=== NOTES 3:0 | Basic Characteristics of the Indian Economy – Features of A Developing Economy
## SUB 0 | Economic Systems – India's Mixed Economy
[0:0:0] # Types of economy
[0:0:1] TABLE head: Type | Who owns / who decides | Example
  [0:0:1.0] Capitalist (market, free) | Production and distribution in the hands of private individuals; prices by market forces; economic inequality is a feature | USA
  [0:0:1.1] Socialist | All productive resources owned and controlled by the government; collective ownership, equitable distribution | Former USSR
  [0:0:1.2] Command (controlled, planned) | A central plan replaces the market; the government decides what, how and for whom | Former USSR, Cuba, North Korea
  [0:0:1.3] Traditional | Custom and tradition decide what, how and for whom | –
  [0:0:1.4] Gandhian | Decentralised, self-contained villages, cottage industries | Gandhian Plan 1944 – S.N. Agarwal
  [0:0:1.5] Mixed | Coexistence of public and private sectors | India, UK
  [0:0:1.6] Dual | Modern sector beside a traditional sector | Lewis model
[0:0:2] # India = mixed economy
[0:0:3] - **After Independence India followed the path of a mixed economy** – public and private sectors coexist under State regulation; it is neither purely capitalist, socialist, Gandhian nor free (asked about 12 times: APPSC ASO 2017, AEs 2009, G2, Constable 2019, CDS 2019, UPPSC).
[0:0:4] - **Meaning:** co-existence of **public and private sectors** – NOT co-existence of small and large industries, labour- and capital-intensive industries, national and foreign companies, agriculture and industry, or military and civilian rule.
[0:0:5] - **How the State regulates** the private sector: **taxes, subsidies and credit**; a high level of public investment in infrastructure is a precondition for private-sector growth.
[0:0:6] - **Socialistic pattern of society** (Avadi 1955, IPR 1956) was to come about **through the mixed economy** (APPSC JL 2004).
[0:0:7] - The Indian model of development protects the interest of **both State and Person** (UP 2013).
[0:0:8] - A **pragmatic middle path** between liberal-capitalist, Soviet and Gandhian models; growth by democratic means with a social order based on justice.
[0:0:9] - **"Commanding heights"** under the State: **heavy industry, infrastructure and finance**; private sector in consumer goods under regulation.
[0:0:10] - **Joint sector** = **one enterprise jointly owned** by government and private investors (a mixed economy is the whole system).
[0:0:11] - **Public sector** = government ownership or control; **private sector** = private ownership or control.
[0:0:12] # Planned, market, open and closed
[0:0:13] - **Centrally planned economy:** the government makes all important decisions on production, exchange and consumption (UPPSC 2002 ✓); in a **market system** prices are set by demand and supply, **not agreed by the government** ✗ → **Only I**.
[0:0:14] - **Closed economy:** **neither exports nor imports** take place (UPSC 2011); open economy trades with others.
[0:0:15] > UPPSC 2024: "Indian economy is underdeveloped" ✓ (a developing economy with underdeveloped features) and "mixed" ✓; "Keynes is the Father of Economics" ✗ → **only 1 and 2**.
[0:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.7-8 (types of economy); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.29-30; Rocket Indian Economy #57 p.85; app notes 3:0 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Features of a Developing (Underdeveloped) Economy
[0:1:0] # The label
[0:1:1] - India is a **developing economy** (APPSC G2 2003; UPPSC 1995, 2011) – not developed, backward or stagnant; it still shows **underdeveloped** features.
[0:1:2] - India is categorised as a "developing country" mainly because of **low per capita income** – not the service-sector share, quality of manpower or lack of industrial growth.
[0:1:3] # Features of the Indian economy
[0:1:4] - **Low per capita income and unemployment** – the salient features; **massive unemployment**.
[0:1:5] - **Predominance of agriculture:** the Indian economy is **primarily an agricultural economy**; **industrial dominance** marks a developed economy, not India (UP 2004: **I, III and IV**).
[0:1:6] - **Low capital formation** (needs a high savings rate) and **low productivity of labour**.
[0:1:7] - **Inequitable distribution of income, high dependency ratio, slower rate of increase in national income** – underdevelopment features (CGPSC 2017 key: all four listed items, incl. change in banking).
[0:1:8] - **NOT a feature: lack of natural resources** – India has resources; they are under-utilised.
[0:1:9] - **Indicators of a developed country:** high literacy, low death rate, high per capita income – a **high proportion of labour in the primary sector is NOT** one.
[0:1:10] - **Dualistic economy** = **coexistence of a modern and a traditional economy** (not inequality, population growth or resource waste).
[0:1:11] - Agriculture of underdeveloped countries has **surplus labour**; their trade = primary exports, manufactured imports.
[0:1:12] # Causes of underdevelopment
[0:1:13] - **Most important cause:** co-existence of **under-utilised manpower and under-utilised natural resources**.
[0:1:14] - Recorded causes: rapid population growth with high dependency ratio, low human development (HDI rank about **130**), high poverty – **NOT mainly the working efficiency of the population** (APPSC G2 Mains 2017).
[0:1:15] - **Vicious circle of poverty (Ragnar Nurkse):** low income → low saving → low investment → low productivity → low income; the vicious circle argument points out the **supply-side connection between productivity and income**.
[0:1:16] - **Labour-surplus economy:** surplus farm labour whose marginal productivity is near zero.
[0:1:17] - **Disguised unemployment:** more workers than needed; marginal productivity of the extra workers **zero**; removing them would **not** reduce output; mainly in **agriculture** and the unorganised sector.
[0:1:18] - Capital formation in a developing economy can rise only with an adequate **savings rate**.
[0:1:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.29-30; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.43 (vicious circle); Rocket Indian Economy #36 p.53, #33 p.49; app notes 3:0 subs 1-3
## SUB 2 | Basic Concepts of Economics and Economists
[0:2:0] TABLE head: Name | Remember for
  [0:2:0.0] Adam Smith (Scottish) | Father of (Modern) Economics / of capitalism – *Wealth of Nations* (1776); not Keynes
  [0:2:0.1] J.M. Keynes | *General Theory*; modern macroeconomics; paradox of thrift – if all save more, income falls and total saving may not rise
  [0:2:0.2] Joan Robinson | *The Accumulation of Capital* (1956)
  [0:2:0.3] W. Arthur Lewis | Dual-sector model: surplus labour from the subsistence to the modern sector
  [0:2:0.4] A.L. Bowley | Averages = "statistical constants which enable us to comprehend in a single effort the significance of the whole"
[0:2:1] - **"Economics"** comes from the **Greek** *oikonomia* (oikos = household, nomos = management).
[0:2:2] # Micro concepts asked
[0:2:3] - **Fixed cost** does not vary with output – **expenditure on machines**; raw material, labour wages and traffic costs vary.
[0:2:4] - **Perfect substitutes** = completely interchangeable goods; perfect complements are used together.
[0:2:5] - **Giffen good:** inferior good; income and substitution effects oppose – demand can be inversely or positively related to price; if the **income effect is stronger**, demand moves **with** price → **both** statements true.
[0:2:6] - **Total and marginal product:** TP rising at an increasing rate → MP rises; at a diminishing rate → MP falls; TP maximum → **MP zero**; TP falling → **MP negative** (not positive).
[0:2:7] - **Law of increasing returns = law of decreasing cost.**
[0:2:8] - **Marginal revenue:** MR > 0 → TR rises; **MR = 0 → TR maximum**; MR < 0 → TR falls (all three true).
[0:2:9] - **Price elasticity of demand** depends on the **nature of the good** and the **availability of close substitutes**.
[0:2:10] - **Economic models** simplify reality, represent a whole or part of a theory and show cause and effect; they can be expressed in words, diagrams, tables or equations – **not only equations**.
[0:2:11] - **Unit root** is a concept of **time-series models** (Dickey-Fuller test): a series with a unit root is non-stationary – not of cross-section or structural-form models.
[0:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.30 (Adam Smith); Rocket Indian Economy #36 p.53 (economists); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_root (Dickey & Fuller 1979); NCERT Class 12 Introductory Microeconomics ch.2-4; app notes 3:0 sub 3
## SUB 3 | India at Independence and the Colonial Legacy
[0:3:0] - **Colonial rule** (from **Plassey, 1757**) turned India from a textile exporter into a **raw-material supplier and captive market** – India was **NOT a supplier of manufactured goods** under British rule; the economy **stagnated** (UPPSC 2013).
[0:3:1] - **Paul Bairoch:** India made about **24.5% of the world's manufactures in 1750** (APPSC G2 2017) → about **1.7% by 1900** (deindustrialisation).
[0:3:2] - **Angus Maddison:** India's share of world GDP **22.6% (1700) → 3.8% (1952)**.
[0:3:3] - **First National Income Committee (1951):** 1948-49 national income **₹8,710 crore**; per capita **₹225**.
[0:3:4] - **Agriculture:** about **72% of the workforce (1951)**; about half of GDP.
[0:3:5] - **Weak industrial base:** capital goods only **one-fourth** of industrial output.
[0:3:6] - **Literacy below 16%**; **life expectancy 32 years** (1947).
[0:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.30; P. Bairoch, "International Industrialization Levels from 1750 to 1980" (J. European Econ. Hist. 1982) via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_India; app notes 3:0 sub 3, 3:1 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Ownership, Institutional Sectors and Savings
[0:4:0] TABLE head: Sector | Ownership
  [0:4:0.0] Public | Government (general government + public corporations)
  [0:4:0.1] Private | Private corporations + households
  [0:4:0.2] Joint | Government + private investors in one firm
  [0:4:0.3] Cooperative | Owned by its members
[0:4:1] - **Largest share of national income** in India's mixed economy: **private sector**.
[0:4:2] - GVA is compiled for **four institutional sectors**: general government, public corporations, private corporations, households – **cooperatives are not a separate one**.
[0:4:3] - **Gross domestic savings:** the **household sector** contributes the largest share (APPSC G1 2007) – household > private corporate > public.
[0:4:4] - **SI 2017 match:** gross domestic savings (2011) **31.1%**; gross capital formation (2011) **36.6%**; unemployment rate (2004-05) **8.36%**; population growth (2001-11) **1.64%** a year → **A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III**.
[0:4:5] - **Private corporate investment:** **12.3% of GDP (FY23) → 11.2% (FY24)**; its share of GFCF at a decadal low of **33%** (Aug 2026).
[0:4:6] ~~ Sources: NSO National Accounts Statistics (institutional sectors, savings); Census 2011 (1.64% exponential growth); app notes 3:0 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Dual Economy – Organised vs Unorganised; Regional and Demographic Features
[0:5:0] - **Organised sector:** formal, regulated work with **social security**; **unorganised:** informal, largely **cash-based**.
[0:5:1] - Unorganised sector: **over 80% of workers**, about **45% of output**.
[0:5:2] - **Census 2011:** population **121.09 crore**; **68.8% rural, 31.2% urban**; sex ratio **940** (933 in 2001).
[0:5:3] - **Work participation rate 39.8%** (Census 2011) – higher in less developed States such as AP and Chhattisgarh because **subsistence activities need more manual work**.
[0:5:4] - **Regional imbalance:** inter-state Gini of per capita income **0.230 (1994-95) → 0.261**; Telangana's PCI = **1.35 times** AP's (2024-25).
[0:5:5] - **Demography:** TFR **1.9**, below the **replacement level 2.1**; median age about **36 by 2036**; dependency ratio expected to fall from **65% to 54%** over a decade; **demographic dividend peaks around 2030**.
[0:5:6] ~~ Sources: Census 2011 (Primary Census Abstract); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.19; app notes 3:0 subs 7-8
## SUB 6 | India's World Standing and the AP Profile
[0:6:0] TABLE head: Measure | Position
  [0:6:0.0] Nominal GDP | 6th (IMF WEO, April 2026)
  [0:6:0.1] PPP GDP | 3rd, after the USA and China
  [0:6:0.2] World Bank income group | Lower-middle income (July 2026)
[0:6:1] - **World Bank classification:** by **GNI per capita** (not GDP) using the **Atlas method** (exchange rate averaged over **three years**); revised every **1 July**.
[0:6:2] - **World Development Report (1996):** low-income economies = per capita GNP in 1994 of **US $725 or less** (IAS 1998).
[0:6:3] - **GDP growth** (2022-23 base): **7.2% (2023-24), 7.1% (2024-25), 7.7% (2025-26)**.
[0:6:4] TABLE head: Indicator (2025-26) | Andhra Pradesh
  [0:6:4.0] Per capita income | ₹2,94,507
  [0:6:4.1] GVA shares | Services 43%, agriculture & allied about 33%, industry 24%
  [0:6:4.2] Top district in PCI | Visakhapatnam
[0:6:5] - **State per capita income = NSDP ÷ population.**
[0:6:6] ~~ Sources: World Bank, World Development Report 1996 (classification of economies); World Bank country classification (July 2026); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025-26 via app notes 3:0 subs 9-10

3. It is found mainly in agriculture.

  x: Under disguised unemployment extra workers add nothing, so removing them would not cut output; it is mainly found in agriculture.

=== NOTES 3:1 | Structural Change – Sectoral Composition of Output and Employment
## SUB 0 | Sectoral Shares of GDP – Trend and Ranking
[1:0:0] # Order and trend
[1:0:1] - **Decreasing order of contribution to GDP now: services > industry > agriculture** (UPSC 2007, NDA 2014, UPPCS 2017) – the **tertiary (service) sector is the largest source of national income** in the 21st century.
[1:0:2] - **At Independence agriculture** was the largest contributor (about half of GDP); over the plan period the composition **shifted in favour of the service sector**.
[1:0:3] - **As the economy develops the tertiary share rises**; since 1980 it has shown an **increasing trend**; agriculture's contribution is **decreasing**.
[1:0:4] TABLE head: Year | Agriculture / primary | Industry | Services
  [1:0:4.0] 1950-51 | over half (SI 2017 key: 56.5%) | about 13% | 30.3%
  [1:0:4.1] 1980-81 → 1990-91 | 38.1% → 34.0% | 25.9% → 24.9% | 37.65% → 42.55%
  [1:0:4.2] 1991 | about 29% | – | –
  [1:0:4.3] 2001-03 | about 26% (APPSC JL 2003 key) | – | 50.37% (2000-01)
  [1:0:4.4] 2006-07 (Economic Survey 2006-07) | 18.5% | 26.4% (between 25 and 30) | 55.1%
  [1:0:4.5] 2012-13 | about 13.7% (SI 2017 key 13.6%) | – | –
  [1:0:4.6] 2017-18 | about 17% | 29.2% | about 54-55% (55.2% AE; APPSC key 54.4%)
  [1:0:4.7] 2025-26 | 17.88% (about 18%) | manufacturing stagnant | 54.3%
[1:0:5] - **Agriculture around 2008-13: about 15%** of GDP (BPSC 2008, UPRO 2013 key) – now about 18% after the revisions.
[1:0:6] # New GDP series (base 2022-23, Feb 2026)
[1:0:7] - **2024-25, current prices: primary 21.4%, secondary 25.8%, tertiary 52.9%** – figures to quote now; the new series shows higher agriculture and industry shares, lower services.
[1:0:8] - **The 21.4% primary share includes mining**, so it is not comparable with the old agriculture-forestry-fishing share.
[1:0:9] - **Manufacturing 14.7%** in the new series (not 14.3%); built from **ASI** (factories) + **ASUSE** (unincorporated units).
[1:0:10] # Sub-sectors
[1:0:11] - **2000-01 (constant prices) order:** agriculture-forestry-fishing > trade-hotels-transport-communication > manufacturing > finance-insurance-real estate-business services (UPSC 2002: **1, 3, 2, 4**).
[1:0:12] - **Highest services share in 2006:** trade, hotels, transport and communication; **fastest-growing service 2006-2010: communication**.
[1:0:13] - **Mining and quarrying ≈ 3% of GVA** in 2016-17 at 2011-12 prices (about 2.4% at current prices) – small output share, key raw-material supplier.
[1:0:14] - **1999-2008 (1999-2000 prices):** within the primary sector the share of **forestry** declined steeply (APPSC G2 2011 key).
[1:0:15] - **Fishing and aquaculture** (old series): **0.8% (2011-12) → 1.3% (2022-23)**; manufacturing 17.4% → 14.3%.
[1:0:16] - **Agriculture's importance** shows in its contribution to **national income and employment, industrial raw materials, trade and foodgrains – all**; its large contribution to GNP is in terms of **value of output**, not exports or revenue.
[1:0:17] - **Highest growth in industrial production** (APPSC G1 2003): **manufacturing**.
[1:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.4; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.12; Economic Survey 2006-07 ch.1 (indiabudget.gov.in/budget_archive/es2006-07); Economic Survey 2017-18 Vol.2 ch.9 (services 55.2%); NSO Second Advance Estimates 2025-26 (27 Feb 2026); app notes 3:1 subs 3-4
## SUB 1 | Sector Classification – Primary, Secondary, Tertiary and Beyond
[1:1:0] TABLE head: Sector | Other name | Activities
  [1:1:0.0] Primary | Agricultural sector; most dependent on natural resources | Agriculture, livestock, dairy farm, forestry, fishing, mining and quarrying, mineral exploration
  [1:1:0.1] Secondary | Industrial sector | Manufacturing (large, medium, small), textile mills, weaving cloth, processing, construction, electricity, gas, water supply
  [1:1:0.2] Tertiary | Service sector | Trade, marketing, transport, storage (incl. storage of farm produce), communication, hotels, banking, finance, real estate, public administration and defence, education, health, social work, personal services
  [1:1:0.3] Quaternary | Knowledge sector | R&D, information, software, consulting
  [1:1:0.4] Quinary | Top decision-making | Government policy, scientific research
[1:1:1] - **Water supply = secondary** (industrial) sector (APPSC G1), not tertiary.
[1:1:2] - **Real estate** is a tertiary activity – **not part of manufacturing**.
[1:1:3] - **Service sector** includes **transport and communication and hotels** – not mining and quarrying, forestry or fishing (UPPCS 2004: **II and III**).
[1:1:4] - **UPSC 2024 pairs:** storage = secondary ✗ (tertiary); dairy farm = primary ✓; mineral exploration = tertiary ✗ (primary); weaving cloth = secondary ✓ → **only two**.
[1:1:5] # Real sector vs financial sector
[1:1:6] TABLE head: Basis | Real sector | Financial sector
  [1:1:6.0] Involves | Production and flow of goods and services | Money and financial assets
  [1:1:6.1] Examples | Farmers harvesting crops, textile mills making fabric | Bank lending, rupee-denominated bonds overseas
[1:1:7] - UPSC 2022: real sector = **1 and 2 only**.
[1:1:8] # GVA groups (national accounts)
[1:1:9] TABLE head: Group | Components
  [1:1:9.0] Agriculture and allied | Agriculture, livestock, forestry, fishing
  [1:1:9.1] Industry | Mining and quarrying, manufacturing, electricity-gas-water supply, construction
  [1:1:9.2] Services | Trade-hotels-transport-communication; finance-real estate-professional services; public administration, defence, other services
[1:1:10] - **Mining = primary** in the three-sector scheme but counted under **Industry** in GVA groups and the AP Socio-Economic Survey.
[1:1:11] - **Compilers:** GDP and sectoral GVA – **CSO, now NSO (MoSPI)**; State GSDP and sector GVA – **Directorate of Economics and Statistics** of each State; ASI and ASUSE – **NSO** (not the State DES).
[1:1:12] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy #57 p.84-85; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.59-61; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.11; NCERT Class 10 Economics ch.2; app notes 3:1 subs 0-1
## SUB 2 | Output vs Employment – the Mismatch
[1:2:0] - **The maximum number of people work in the primary sector** (agriculture) – the **largest employer**, though it gives the least output; the tertiary sector gives the most output (APPSC JL 2004, AD 2017).
[1:2:1] - Agriculture employs **46.1%** of workers (PLFS 2023-24); earlier **more than 50%** of the working population depended on the primary sector (WBCS 2017).
[1:2:2] TABLE head: Sector (2021-22) | Share of GDP | Share of workforce
  [1:2:2.0] Primary | 21.82% | 43.96%
  [1:2:2.1] Tertiary | 53.89% | 33.80%
[1:2:3] - Services were **22.82%** of employment in 1993-94 (agriculture 64.75%).
[1:2:4] - **Manufacturing** employs only **11.4%** of workers (2023-24); **MSMEs** are the second-largest employer after agriculture.
[1:2:5] - **Organised-sector employment growth declined** in recent years mainly because the **manufacturing share of GDP did not increase** (APPSC AD 2017).
[1:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.12; PLFS Annual Report 2023-24 (MoSPI); app notes 3:1 sub 5
## SUB 3 | Structural Change and Services-led Growth
[1:3:0] - **Structural change** = changing shares of the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors in national income; it occurred **because the process of economic growth was initiated** (APPSC G1: A and R true, **R explains A**).
[1:3:1] - **Shifting of workers from agriculture to other sectors** = an indication of **economic growth** (APPSC G2 2011), not backwardness.
[1:3:2] TABLE head: Model | Author | Prediction
  [1:3:2.0] Three-sector | Colin Clark and Allan Fisher | As income rises, labour and output shift primary → secondary → tertiary
  [1:3:2.1] Dual-sector | W. Arthur Lewis (1954) | Surplus farm labour moves to modern industry until it runs out – the Lewis turning point
[1:3:3] - **Post-1991 growth was service-led** – not import-, export- or agriculture-led (APPSC 2018); in **1992-2001 services** grew fastest and contributed most to GDP.
[1:3:4] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [1:3:4.0] Missing middle | Agriculture → services without a manufacturing-led stage
  [1:3:4.1] Premature deindustrialisation | Services generally require high skills and may not absorb semi-skilled farm workers → jobless growth
  [1:3:4.2] Premature leapfrogging | Services absorb value while manufacturing fails to absorb surplus farm labour
  [1:3:4.3] Nominal vs real share | Fall in manufacturing's nominal share = relative-price effect (Economic Survey 2025-26)
  [1:3:4.4] Share logic | A sector growing slower than GDP loses share even if its output rises
[1:3:5] - **EAC-PM Chairman** (Nov 2025): services-led growth cannot be sustained without a manufacturing base.
[1:3:6] - India: **2.9%** of global manufacturing value added; **1.8%** of world merchandise exports; **44th** on the Economic Complexity Index.
[1:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.12; Economic Survey 2025-26 (economic-survey-2025-26-full); app notes 3:1 subs 2, 6
## SUB 4 | Manufacturing Targets and Recent Sectoral Growth
[1:4:0] TABLE head: Policy | Year | Target
  [1:4:0.0] National Manufacturing Policy | 2011 | Manufacturing 25% of GDP by 2022; 100 million jobs
  [1:4:0.1] Make in India | 25 Sep 2014 | 25% of GDP – deadline extended from 2022 to 2025
[1:4:1] - Target not met: the share fell to 14.3% (2022-23, old series).
[1:4:2] TABLE head: Agriculture growth | 9th Plan | 10th Plan | 11th Plan
  [1:4:2.0] Growth | 2.5% | 2.4% | 3.6% (highest)
[1:4:3] - **11th Plan target:** **4%** agricultural growth (achieved about 3.6-3.7%).
[1:4:4] TABLE head: Sector (real) | 2025-26 | Q1 2026-27
  [1:4:4.0] Manufacturing | 12.5% | 9.2%
  [1:4:4.1] Services | 8.9% | 10.0%
[1:4:5] - Q1 2026-27 leaders: **finance, real estate, IT and professional services (12.1%)**.
[1:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.4 (11th Plan 3.6%); NSO quarterly estimates (Aug 2026) via app notes 3:1 subs 7-8
## SUB 5 | Andhra Pradesh – GSVA Composition
[1:5:0] TABLE head: Year (source) | Agriculture & allied | Industry | Services
  [1:5:0.0] 2024-25 (AP Budget 2026-27) | 37% | 21% | 42%
  [1:5:0.1] 2025-26 (AP SES 2025-26) | about 33% | 24% | 43%
[1:5:1] - AP has **a farm share well above the national share** (India below 20%).
[1:5:2] - **AP growth 2025-26 (constant prices):** fishing and aquaculture fastest within agriculture (17.69%); **construction** fastest within industry (14.18%); **public administration** lowest (0.05%).
[1:5:3] - **Manufacturing only about 11% of GSDP** → **Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29)**.
[1:5:4] - Telangana's services grew from 1.25 to 1.47 times AP's (2013-14 to 2024-25), led by **real estate, IT and trade-hotels**.

  x: Both are true: banking is tertiary because the tertiary sector provides services, and banking is a service. R explains A.

=== NOTES 3:2 | Services Sector – Growth, Composition and Contribution
## SUB 0 | Share in GVA, Growth and Jobs – the Mismatch
[2:0:0] # Share of output
[2:0:1] - **Services = more than 50% of GVA** (Economic Survey 2025-26) – the **highest** contributor to GDP (WBCS 2017: "more than **50%**").
[2:0:2] TABLE head: Sector (2021-22) | Share of GDP | Share of workforce
  [2:0:2.0] Secondary | 24.29% | 22.24%
  [2:0:2.1] Tertiary | 53.89% | 33.80%
[2:0:3] - **Employment-output paradox** (**NITI Aayog**): services give over half of output but only about **one-third** of jobs; high-end services (IT, finance) need high skills, so most new jobs are in low-value trade, hospitality, transport.
[2:0:4] - **Regular wages: 51.5%** of service workers vs about 1% in agriculture.
[2:0:5] # Share of growth
[2:0:6] - **Contribution of services to GVA growth, 2011-12 to 2015-16: about 69%** (CGPSC 2017 key); in 2015-16 alone **66.1%** (Economic Survey 2015-16); 2017-18 about 72.5%.
[2:0:7] - Growth: **9.1%** in FY2025-26 (FAE; new series 8.9%); **10%** in Q1 FY2026-27, led by finance, real estate, IT and professional services (**12.1%**).
[2:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.4-5; Economic Survey 2015-16 Vol.2 ch.7 (services 66.1% of GVA growth); Economic Survey 2025-26; app notes 3:2 sub 1
## SUB 1 | What Is (and Is Not) a Service
[2:1:0] TABLE head: Tertiary (services) | Not services
  [2:1:0.0] Trade, hotels, restaurants | Mining & quarrying (primary)
  [2:1:0.1] Transport, storage, communication | Forestry, fishing (primary)
  [2:1:0.2] Finance, insurance, real estate, business services | Manufacturing, construction, utilities (secondary)
  [2:1:0.3] Public administration, defence, other services | Agriculture (primary)
[2:1:1] - **Construction is secondary**, not a service (CDS 2015); transport, hotels and restaurants and insurance are tertiary.
[2:1:2] - **NIC** lists **15** types of services; **WTO** uses the UN's **UNCPC** (Central Product Classification); AP Survey uses **8** service sub-sectors.
[2:1:3] TABLE head: Constitution list | Services
  [2:1:3.0] Union | Telecom, postal, broadcasting, financial services, insurance
  [2:1:3.1] State | Health, real estate
  [2:1:3.2] Concurrent | Education, accounting, engineering, electricity
[2:1:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.36 (NIC 15 types; three Lists); NCERT Class 10 Economics ch.2; app notes 3:2 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Services Exports, FDI and Digital Services
[2:2:0] # Exports
[2:2:1] - India's share of world services trade: **2% (2005) → 4.3% (2024)**; older target: **4.2% of world services exports by 2022**.
[2:2:2] - **Digitally delivered services exports:** India's share of the world total about **6% in 2023** (Economic Survey 2023-24).
[2:2:3] - Rank: **8th**-largest services exporter (WTO, April 2025 data); also 8th in 2014.
[2:2:4] - 2024-25: exports **USD 387.5 bn** vs imports USD 198.7 bn → surplus; **software and business services = 77.8%** of services exports.
[2:2:5] - Target: services exports **USD 1 trillion** within the USD 2 trillion export goal by **2030**.
[2:2:6] # FDI
[2:2:7] - **1997-2000:** largest FDI share – **services sector** in most books' keys (UPSC 2001; some keys say engineering).
[2:2:8] - **Last decade (to 2006):** services sector attracted the highest FDI among chemicals, food processing and telecom; April 2000-December 2025 cumulative: **services 16.38%**, computer software and hardware 15.63%, trading, telecom, automobiles.
[2:2:9] - FY2024-25: **services sector** again the **top** FDI equity recipient (~19%, about $9.35 bn), ahead of computer software and hardware (16%).
[2:2:10] - Large foreign investment came into **life insurance, banking and automobiles** (UPPCS 2009).
[2:2:11] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2023-24 ch.9 (digitally delivered services 6%); DPIIT FDI Factsheet Dec 2025; app notes 3:2 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Andhra Pradesh and the States
[2:3:0] - **AP:** services = **AP's largest sector** – about **43%** of GVA (current prices) (APPSC DL 2020).
[2:3:1] - Yet AP is **basically an agricultural economy** (APPSC Panchayat Secretary): agriculture is its main employer, so the success of its Five Year Plans depended mainly on **agriculture** (APPSC G2 2011).
[2:3:2] - AP 2025-26: services **Rs 3,59,931 crore (+10.67%)**; **communications** fastest (**15.13%**).
[2:3:3] - **Villaments** (villa + apartment) = new urban-housing trend in AP real estate (APPSC G2 Mains 2019).
[2:3:4] - Kerala **64.3%**, **Bihar 58.7%** of GSVA from services; Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Telangana = about **40%** of India's services output.
[2:3:5] - Largest services share in State GDP, 2008-09: **Delhi** > Chandigarh > Kerala > Maharashtra; 2023-24 (NITI Aayog, Oct 2025): Chandigarh 88.8%, Delhi 84.1%.
[2:3:6] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 (GVA by sector); NITI Aayog "India's Services Sector" (Oct 2025); app notes 3:2 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Service-led Growth and the 1991 Reforms
[2:4:0] - Boom began in the **mid-1980s**; sped up after the **1990s reforms** – services gained most from globalisation.
[2:4:1] - The 1991 reforms **did not bring much benefit to agriculture** (public investment in agriculture fell; APPSC ASO 2017) – unlike services, stock markets and power.
[2:4:2] - **Software** is a major export, but India **lacks a strong hardware base** (UPSC 1999: A true, R false).
[2:4:3] - **EAC-PM Chairman** (Nov 2025): service-led growth cannot last without a **manufacturing base**; manufacturing creates demand for logistics, IT, finance and steadies GDP cycles.
[2:4:4] - **Paradox of thrift** – popularised by **Keynes**.
[2:4:5] ~~ Sources: NCERT Class 11 Indian Economic Development ch.3 (reforms and agriculture); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 14 p.9; app notes 3:2 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Indices and Terms
[2:5:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [2:5:0.0] PMI | Survey of purchasing managers; indicator of the health of the manufacturing (and services) sector; above 50 = expansion, below 50 = contraction
  [2:5:0.1] Index of Services Production (ISP) | MoSPI's first trial (for April 2026) – services counterpart of the IIP; monthly, within 60 days; base 2024-25; Laspeyres index
  [2:5:0.2] GCC | Offshore unit of an MNC doing its own core work (not a third-party vendor); over 1,800 in India
[2:5:1] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.34 (PMI); app notes 3:2 sub 4
## SUB 6 | GATS Modes of Supply
[2:6:0] TABLE head: Mode | Meaning | Example
  [2:6:0.0] Mode 1 | Cross-border supply | Software sent online
  [2:6:0.1] Mode 2 | Consumption abroad | Medical tourism
  [2:6:0.2] Mode 3 | Commercial presence | Foreign branch/subsidiary
  [2:6:0.3] Mode 4 | Presence of natural persons | IT professionals on visas
[2:6:1] ~~ Sources: WTO GATS Article I; app notes 3:2 sub 5

=== NOTES 3:3 | Role of the It and Ites Industry in India's Development
## SUB 0 | Firms, Exports and Destinations
[3:0:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [3:0:0.0] Largest software company | TCS (largest exporter in 2002-03 and by market cap), then Infosys, Wipro
  [3:0:0.1] First Indian company on NASDAQ | Infosys (March 1999)
  [3:0:0.2] Biggest tech employers (2018) | Large Indian IT services firms (TCS, Infosys) – not Oracle, Apple or Microsoft
  [3:0:0.3] Destinations | USA and Europe; 2022-23: USA first, UK second (US and Canada 56%, Europe 30.8%, half of it the UK)
  [3:0:0.4] Major hubs (2012) | Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Pune, NCR = ~90%
  [3:0:0.5] Export concentration | Seven cities = 70%; Bengaluru 38%
  [3:0:0.6] Tier-2/3 | Coimbatore, Indore, Jaipur, Bhubaneswar
  [3:0:0.7] AP | IT Park, Madhurawada (Rushikonda), Visakhapatnam – AP IT & GCC Policy 4.0
[3:0:1] - **Services (IT and ITES) benefited most from globalisation** after 1991 – outsourcing, FDI, global Indian firms.
[3:0:2] ~~ Sources: NASSCOM Strategic Review 2003 (TCS largest exporter 2002-03); RBI Survey on Computer Software & ITES Exports 2022-23 (Oct 2023); Infosys history (NASDAQ listing 1999); app notes 3:3 sub 3
## SUB 1 | Revenue and Export Growth
[3:1:0] - 1990s boom: software exports grew **over 50% a year after 1995-96** because Indian firms were **cost-effective with international quality** (UPSC 2001: A and R true, R explains A); IX Plan (1997-2002) CAGR **52%** (exports 57%).
[3:1:1] - Question-period data (UPSC 2003): exports CAGR about **60%** over five years ✓; software and services growth about **28%** in rupee terms in 2001-02 ✓ → **both**.
[3:1:2] - Software services exports **2022-23: US $185.5 bn** (RBI, +18.4%); computer services 67.3%, ITES/BPO 32.7%.
[3:1:3] - **FY2025 (NASSCOM):** revenue **USD 282.6 bn** (+5.1%); exports **USD 224.4 bn** (~**79%**); domestic USD 58.2 bn.
[3:1:4] - Software/computer services = India's **largest services export** and **largest services forex earner** → offsets the **merchandise trade deficit**.
[3:1:5] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2002-03 (software exports); RBI Bulletin Oct 2023; NASSCOM Strategic Review 2025; app notes 3:3 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Origins – Policies and Institutions
[3:2:0] TABLE head: Policy / institution | Year | Role
  [3:2:0.0] Department of Electronics | 1970 | Foresaw India's export potential in software as early as the mid-1970s
  [3:2:0.1] Software Export Scheme | 1972 | Computers imported against an export obligation
  [3:2:0.2] Computer Policy / Software Export Policy | 1984 / 1986 | Liberalised imports and data links
  [3:2:0.3] NASSCOM | 1988 | Industry body; annual Strategic Review = data source
  [3:2:0.4] STPI | 1991 | Under the Department of Electronics; satellite data links + single-window clearances; India's first export-park model for software
  [3:2:0.5] NPIT 2012 | 2012 | Targets for 2020
  [3:2:0.6] MeitY | separate ministry 2016 | Earlier DeitY
[3:2:1] - **NPIT 2012** targets (2020): revenue USD 100 bn → 300 bn; exports USD 69 bn → **200 bn**; 10 million more skilled workers; **one e-literate person in every household** (not two).
[3:2:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.2 (software technology parks); app notes 3:3 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Employment
[3:3:0] - **~58 lakh (5.8 million)** direct jobs (FY2025); mostly **organised** jobs with contracts and social security; high share of women.
[3:3:1] - **Quarterly Employment Survey (QES)** – **Labour Bureau**; **9 non-farm sectors**; in 2021 rounds **manufacturing** had the largest share (~39-41%); IT/BPO ~7% but fastest growth (152%).
[3:3:2] ~~ Sources: NASSCOM Strategic Review 2025; Labour Bureau QES 2021; app notes 3:3 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Challenges and Role in Development
[3:4:0] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [3:4:0.0] External dependence | Visa rules, protectionism, client spending cycles
  [3:4:0.1] Automation | Routine ITES/BPM most exposed to generative AI
  [3:4:0.2] Jobs paradox | Fast GVA growth, few jobs – skill-intensive and automated
  [3:4:0.3] Other risks | Urban concentration, Bengaluru water stress, Chennai floods 2015, digital divide
[3:4:1] - IT **earns forex and formal jobs** but serves a **skilled few in a few cities** → cannot deliver broad development alone; a forex shortage is **not** one of its problems.
[3:4:2] - Skill gap: employers want AI-ready skills – cloud, GenAI, data analytics (May 2026).
[3:4:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:3 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Digital India and Data Protection
[3:5:0] - **Digital India**: launched **1 July 2015** (MeitY); **nine pillars**, first = **Broadband Highways**.
[3:5:1] - **BharatNet**: renamed from **NOFN** (2015); optical fibre to about 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats.
[3:5:2] - **IndiaAI Mission**: Cabinet approval March 2024, outlay **Rs 10,372 crore**.
[3:5:3] - **DPDP Act 2023**: assent **11 August 2023**; **Data Protection Board of India** imposes penalties up to **Rs 250 crore**; **DPDP Rules 2025** notified November 2025.
[3:5:4] ~~ Sources: MeitY (digitalindia.gov.in); PIB 7 Mar 2024 (IndiaAI); DPDP Act 2023; app notes 3:3 sub 5

=== NOTES 3:4 | Other Services – Tourism, Banking, Insurance, Health and Education
## SUB 0 | Insurance – Milestones, Companies and Regulator
[4:0:0] TABLE head: Act / body | Year | Provision
  [4:0:0.0] LIC Act | 1 September 1956 | LIC formed; life insurance nationalised (over 240 insurers merged)
  [4:0:0.1] GIC | 1972 | General insurers nationalised; National, New India, Oriental, United India became GIC subsidiaries
  [4:0:0.2] Malhotra Committee | 1993-94 | Open insurance to private companies + independent regulator (not the Gadgil Committee)
  [4:0:0.3] IRDA Act | 1999 | Set up IRDAI – statutory regulator, HQ Hyderabad; set up April 2000
  [4:0:0.4] Agriculture Insurance Company of India (AIC) | 2002 | Implements crop insurance (RKBY/NAIS) in AP and other States; before it the GIC ran crop insurance
  [4:0:0.5] PMFBY | 2016 | Replaced NAIS (Rashtriya Krishi Bima Yojana) and MNAIS
  [4:0:0.6] Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act | Passed 17 Dec 2025 | FDI cap 74% → 100%
[4:0:1] - **LIC is not the oldest insurer** (Oriental Life 1818; National Insurance 1906); **National Insurance** was nationalised in 1972 and made a GIC subsidiary; **United India** HQ = **Chennai** (UPSC 2006 → B and C).
[4:0:2] - The **2025 Act** amends the Insurance Act 1938, LIC Act 1956 and IRDA Act 1999 and creates a Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund.
[4:0:3] - IRDAI vision: **"Insurance for All by 2047"**; FY25 premium income **Rs 11.9 lakh crore**; **health** passed **motor** as the top non-life segment.
[4:0:4] - IRDAI panel on a standard **cyber liability** insurance product (Oct 2020): chaired by **P. Umesh**.
[4:0:5] - Only about **5%** of Indians had insurance cover in the 2000s (APPSC G1 2008 key).
[4:0:6] - AP enrolment under PMFBY, 2016-17: about **15 lakh** farmers (APPSC ASO 2017 key).
[4:0:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy #30 p.44 (LIC 1 Sept 1956); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.32 (IRDA Act 1999); GIC Re history (gicre.in); aicofindia.com (AIC 2002, RKBY); app notes 3:4 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Insurance Terms and Principles
[4:1:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [4:1:0.0] Insurance penetration | Total premium as % of GDP – not "insured persons per 100 people" (APPSC G2 2017 → none of these)
  [4:1:0.1] Insurance density | Premium per capita (USD 97 in FY25)
  [4:1:0.2] Principle of indemnity | Restores the insured to the pre-loss position, no profit; applies to fire, marine, motor, health – not life insurance
  [4:1:0.3] Actuary | Insurance expert who judges risk and estimates the premium
  [4:1:0.4] Cyber insurance | Data breach, hacking, ransomware, identity theft
  [4:1:0.5] Aviation hull | Physical damage to the aircraft itself
  [4:1:0.6] P&I | Shipowners' third-party liabilities; first sovereign-backed cover: Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool (Jul 2026)
[4:1:1] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary - Part 1 p.33-34 (penetration, density); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.33; app notes 3:4 sub 1

## SUB 5 | Para-banking
[4:5:0] - Legal basis: **Section 6, Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, with **RBI** approval; run **departmentally or through subsidiaries** (subsidiary route: **Section 19(1)**).

=== NOTES 3:5 | Occupational Structure of India – Trends and Inter-state Variation
## SUB 0 | Census – History and Worker Data
[5:0:0] # History
[5:0:1] - First Census of the modern (non-synchronous) system: **1872** under Lord **Mayo** – the Viceroy who arranged the first Census; first **regular**, synchronous and scientific Census: **1881** under Lord **Ripon**.
[5:0:2] - **Census 2011** = **15th** since 1872, **7th** after Independence; covered **6,40,867 villages**. **Census 2027** = first **app-based digital** Census.
[5:0:3] # Worker categories
[5:0:4] TABLE head: Category | Meaning
  [5:0:4.0] Main worker | Worked 6 months or more in the reference year
  [5:0:4.1] Marginal worker | Worked less than 6 months
  [5:0:4.2] Cultivator | Works on own/leased land
  [5:0:4.3] Agricultural labourer | Works on another person's land for wages
  [5:0:4.4] Household industry | Production in the household, by family members
  [5:0:4.5] Other workers | All other work – services, trade, factories
[5:0:5] # Census 2011 numbers
[5:0:6] - Total workers **48.19 crore** (481.9 million, not 382 million); **main workers 36.26 crore**; male workers about **332 million**.
[5:0:7] - **Work participation rate 39.8%** (39.79%) – not 39.1, 42.3 or 43.6.
[5:0:8] - Census 2001: AP's female WPR **35.1%**; rural female WPR in AP about **43.3%** (APPSC G2 2011 key); mining and quarrying employed about **0.6%** of workers.
[5:0:9] ~~ Sources: Census of India 2011, Primary Census Abstract – Data Highlights (censusindia.gov.in); Census 2001 Final Population Totals; app notes 3:5 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Workforce Share by Sector Over Time
[5:1:0] TABLE head: Year / survey | Agriculture share of workers
  [5:1:0.0] 1951 | 72%
  [5:1:0.1] Census 2001 | 58.2% (labour force in agriculture 56.7%)
  [5:1:0.2] NSS 2011-12 | 48.9%
  [5:1:0.3] Census 2011 | 54.6%
  [5:1:0.4] PLFS 2023-24 | 46.1%
  [5:1:0.5] PLFS Q2 FY26 | 42.4%
[5:1:1] - **Agriculture** = always the **highest employment share** (falling); the main livelihood **on the eve of Independence**. Direct employment in agriculture: about **55%** of the labour force (Census 2011), so 20, 30, 40 and 65% are all off (UPPCS Mains 2012).
[5:1:2] - Now: agriculture about **18% of GVA** but **42.4%** of the workforce.
[5:1:3] - 2021-22 workforce: primary 43.96%, secondary 22.24%, tertiary **33.80%**; urban employment: services **62.0%** (Q2 FY26).
[5:1:4] - PLFS Jan-Mar 2026: rural agricultural employment 58.5% → 55.8%; workforce **61.6 crore** (PLFS 2025).
[5:1:5] - **Agricultural households = 57.8%** of rural households (NSSO 70th round, 2013).
[5:1:6] - **NSS 2011-12: self-employed** = largest category of workers (about 52%), then casual labour, then regular salaried.
[5:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 22 p.12 (occupational structure); NSS 68th round Report 554 (2011-12); PLFS Annual Report 2023-24; app notes 3:5 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Informal and Unorganised Employment
[5:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [5:2:0.0] Unorganised sector (general) | Small and scattered units largely outside the control of the government; low pay, no job security (APPSC GS, SSC 2017)
  [5:2:0.1] Unorganised sector (NCEUS) | Unincorporated private enterprises of individuals/households, fewer than 10 workers
  [5:2:0.2] Organised manufacturing | Registered factories – 10+ workers with power / 20+ without
  [5:2:0.3] Informal worker (NCEUS) | Unorganised-sector workers + organised-sector workers without social security
  [5:2:0.4] Informalisation of formal enterprises | Contract and outsourced workers inside formal firms
  [5:2:0.5] "Formal informality" | New EPFO 'formal' jobs that are short-term, low-wage or contractual
[5:2:1] - **NCEUS**: chaired by **Dr. Arjun Sengupta**; formed **20.09.2004**, term ended 30.04.2009; found **77%** of Indians lived on less than **Rs 20 a day**.
[5:2:2] - Informal employment: **over 80%** of the workforce (Mar 2026); non-farm informal share about **78%** (PLFS 2022-23).
[5:2:3] - **NSS 73rd round (2015-16)**: unincorporated non-agricultural enterprises employed about **11 crore**.
[5:2:4] - **e-Shram**: **31 crore+** registered; **four Labour Codes** merged **29** laws (Code on Wages **2019**; others 2020).
[5:2:5] - Social-protection coverage: 19% (2015) → **64.3%** (2025) – India 2nd after China.
[5:2:6] - Direct factory employment 61% → **47%** (2011-2023); contract workers = 42%; small and marginal farmers ~**86%**.
[5:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.7 (Arjun Sengupta, Rs 20 a day); NCEUS Report 2007; NCERT Class 10 Economics ch.2; app notes 3:5 sub 6
## SUB 3 | Meaning and Theory of Occupational Structure
[5:3:0] - **Occupational structure** = **distribution of the working population among different occupations** – primary, secondary and tertiary.
[5:3:1] - **Clark-Fisher thesis**: as income rises, labour shifts primary → secondary → tertiary; India moved from agriculture **directly to services** with no manufacturing-led stage.
[5:3:2] - **Structural retardation**: the occupational structure changed far more slowly than output – because **investment was directed towards capital-intensive industries** (UPSC 1995).
[5:3:3] - **Premature deindustrialisation**: manufacturing fails to absorb enough farm labour.
[5:3:4] - An **increase in the working population** is **not** an adverse effect of population growth (smaller holdings, unemployment, less food per head are).
[5:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.21 (occupational structure); app notes 3:5 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Cultivators vs Agricultural Labourers
[5:4:0] TABLE head: Category | Census 2001 | Census 2011 | Share 2011
  [5:4:0.0] Cultivators | 127.3 million | 118.8 million (11.87 crore) ↓ | 24.7%
  [5:4:0.1] Agricultural labourers | 106.8 million | 144.3 million (14.43 crore) ↑ | 30.0%
[5:4:1] - **2011** = first Census in which **labourers outnumbered cultivators**.
[5:4:2] - Cause – **fragmentation**: average holding **2.28 ha (1971) → 1.08 ha (2015-16)**.
[5:4:3] ~~ Sources: Census of India 2011, Primary Census Abstract; Agriculture Census 2015-16; app notes 3:5 sub 3
## SUB 5 | Rural Workers and Women Workers
[5:5:0] - Census 2011: **72.4%** of workers in **rural** areas, against **68.8%** of population.
[5:5:1] - **Feminisation of agriculture:** female workers **55%** agricultural labourers, 24% cultivators; women hold only **12.8%** of operational holdings; driven by **subsistence farming, unpaid family work, distress employment** (not formal manufacturing jobs).
[5:5:2] - Rural women self-employed: 60% (2011-12) → **73%** (2023-24); UN: **2026 = International Year of the Woman Farmer**.
[5:5:3] - Female LFPR (15+): 23.3% (2017-18) → **30%** (2019-20) → **40%** (2025); rural 33.0% → **45.9%**; women = **32.5%** of employment (2025).
[5:5:4] - Labour participation of women about **32%** (APPSC AEE 2012 key, ILO estimate); Census 2011 female WPR 25.5%.
[5:5:5] ~~ Sources: Census of India 2011; PLFS Annual Reports 2017-18 to 2023-24; app notes 3:5 sub 4
## SUB 6 | Labour Indicators and Employment Status
[5:6:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Meaning
  [5:6:0.0] LFPR | % of population working or seeking/available for work
  [5:6:0.1] WPR | % of population employed
  [5:6:0.2] Unemployment rate | % of the labour force that is unemployed
  [5:6:0.3] Usual status (ps+ss) | Reference period 365 days
  [5:6:0.4] Current weekly status | Reference period 7 days – monthly/quarterly bulletins
[5:6:1] - Monthly PLFS from April 2025; July 2026 rural unemployment 5% → **4.5%**.
[5:6:2] - PLFS 2025: regular wage/salaried 22% → **24%**; **self-employment 58% → 56%**.
[5:6:3] - **India Employment Report 2024:** March 2024, **IHD with the ILO**; focus on **youth employment, education and skills**.
[5:6:4] ~~ Sources: PLFS methodology (MoSPI); ILO-IHD India Employment Report 2024; app notes 3:5 sub 5
## SUB 7 | Jobless Growth and the Slow Shift Out of Agriculture
[5:7:0] - **Jobless growth**: output grows without a matching rise in quality employment – **late 1990s**.
[5:7:1] - **Employment elasticity:** **negative in agriculture**; **construction** and services most employment-intensive (RBI study, 2014).
[5:7:2] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [5:7:2.0] History | Colonial deindustrialisation pushed artisans onto land
  [5:7:2.1] Capital intensity | Growth failed to absorb surplus farm labour
  [5:7:2.2] Skills | Only 4.2% had formal vocational training
  [5:7:2.3] Job deficit | ~20 million entrants a year vs ~2 million new jobs
[5:7:3] ~~ Sources: RBI study on employment elasticity (2014); app notes 3:5 sub 8
## SUB 8 | Gig and Platform Work
[5:8:0] - **Gig worker**: earns outside the traditional employer-employee relationship; defined **for the first time** in the **Code on Social Security, 2020**.
[5:8:1] - **Platform work**: uses an **online platform** to reach others or provide services; gig workers = about **2%** of the 61.6 crore workforce; **not yet a separate PLFS category**.
[5:8:2] ~~ Sources: Code on Social Security 2020 s.2(35), 2(61); app notes 3:5 sub 7
## SUB 9 | Types of Unemployment
[5:9:0] TABLE head: Type | Feature | Linked with
  [5:9:0.0] Disguised | More people than needed; marginal productivity near zero | Agriculture
  [5:9:0.1] Seasonal | Work only in sowing/harvest | Agriculture
  [5:9:0.2] Structural | Skill-job mismatch (new technology) | Industry, educated
  [5:9:0.3] Frictional | Short gap between jobs | Urban/organised
  [5:9:0.4] Cyclical | Demand falls in a business-cycle slump | Industry
[5:9:1] ~~ Sources: NCERT Class 11 Indian Economic Development ch.7; app notes 3:5 sub 9
## SUB 10 | Inter-state Variation and Andhra Pradesh
[5:10:0] TABLE head: Census 2011 | Andhra Pradesh (13 districts) | India
  [5:10:0.0] Cultivators | 14.5% | 24.7%
  [5:10:0.1] Agricultural labourers | 47.9% | 30.0%
  [5:10:0.2] All agriculture | 62.4% | 54.6%
[5:10:1] - AP labourers : cultivators about **3:1** (India about 1.2:1).
[5:10:2] - High **"other workers"** (services): urbanised **Delhi, Chandigarh, Puducherry**; highest share of cultivators: **Himachal Pradesh** (57.9%); of agricultural labourers: **Bihar** (52.8%).
[5:10:3] - AP (PLFS 2023-24): agriculture **45.6%** (India 46.1%); youth (15-29) unemployment **17.5%**; rural casual labour **AP 33.8% vs India 22.5%**.
[5:10:4] - 2026 rural female LFPR gains: **West Bengal, UP, Bihar**.
[5:10:5] ~~ Sources: Census 2011 PCA (AP); PLFS Annual Report 2023-24; app notes 3:5 sub 10

=== NOTES 3:6 | Economic Development Since Independence – Phases, Growth Rates and the Hindu Rate of Growth
## SUB 0 | Hindu Rate of Growth
[6:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [6:0:0.0] Coined by | Prof. Raj Krishna (not V.K.R.V. Rao, Mahalanobis, Amartya Sen)
  [6:0:0.1] Year | 1978 (some books: 1976)
  [6:0:0.2] Variable | Growth of national income / real GDP – not per capita income, population or money
  [6:0:0.3] Rate | About 3.5% a year (3.52%, 1950-1980) – not 5.5%
  [6:0:0.4] Period | 1950s to early 1980s (pre-reform planning era)
  [6:0:0.5] Per capita growth | Only 1.37% a year – barely above population growth
[6:0:1] - It describes **stagnant / low growth** of the Indian economy in 1950-80 – nothing to do with the Hindu population, faster growth or inequality.
[6:0:2] - Broken in the **1980s** (5.1-5.5%); 2026 echo: a **"Bharat rate of growth"** of 8%+ through AI-led "Reforms 3.0" (Jun 2026).
[6:0:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy p.98 (Hindu rate: Raj Krishna, national income/GDP, 3.5%, 1950s-early 1980s); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.11 (3.52%, per capita 1.37%); app notes 3:6 sub 0
## SUB 1 | The 1991 Reforms – Trigger and Record
[6:1:0] - **Economic reforms (LPG / New Economic Policy): July 1991** – opened the economy to foreign and private investment.
[6:1:1] - **Trigger: balance-of-payments crisis** – reserves for only about **two weeks** of imports (under $1 bn); fiscal deficit **8.4%** (1990); the **Gulf War (1990-91)** raised oil prices and cut remittances.
[6:1:2] - Shortcomings: faster growth did not cut poverty enough, few quality jobs, unbalanced regional development; **rising consumer-goods imports is not usually listed** as a shortcoming.
[6:1:3] - 1997-98 slowdown – **East Asian financial crisis**; currency devaluation there was **unfavourable** for Indian exports.
[6:1:4] TABLE head: View | Argument
  [6:1:4.0] 1980s turn | Rodrik-Subramanian (2004): transition around 1980 from a pro-business (not pro-market) shift; DeLong (2003): take-off in the 1980s
  [6:1:4.1] 1991 turn | 1980s growth was debt-fuelled → 1991 crisis → sustained high growth after reforms
[6:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.32 (two weeks of imports, reforms 1991); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 13 p.6-11 (LPG); app notes 3:6 subs 7-8
## SUB 2 | Policy Orientation 1947-1991 – Planning and Import Substitution
[6:2:0] TABLE head: Policy / plan | Year | Provision
  [6:2:0.0] First Industrial Policy | 1948 | IFCI set up
  [6:2:0.1] IPR 1956 ("Economic Constitution") | 1956 | Schedule A = 17 industries for the State; Schedule B = 12; rest private under licensing
  [6:2:0.2] Second Plan (Mahalanobis) | 1956-61 | Heavy industries; import substitution adopted as the strategy of industrialisation
  [6:2:0.3] Third Plan | 1961-66 | Continued import substitution (did not introduce it)
  [6:2:0.4] 1980s reforms | 1980s | Pro-business: broad-banding, MRTP limit raised to Rs 100 crore
  [6:2:0.5] 1991 reforms | 1991 | Reserved industries 17 → 8; delicensing
[6:2:1] - Major focus 1947-1991: **import substitution** with a large public sector – not export promotion, deregulation or less public investment.
[6:2:2] - UPSC 2009: Second Plan heavy industry ✓; "Third Plan introduced import substitution" ✗ → **a only**.
[6:2:3] - **Bombay Plan (1944)**: industrialists themselves sought **state protection** and planning support.
[6:2:4] ~~ Sources: NCERT Class 11 Indian Economic Development ch.2 (import substitution, first seven Plans); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.25 (IPR 1956 "Economic Constitution"); app notes 3:6 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Phases and Growth Rates
[6:3:0] TABLE head: Phase | Average growth
  [6:3:0.0] Before Independence | about 1% a year; agriculture 0.3%; agriculture the main livelihood on the eve of Independence
  [6:3:0.1] Plan era (Plans 1-11) | about 4.5%; agriculture 2-3%, industry 6-8%
  [6:3:0.2] 1950-1980 ("Hindu rate") | ~3.5%
  [6:3:0.3] 1980-81 to 1989-90 | 5.13-5.18%
  [6:3:0.4] Post-reform | ~6.5%; peak 8.5% in 2003-08
  [6:3:0.5] Post-Covid (2022-23 series) | 7.2% (2023-24), 7.1% (2024-25), 7.7% (2025-26 PE)
[6:3:1] - **Expected growth 2012-13** (Economic Survey 2011-12 / Budget 2012-13): **7.6%** (±0.25); 2008-09 expected about **9%** (actual 6.7%).
[6:3:2] - UPSC 2011: GDP and per capita growth did **not** rise steadily in 2006-11 (growth fell from 9.6% in 2006-07 to about 6.7% in 2008-09 and then recovered) → **neither**.
[6:3:3] - **High growth** depends on savings and their **optimal allocation** (APPSC G1 1990-91 key).
[6:3:4] - **Worst years:** **1979-80: -5.2%** (drought, oil shock); **2020-21: -5.8%** (Covid-19).
[6:3:5] - RBI outlook 2026-27: **6.6%** (Jun 2026); **Arvind Subramanian**: 2011-17 growth about **4.5%**, not 7%; AP **9.88%** vs India 7.4% (2025-26).
[6:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.11; Economic Survey 2011-12 ch.1 (7.6% for 2012-13); NSO; app notes 3:6 subs 1, 4-5
## SUB 4 | Investment and Growth – ICOR
[6:4:0] - **ICOR** = change in capital ÷ change in output; **lower ICOR = more efficient** investment.
[6:4:1] - **Harrod-Domar** (First Plan): **g = s/v**; a higher capital-output ratio with the same savings → **lower growth**.
[6:4:2] - **Second Plan**: investment 7% → 11% of national income; **heavy, capital-intensive** industry (not light consumer goods) with long gestation → high ICOR.
[6:4:3] - GFCF about **30%** of GDP (2025-26).
[6:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 (plans); app notes 3:6 sub 3
## SUB 5 | Chronology of Milestones
[6:5:0] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [6:5:0.0] 1938 | First National Planning Committee
  [6:5:0.1] 1 Jan 1949 | RBI nationalised
  [6:5:0.2] 1951 | First Five Year Plan; First Finance Commission (K.C. Neogy)
  [6:5:0.3] 1952 | Community Development Programme (2 October 1952)
  [6:5:0.4] 1955 | SBI and ICICI
  [6:5:0.5] 1960 | First Agricultural University – Pantnagar
  [6:5:0.6] 1964 | IDBI and UTI
  [6:5:0.7] 1966-69 | Plan Holiday – wars (1962, 1965) and droughts; rupee devalued 36.5% on 6 June 1966
  [6:5:0.8] July 1969 | Nationalisation of 14 banks
  [6:5:0.9] 1971 | Garibi Hatao; Dandekar-Rath poverty study
  [6:5:0.10] 1974 / 1975 | First KVK (Puducherry) / first RRB – Prathama Grameen Bank
  [6:5:0.11] 1977-78 | Food-for-Work; Antyodaya in Rajasthan
  [6:5:0.12] 1978-79 | IRDP introduced (trial); nationwide 1980
  [6:5:0.13] 1980 | Second bank nationalisation; NREP
  [6:5:0.14] 1982 | NABARD; DWCRA
  [6:5:0.15] 1990 | SIDBI; first Human Development Report (UNDP, Mahbub-ul-Haq)
  [6:5:0.16] 1993 | First private-sector mutual fund
[6:5:1] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian Economy #30 p.44 (banking milestones); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.12-14; app notes 3:6 subs 6-7

=== NOTES 3:7 | Economic Planning in India – Origins, Planning Commission, National Development Council
## SUB 0 | Planning Commission – Set-up, Status, Chairman
[7:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [7:0:0.0] Set up | 15 March 1950 (began work 28 March 1950), with the Budget of 1950-51
  [7:0:0.1] How | Cabinet (executive) resolution of the Government of India – "a resolution of the Government of India"
  [7:0:0.2] Recommended by | Advisory Planning Board (1946), chaired by K.C. Neogy – not the Congress National Planning Committee
  [7:0:0.3] Basis | In line with Article 39 (DPSP) objectives
  [7:0:0.4] Status | Non-constitutional, non-statutory, advisory body (Rocket: also "quasi-political")
  [7:0:0.5] Chairman | Prime Minister, ex officio; first – Jawaharlal Nehru (as first PM)
  [7:0:0.6] Model | Broadly the Soviet Gosplan
  [7:0:0.7] Replaced by | NITI Aayog, 1 January 2015 (also a Cabinet resolution); last Plan = Twelfth (2012-17)
[7:0:1] - Body set up after Independence to prepare a **common plan** for the country = **Planning Commission**.
[7:0:2] - **Five-Year Plan idea in India: Jawaharlal Nehru** (as PM and first Chairman); planned development began with the **First Plan from 1 April 1951**.
[7:0:3] - **Functions:** assess material, capital and human resources; **formulate** plans; fix stages and priorities; determine resources; **appraise progress**; recommend on policy and administration; **perspective planning**.
[7:0:4] - **Execution is NOT its function** – plans were executed by ministries and States.
[7:0:5] - No mention in the Constitution; **no fixed tenure or qualifications** for the Deputy Chairman and members.
[7:0:6] - Was the **nodal agency for poverty estimation** at national and state level (now NITI Aayog, its successor).
[7:0:7] - **UIDAI** (Unique Identification Authority, 2009) began as an **attached office of the Planning Commission**; statutory since the Aadhaar Act 2016, under **MeitY**.
[7:0:8] - **National Planning Council (1965):** expert advisory body attached to the Commission.
[7:0:9] > 1950 = Planning Commission; 1952 = NDC; 2015 = NITI Aayog. "Advisory body" is the keyed status.
[7:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.4-5; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.28; Rocket Indian Economy #23 p.33; app notes 3:7 sub 1, 3:8 sub 1
## SUB 1 | National Development Council (NDC)
[7:1:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [7:1:0.0] Set up | 6 August 1952 – executive resolution, on the recommendation of the draft outline of the First Plan
  [7:1:0.1] Status | Neither constitutional nor statutory; extra-constitutional; advice not binding; to meet at least twice a year
  [7:1:0.2] Chairman | Prime Minister (presides over meetings)
  [7:1:0.3] Members | PM, all Union Cabinet Ministers (since 1967), Chief Ministers of all States, UT administrators, members of the Planning Commission
  [7:1:0.4] Secretary | Secretary of the Planning Commission
  [7:1:0.5] NOT members | President, Vice-President, Governors, Chairman of the Finance Commission, Secretary of the Ministry of Planning and Programme Implementation
[7:1:1] - **Objectives:** **chief – secure cooperation of the States in executing the plan** (NextGen); strengthen and mobilise the nation's efforts and resources for the plan; promote common economic policies; ensure **balanced and rapid development** of all regions.
[7:1:2] - **Functions:** prescribe **guidelines for the national plan, including assessment of resources**; consider and **approve the draft Five-Year Plan** – the **apex / final authority** that approves plans (can modify the draft).
[7:1:3] - **Sarkaria Commission:** constitutional status under **Article 263**, rename it "**National Economic and Development Council**".
[7:1:4] - Now inactive; its role passed to **NITI Aayog's Governing Council** (formal abolition pending).
[7:1:5] - **Chronology (UPPCS 2003):** India joins IMF (**Dec 1945**) → first devaluation (**Sept 1949**) → First Plan submitted to Parliament (**draft outline July 1951**) → NDC (**Aug 1952**).
[7:1:6] > NDC is NOT 1950 and NOT statutory; "guidelines incl. assessment of resources" = NDC, "assess resources and draft" = Planning Commission.
[7:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC 20 (NDC: composition, objectives); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.28, p.53 (NDC finally approves plans); app notes 3:7 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Origins – Pre-independence Plans
[7:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Effort | Person / idea
  [7:2:0.0] 1931 | Karachi Resolution (INC) | Economic freedom; state ownership / control of key industries
  [7:2:0.1] 1934 | Planned Economy for India | M. Visvesvaraya – first blueprint; ten-year plan to double national income; "Father of Indian Planning"; Bharat Ratna 1955
  [7:2:0.2] 1934 | FICCI | Called for national planning (Depression, New Deal, Soviet experiment)
  [7:2:0.3] 1938 | National Planning Committee (Congress) | Initiated by Subhas Chandra Bose (Haripura); chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru; final report 1949
  [7:2:0.4] 1944 | Bombay Plan | Eight industrialists (J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla, Kasturbhai Lalbhai, Purshottamdas Thakurdas, Ardeshir Dalal, John Mathai) – state-led industrialisation with protection
  [7:2:0.5] 1944 | Gandhian Plan | Shriman Narayan Agarwal (not Kripalani) – decentralised, self-contained villages
  [7:2:0.6] 1944 | Planning and Development Department | Ardeshir Dalal; abolished 1946
  [7:2:0.7] 1945 | People's Plan | M.N. Roy (Indian Federation of Labour) – Marxist; priority to agriculture
  [7:2:0.8] 1946 | Advisory Planning Board | K.C. Neogy – recommended the Planning Commission
  [7:2:0.9] 1947 | Economic Programme Committee | Jawaharlal Nehru
  [7:2:0.10] 1950 | Sarvodaya Plan | Jayaprakash Narayan (inspired by Gandhi and Vinoba)
[7:2:1] - **First Five-Year Plan in the world: USSR (1928, Stalin)**; India from 1951.
[7:2:2] - Indian planning drew on **Soviet planning** and the **Fabian socialism of Sidney and Beatrice Webb** (Nehru) – not Lenin's NEP.
[7:2:3] - **Mahatma Gandhi opposed centralised planned development** – self-reliance meant simple living, local resources and local production.
[7:2:4] - Supporters of planning: industrialists (Bombay Plan) and socialists; Gandhian and Sarvodaya plans = **decentralised alternative**.
[7:2:5] > Bose initiated, Nehru chaired the NPC; M.N. Roy = People's Plan, not a Bombay Plan signatory.
[7:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.1-4; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.28 (Visvesvaraya first attempt; NPC 1938 Nehru); app notes 3:7 sub 0, 3:8 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Which Body Did What – PC, NDC, Finance Commission, Finance Ministry
[7:3:0] TABLE head: Task | Body
  [7:3:0.0] Assess resources; prepare the draft plan | Planning Commission
  [7:3:0.1] Guidelines incl. assessment of resources; final approval of the plan | NDC
  [7:3:0.2] Plan becomes operative | Union Cabinet, then Parliament
  [7:3:0.3] Share of States in taxes; principles of distribution of net tax proceeds; grants | Finance Commission (Article 280, constitutional)
  [7:3:0.4] Suggestions on transfer and allocation of financial resources to Union and States | Finance Commission
  [7:3:0.5] Control of government expenditure; budgetary allocation | Finance Ministry
  [7:3:0.6] Allocation of central funds to States now (after the Planning Commission) | Union Finance Ministry (devolution on Finance Commission advice)
[7:3:1] - **Flow:** Commission drafts → **NDC approves** → Cabinet → Parliament. So the bodies "associated with planning" = **NDC and Parliament** (UPSC 2014), not the Finance Commission or the line ministries.
[7:3:2] TABLE head: Basis | Planning Commission | Finance Commission
  [7:3:2.0] Nature | Non-constitutional, permanent | Constitutional (Art. 280), periodic
  [7:3:2.1] Dealt with | Plan resources, planning | Tax devolution, grants (old non-Plan)
[7:3:3] - Finance Commission decides the **method and formula** for sharing tax proceeds between Centre and States.
[7:3:4] - **State plans:** State Planning Board (**CM as Chairman**, Vice-Chairman, 6-9 members) drafts; the **Chief Minister** sends the State draft plan to the Planning Commission.
[7:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.4; Rocket Indian Economy #23 p.33 (PC vs FC); NextGen Polity - APPSC 20; app notes 3:7 sub 3, sub 6
## SUB 4 | Planning, the Constitution and Decentralised Planning
[7:4:0] - "**Economic and social planning**" = **Concurrent List (List III), Entry 20**, Seventh Schedule.
[7:4:1] - **Article 39** (DPSP) – source of plan objectives; **Article 40** – village panchayats, the village as the primary unit.
[7:4:2] - **Not mentioned in the Constitution:** **NDC, Planning Commission, Zonal Councils** (all three; Zonal Councils are **statutory** – States Reorganisation Act 1956); NITI Governing Council is not statutory.
[7:4:3] - **Bottom-up planning** is a goal not yet achieved; the village is accepted as a suitable unit (UPPSC 1998 key: A and R true, R explains A).
[7:4:4] TABLE head: Body | Article | Rule
  [7:4:4.0] District Planning Committee | 243ZD | Four-fifths elected from elected members of district panchayat and municipalities; chairperson sends the draft district plan to the State
  [7:4:4.1] Metropolitan Planning Committee | 243ZE | Metro areas of 10 lakh+; two-thirds elected
[7:4:5] - **74th Amendment (1992)** inserted **Part IXA** (municipalities), which holds the DPC and MPC.
[7:4:6] - **Balwantrai Mehta (1957):** planning to PRIs (accepted Jan 1958); **JP Narayan Committee (1961):** flagged centralisation; **Thungon (1988):** **Zila Parishad** the pivot of planning.
[7:4:7] - **SFDA, DPAP, ITDP, IADP** ran **outside the panchayats**; **73rd and 74th Amendments** restored local bodies' role.
[7:4:8] - Levels: Centre (Planning Commission → NITI Aayog) → State Planning Boards → DPC / MPC → Mandal plans, **GPDP**.
[7:4:9] - **AP:** State Planning Commission in the **Fifth Plan**; first district-level planning in the **Sixth Plan – Rs 1 crore to each of 23 districts**; Economic Regions – **Visakhapatnam 10 districts** (NITI-assisted, launched 13 Nov 2025), **Amaravati 9**, Tirupati 10.
[7:4:10] - **Kerala People's Plan Campaign:** 17 Aug 1996; 35-40% of plan outlay to local bodies.
[7:4:11] - **NITI State Support Mission** (2026) helps States set up **State Institutions for Transformation**.
[7:4:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.4 (JP Committee, 73rd/74th); Constitution of India (List III Entry 20; Arts 40, 243ZD, 243ZE); app notes 3:7 sub 4, 6, 7, 3:8 sub 9
## SUB 5 | Deputy Chairmen and Members
[7:5:0] TABLE head: Deputy Chairman | Period / note
  [7:5:0.0] Gulzarilal Nanda | First (1950)
  [7:5:0.1] V.T. Krishnamachari | 1953-60 – Second Plan period
  [7:5:0.2] D.T. Lakdawala | 1977-80 – Rolling Plan (Janata)
  [7:5:0.3] Manmohan Singh | Jan 1985 – Aug 1987
  [7:5:0.4] Pranab Mukherjee | June 1991 – May 1996
  [7:5:0.5] Montek Singh Ahluwalia | July 2004 – May 2014 – last
[7:5:1] - **P. Chidambaram** was never Deputy Chairman; **A.M. Khusro, N.K.P. Salve, M.S. Ahluwalia** were never **Chairman** (only the PM is).
[7:5:2] - Deputy Chairman = de facto head, **Cabinet-minister rank**, attended Cabinet without a vote.
[7:5:3] - Composition: PM, Deputy Chairman, Finance and Planning Ministers ex officio, expert members, Member-Secretary; **States / Governors not represented**.
[7:5:4] - Last Plan: **Twelfth (2012-17)**.
[7:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.28 (first and last Deputy Chairman); Planning Commission list of Deputy Chairmen (planningcommission.nic.in, archived); app notes 3:8 sub 1
## SUB 6 | Criticism and the Shift to NITI Aayog
[7:6:0] - Epithets: "**super cabinet**", "economic cabinet", "parallel cabinet", "**fifth wheel of the coach**" – for **centralising decisions** and eroding **State autonomy**.
[7:6:1] - **Nehru (1958)** admitted the Commission had become a kind of "super-cabinet"; the Advisory Planning Board's "**common plan**" idea bred lasting Centre-State tension.
[7:6:2] - **NITI Aayog:** think tank; **bottom-up**, **cooperative (and competitive) federalism**; **no financial powers** – not a fund allocator.
[7:6:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.5; Rocket Indian Economy #24 p.34; app notes 3:7 sub 5

=== NOTES 3:8 | Objectives of Indian Planning; Types of Planning (imperative, Indicative, Perspective, Rolling)
## SUB 0 | Rolling Plan (1978-80)
[8:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [8:0:0.0] Suggested by | Gunnar Myrdal, for backward countries – "Indian Economic Planning in its Broader Setting"
  [8:0:0.1] Introduced by | Janata Party government (ended the Fifth Plan a year early)
  [8:0:0.2] Deputy Chairman then | D.T. Lakdawala – credited with introducing it in India
  [8:0:0.3] Period | April 1978 – March 1980 (1978-80)
  [8:0:0.4] Name | Janata Sixth Plan (1978-83) = "the rolling plan" – the novel idea of the draft Sixth Plan
  [8:0:0.5] Outlay | Rs 12,177 crore; stressed employment
  [8:0:0.6] End | Janata fall → 1979-80 annual plan → Congress Sixth Plan from 1 April 1980
[8:0:1] # Three plans in one (all four book statements are correct)
[8:0:2] - 1. A plan for the **current year** (with the annual budget).
[8:0:3] - 2. A plan for a fixed number of years (**3, 4 or 5**), **revised every year** as the economy requires and extended by one year.
[8:0:4] - 3. A **perspective plan** of **10, 15 or 20 years**.
[8:0:5] - Rolling plan **changes both its allocations and its targets every year** → flexibility; criticism: yearly revision **weakened commitment** to targets.
[8:0:6] > Myrdal suggested – Janata introduced – Lakdawala Deputy Chairman – 1978-80. Not Indira, Rajiv or the National Front; Madhu Dandavate was Deputy Chairman only in 1990-91.
[8:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.16 (Rolling Plan 1978-80); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.38 (Myrdal; April 1978 – April 1980); app notes 3:8 sub 8
## SUB 1 | Objectives of Planning
[8:1:0] - **Four long-term objectives:** **growth, modernisation, self-reliance, social justice (equity)** – plus employment and removal of poverty; the long-term objective = **all** of high standard of living, social justice and self-reliance.
[8:1:1] - **Economic growth = principal objective**; the others are supporting.
[8:1:2] - Chief objectives also listed in the Plans: **reduce inequalities of income and wealth**, higher growth, **removal of poverty**, employment. "**To achieve social equality**" is not a stated economic objective of the Plans.
[8:1:3] - Major objective of the Five Year Plans (book key): **self-reliance** and less dependence on foreign sources.
[8:1:4] - Declared aim (1950 resolution): rapid rise in the **standard of living** through efficient use of resources, more production and **employment for all**.
[8:1:5] - **Planning** = a conscious effort of the State with a **set of goals**, a **set of means** and a **specific time period**.
[8:1:6] - Initial strategy of the 1950s: **rapid industrialisation** (Second Plan); cornerstone = **central economic planning**.
[8:1:7] # Socialistic pattern of society
[8:1:8] - Adopted at the **Avadi Congress (1955)** → **Second Plan (1956-61)** and **IPR 1956**.
[8:1:9] - Core element: **social gain, not private profit**, as the test of development (not communes or nationalising all firms).
[8:1:10] - Planning for socialism aims at a **national minimum standard of living** for all (NPC 1938, Bombay Plan).
[8:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.4-6; NCERT Class 11 Indian Economic Development ch.2 (goals of Five Year Plans); Second Five Year Plan ch.2 (socialist pattern – social gain, reduction of inequalities); app notes 3:8 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Imperative vs Indicative Planning
[8:2:0] TABLE head: Feature | Imperative (directive / target) | Indicative
  [8:2:0.0] Market mechanism | Entirely replaced by a command hierarchy | Plan improves the market
  [8:2:0.1] Ownership | State / collective | Mixed
  [8:2:0.2] Targets | Binding quotas, allocation, prices | Guidelines and signals
  [8:2:0.3] Examples | USSR (1928, Stalin), China | Mixed economies; France
  [8:2:0.4] India | Public sector in early Plans | From the Eighth Plan (1992-97) after 1991
[8:2:1] - A **Five-Year Plan** is an **indicative plan of action** reflecting the government's intent.
[8:2:2] - Soviet collectivisation (Stalin): collective farms = **Kolkhoz** (state farms = sovkhoz).
[8:2:3] - **Regional planning** first in the USA (1916+; Tennessee Valley).
[8:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.28, p.58 (imperative vs indicative); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.6; Britannica "kolkhoz"; app notes 3:8 sub 5
## SUB 3 | Perspective Planning and Plan Horizons
[8:3:0] TABLE head: Plan | Horizon
  [8:3:0.0] Annual plan | Short term – one year
  [8:3:0.1] Five Year Plan | Medium term
  [8:3:0.2] Perspective plan | Long term – 15 to 20 years or more; five-year and annual plans carved out of it
[8:3:1] - Perspective planning was a **Planning Commission function**.
[8:3:2] - **Long-term perspective plan 1985-2000** accompanied the **Seventh Plan**.
[8:3:3] - **AP now:** **Swarna Andhra Vision 2047** – GSDP **Rs 308.11 lakh crore by 2047-48**; ten "**Padi Sutralu**"; targets (10 Feb 2026): **15%** growth, GSDP **Rs 31 lakh crore**, PCI Rs 5.15 lakh by 2030.
[8:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.5, p.20 (15-year perspective 1985-2000); app notes 3:8 sub 7
## SUB 4 | Other Types of Planning
[8:4:0] TABLE head: Pair | Distinction
  [8:4:0.0] Centralised vs decentralised | One central authority, top-down vs decisions shared with lower governments / private units within a broad policy
  [8:4:0.1] Financial vs physical | Allocation in money terms vs in real terms (materials, manpower, output)
  [8:4:0.2] Direction vs inducement | Command (imperative) vs incentives guiding private units (indicative)
  [8:4:0.3] Democratic vs totalitarian | Through elected bodies and consent (India) vs state command
[8:4:1] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.58; app notes 3:8 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Plans – Thrust, Models and Financing
[8:5:0] TABLE head: Plan | Main thrust / model
  [8:5:0.0] First (from 1 April 1951) | Agriculture, irrigation, power; Harrod-Domar (growth = savings rate ÷ capital-output ratio); 3.6% achieved vs 2.1% target
  [8:5:0.1] Second (1956-61) | Rapid industrialisation, socialistic pattern – Feldman-Mahalanobis (heavy industry, public sector, import substitution; not export promotion); forex crisis cuts 1958
  [8:5:0.2] Third (1961-66) | Self-reliance, food self-sufficiency
  [8:5:0.3] Fourth (1969-74) | Target-group approach (SFDA, MFAL, DPAP); reduce dependence on foreign aid
  [8:5:0.4] Fifth (1974-79) | Self-reliance + raising consumption of the poor; direct attack on poverty; Tribal Sub-Plan
  [8:5:0.5] Sixth (1980-85) | Poverty alleviation; Minimum Needs Programme, IRDP
  [8:5:0.6] Ninth (1997-2002) | Seven Basic Minimum Services
  [8:5:0.7] Twelfth (2012-17) | Faster, sustainable, more inclusive growth – last
[8:5:1] - **Trickle-down** (First–Third Plans; Community Development Programme 1952) → target-group (Fourth) → direct attack (Fifth, Sixth).
[8:5:2] - **Wage-goods model:** **C.N. Vakil and P.R. Brahmananda** – alternative to Mahalanobis.
[8:5:3] - **Plan financing:** domestic budgetary resources, PSU surpluses, **market borrowing**, **deficit financing (borrowing from the RBI = money creation)**, foreign aid.
[8:5:4] - **Eighth Plan (1992-97):** largest source of public sector outlay = **government borrowings** (Rs 2,02,255 crore of Rs 4,34,100 crore, **46.6%**); deficit financing only Rs 20,000 crore.
[8:5:5] - **PURA** (Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas, 2003): idea of **A.P.J. Abdul Kalam**, announced by PM Vajpayee.
[8:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.6-24; Eighth Five Year Plan Vol.1 ch.4 (financing of public sector outlay, 1991-92 prices) via Economic Survey 2000-01 Appendix 2.11; app notes 3:8 sub 3, 4, 10
