=== NOTES 3:9 | Plan Models – Harrod-domar, Mahalanobis, Wage-goods (vakil-brahmananda), Gandhian and Bombay Plans
## SUB 0 | Plan → Model It Was Based On
[9:0:0] TABLE head: Plan | Model / strategy
  [9:0:0.0] First (1951-56) | Harrod-Domar model (with modifications); priority agriculture
  [9:0:0.1] Second (1956-61) | P.C. Mahalanobis model (Nehru-Mahalanobis-Feldman; a modified Soviet / Russian model)
  [9:0:0.2] Third (1961-66), "Gadgil Yojana" | Sandee-Chakravarty model (NextGen); several books say "no specific model"; import substitution
  [9:0:0.3] Fourth (1969-74) | Alan S. Manne – Ashok Rudra (open) consistency model; Gadgil strategy (growth with stability)
  [9:0:0.4] Fifth (1974-79) | Dhar model
  [9:0:0.5] Eighth (1992-97) | John W. Miller model
[9:0:1] - **Order 1-2-3-4-5:** Harrod-Domar – Mahalanobis – Sandee-Chakravarty – Manne-Rudra – Dhar.
[9:0:2] - **Mahalanobis model launched in 1956** (Second Plan) laid the foundation of India's industrial modernisation; Mahalanobis = **architect of the Second Plan**.
[9:0:3] - Second Plan distractors: **wage-goods, Gadgil, CELP, Tendulkar, Kaldor, Joan Robinson, Solow** – the key is **Mahalanobis**. First Plan distractors: Lewis-Fei, Keynesian, Manne-Rudra, Gandhian, Sarvodaya – the key is **Harrod-Domar**.
[9:0:4] - **Solow (Solow-Swan):** neoclassical model on a **Cobb-Douglas** production function; **no Indian plan was based on it.**
[9:0:5] TABLE head: Model | Bottleneck it assumed | Priority
  [9:0:5.0] Harrod-Domar (Roy Harrod, Evsey Domar) | Limited savings | Raise savings and investment
  [9:0:5.1] Feldman-Mahalanobis | Capital goods | Heavy industry (steel, machinery)
  [9:0:5.2] Wage-goods (Vakil-Brahmananda, 1956) | Food / wage goods | Agriculture, employment
[9:0:6] > Match question (APPSC): Mahalanobis → Second; open consistency (Manne-Rudra) → Fourth; "no specific model" → Third; Harrod-Domar → First.
[9:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.28 (plan models); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.6-10; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #1 p.2; app notes 3:9 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Pre-independence Plans – Author and Year
[9:1:0] TABLE head: Plan | Year | Author(s) | Core idea
  [9:1:0.0] Visvesvaraya Plan ("Planned Economy for India") | 1934 | M. Visvesvaraya – "Father of Indian Planning" | First blueprint; double national income in a decade via industrialisation
  [9:1:0.1] FICCI proposal | 1934 | FICCI | Need for national planning
  [9:1:0.2] National Planning Committee (Congress) | 1938 | Set up under Subhas Chandra Bose; chaired by Nehru | Final report 1949
  [9:1:0.3] Bombay Plan ("A Plan of Economic Development for India") | 1944 (January; Part 2 Dec 1944) | 8 industrialists: J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla, Purshottamdas Thakurdas, Kasturbhai Lalbhai, Ardeshir Dalal, Lala Shri Ram, A.D. Shroff, John Mathai | Big State role: public investment in infrastructure and heavy/basic industry; protection of infant industry; treble national income in 15 years
  [9:1:0.4] Gandhian Plan | 1944 | Shriman Narayan Agarwal (not Gandhi himself) | Agriculture, cottage and village industries, decentralised self-contained villages
  [9:1:0.5] People's Plan | 1945 | M.N. Roy, for the Post-War Reconstruction Committee of the Indian Federation of Labour | Marxist socialism; basic necessities; equal weight to agriculture and industry
  [9:1:0.6] Sarvodaya Plan | 1950 | Jayaprakash Narayan | Gandhian constructive work + Vinoba Bhave's Sarvodaya
[9:1:1] - **Wrong pairs asked:** Bombay Plan – **Rajaji** ✗; Bombay Plan – **Dhirubhai Ambani** ✗ (he was not an architect); People's Plan – Gandhi/Mahalanobis ✗.
[9:1:2] - **All correct (APPSC Group 1):** Bombay Plan – **John Mathai** ✓ (a signatory), People's Plan – M.N. Roy ✓, Gandhian Plan – **Shriman Narayan** ✓, Second Plan – Mahalanobis ✓.
[9:1:3] - **Chronology:** NPC (1938) → Bombay and Gandhian Plans (1944) → People's Plan (1945) → Sarvodaya (1950) → First Plan (1951).
[9:1:4] - Precursors: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**; **Planning and Development Department (1944)** under **Ardeshir Dalal**; **Advisory Planning Board (1946)** headed by **K.C. Neogi**.
[9:1:5] - People's Plan echoed in the 1990s slogan "**reforms with a human face**".

## SUB 2 | Mahalanobis Model
[9:2:0] # Strategy and sectors
[9:2:1] - **Heavy sector strategy** / **unbalanced growth**: priority to **heavy capital goods industries** (steel, machinery) – most public-sector investment went there.
[9:2:2] - Originally conceived by **G.A. Feldman** (USSR, **1928**); Mahalanobis (**1953**) developed it independently – so the **Feldman-Mahalanobis** model, based on the **Russian (Soviet)** model.
[9:2:3] - **Four sectors:** (1) capital goods, (2) factory consumer goods, (3) household / small-scale consumer goods, (4) services.
[9:2:4] - **Stalin's USSR** began five-year plans in **1928** – **imperative** planning; India follows **indicative** planning.
[9:2:5] TABLE head: Included / emphasised | Excluded / neglected
  [9:2:5.0] Industrialisation through heavy industries | Foreign trade – assumed a closed economy
  [9:2:5.1] Infrastructure, basic and key industries | Agriculture (not the priority)
  [9:2:5.2] Dominant public sector (socialistic pattern, IPR 1956), self-reliance, import substitution | Exports / export promotion
  [9:2:5.3] Investment from 7% to 11% of national income | Village and cottage industries were not top priority (left consumer goods to them)
[9:2:6] # Criticisms
[9:2:7] - **Neglect of agriculture and small-scale industries**, **over-emphasis on heavy industry**, **neglect of social objectives** (employment, equity) – food and capital shortages, inflation in the late 1950s.
[9:2:8] - The emphasis on **growth** itself was the plan's aim, **not** the criticism (APPSC G2 Mains 2017).
[9:2:9] # Second Plan outcome
[9:2:10] - Growth: target **4.5%**, achieved **4.27%** (most books; NextGen prints 4.21%).
[9:2:11] - Steel plants **Bhilai, Durgapur, Rourkela**; **Chittaranjan** – locomotives; **Perambur** – coaches; Atomic Energy Commission.
[9:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.8-9; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.46 (unbalanced growth); app notes 3:9 sub 3, 8
[9:2:13] - **Closed economy:** for nearly four decades after independence (till the 1991 reforms) India was a largely **closed**, inward-looking economy.
## SUB 3 | Harrod-Domar Model and Capital-Output Ratio
[9:3:0] - **g = s / k** (g = growth rate, s = **savings** rate, k = **capital-output ratio**): growth **rises with savings**, **falls with a higher COR** – so COR fixes growth **along with savings**.
[9:3:1] - **Capital-output ratio** = capital needed to raise output by **one unit** per annum.
[9:3:2] TABLE head: Basis | High COR | Low COR
  [9:3:2.0] Meaning | More capital per unit of output; investment gives less output | Less capital per unit of output
  [9:3:2.1] Capital productivity | Lower | Higher
  [9:3:2.2] Growth | Slower, even with high savings | Higher potential
[9:3:3] - ★ Low growth despite high savings and capital formation = **high capital-output ratio** (UPSC 1995, 2018).
[9:3:4] - ★ Slow per-capita income growth = **high COR + high population growth** (UPSC 1993: "1 and 2").
[9:3:5] # First Plan
[9:3:6] - Started **1 April 1951**; priority **agriculture**, irrigation and power; investment target 7% of national income.
[9:3:7] - Faced refugees, food shortage, inflation; succeeded mainly due to **good harvests in its last two years**.
[9:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.56 (high COR); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.71 (COR); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.6-7; app notes 3:9 sub 2
## SUB 4 | P.C. Mahalanobis – ISI and Statistics Day
[9:4:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [9:4:0.0] Role | Architect of the Second Plan; called the architect of Indian planning
  [9:4:0.1] Indian Statistical Institute | Founded 17 Dec 1931, Kolkata, by P.C. Mahalanobis; journal Sankhya; Institution of National Importance by the ISI Act, 1959
  [9:4:0.2] National Income Committee (1949) | He chaired it → recommended the National Sample Survey; first NSS round 1950-51
  [9:4:0.3] Honours | Padma Vibhushan (1968), FRS (1945)
  [9:4:0.4] National Statistics Day | 29 June (his birth anniversary), since 2007
[9:4:1] - Statistics Day themes: **2018 – "Quality Assurance in Official Statistics"**; 2026 – "**Unlocking the Potential of Administrative Data**".
[9:4:2] - **ISI Bill, 2026** introduced in Lok Sabha on **2 Aug 2026** to replace the 1959 Act; referred to the **Standing Committee on Finance** (1 Sep 2026).
[9:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.33; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.36; MoSPI Statistics Day 2018 release (gktoday summary); app notes 3:9 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Gandhian Economics and the Janata Strategy
[9:5:0] - Gandhian economy rests on **Trusteeship**: the wealthy act as trustees of wealth.
[9:5:1] - "**India's Economic Policy: The Gandhian Blue Print**" – **Charan Singh**; "**Gandhian Constitution for Free India**" – **Shriman Narayan Agarwal** (not M.N. Roy).
[9:5:2] - **Ram Rajya:** rule on moral authority and justice for the poorest; **not a Hindu state**.
[9:5:3] - **Janata alternative strategy (1977-80):** ended the Fifth Plan a year early (1978); **Rolling Plan 1978-80** (Gunnar **Myrdal's** concept); stressed **agriculture, rural development, employment, cottage and village industries, minimum needs** – **not** heavy industry, and **SEZs** (a 2000s idea) had no place in it.
[9:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.3; app notes 3:9 sub 6-7
## SUB 6 | Wage-goods Model
[9:6:0] - Authors: **C.N. Vakil and P.R. Brahmananda** – "**Planning for an Expanding Economy**" (**1956**).
[9:6:1] - Real constraint = supply of **wage goods** (food, essential consumer goods), **not capital goods**.
[9:6:2] - More wage goods → **disguised unemployed** put to productive work; stresses **employment**.
[9:6:3] - Priority: **agriculture and wage goods** vs Mahalanobis's heavy industry.
[9:6:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:9 sub 5
## SUB 7 | Other Growth Theories
[9:7:0] TABLE head: Theory | Name to remember
  [9:7:0.0] Secular stagnation | Alvin Hansen (1938)
  [9:7:0.1] Differential savings propensity (workers vs capitalists) | Nicholas Kaldor (distribution theory of growth)
  [9:7:0.2] Neoclassical growth | Solow (Cobb-Douglas)
[9:7:1] - **Cobb-Douglas** Q = A L^α K^β: **α + β = 1 → constant** returns to scale (>1 increasing, <1 decreasing).
[9:7:2] ~~ Sources: standard macroeconomics (Hansen 1938 AEA address; Kaldor 1956 "Alternative Theories of Distribution"); app notes 3:9 sub 1

  x: Vakil and Brahmananda argued that more wage goods would let the disguised unemployed be put to productive work.
[fa931fa62e615] sub6
  In contrast to Mahalanobis, the wage-goods model held that the real constraint was NOT the supply of:
  *Capital goods | Food | Essential consumer goods | Wage goods
  x: The wage-goods model saw food and essential consumer goods as the constraint, not capital goods.

=== NOTES 3:10 | Five Year Plans I to Xii – Objectives, Targets, Achievements and Failures of Each
## SUB 0 | Plans I to V and the Plan Holiday – Objectives and Firsts
[10:0:0] TABLE head: Plan | Period | Model | Main objective / tagline
  [10:0:0.0] First | 1951-56 (launched 1 April 1951) | Harrod-Domar | Agriculture and irrigation (with power, transport); food, refugee rehabilitation, price stability
  [10:0:0.1] Second | 1956-61 ("Mahalanobis Plan") | Nehru-Mahalanobis | Rapid industrialisation – heavy and basic industries; socialistic pattern of society
  [10:0:0.2] Third | 1961-66 ("Gadgil Yojana") | Sandy-Chakravarty | Self-reliant and self-generating economy ("make the economy independent"); self-sustaining growth; agriculture priority
  [10:0:0.3] Plan Holiday | 1 April 1966 – 31 March 1969 | – | Three Annual Plans; food problem, Green Revolution (1966-67); agriculture and industry equal weight
  [10:0:0.4] Fourth | 1969-74 (finally launched 1969) | Manne-Rudra (Gadgil strategy) | Twin objectives: growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance; 14 banks nationalised 1969
  [10:0:0.5] Fifth | 1974-79 (ended 1978) | Dhar (final draft by D.P. Dhar) | Twin objectives: removal of poverty (Garibi Hatao) and self-reliance; control of inflation; zero net foreign aid
[10:0:1] # First Plan (1951-56)
[10:0:2] - **Draft outline** presented by the Planning Commission in **July 1951**; final plan December 1952.
[10:0:3] - Prepared to face **Partition (refugees)**, **inflation** and **food shortage**; priority **agriculture and irrigation** – about **one-third** of outlay (highest agriculture share of any plan); **Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud**.
[10:0:4] - **Land reform:** the First Plan first proposed **co-operative village management** (village land managed co-operatively) – not the Second Plan.
[10:0:5] - Succeeded mainly due to **good harvests** in its last two years.
[10:0:6] # Second Plan (1956-61)
[10:0:7] - **Mahalanobis** two- and four-sector model; **heavy industry-led development**; **maximum emphasis on the industrial sector**; the **first major industrial plan**; primary responsibility of development shifted to the **public sector** ("public sector plan").
[10:0:8] - From the Second Plan a **determined thrust towards substitution (import substitution) of basic and capital goods** industries.
[10:0:9] - Goal of **socialistic pattern of society** (with IPR 1956).
[10:0:10] - **Targets pruned** because of an **acute shortage of foreign exchange** (1957-58 crisis) and rising prices.
[10:0:11] # Third, Fourth and Fifth Plans
[10:0:12] - **Third:** self-reliant, self-generating economy – self-reliance / self-sustaining growth first made the objective; hit by **two wars (1962, 1965)** and the 1965-66 drought.
[10:0:13] - **Fourth:** "growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance"; **correcting the earlier trend of increased concentration of wealth and economic power**; **exports to grow about 7 per cent a year** for balance on foreign account; **Growth Centre approach** for regional disparities; target-group programmes.
[10:0:14] - **Fifth:** **removal of poverty for the first time** the basic objective; "**Garibi Hatao**" – Indira Gandhi's slogan of the **1971 elections**; **anti-poverty programmes** and serious concern for **unemployment** start here; high priority to **bring inflation under control** and achieve stability.
[10:0:15] - **Financial sector** was **not** first made an integral part of the plan in the Fifth (false statement, UPSC 2019).
[10:0:16] > Twin objectives (APPSC): Fourth = growth with stability + progressive self-reliance; Fifth = poverty removal + self-reliance. Garibi Hatao = Fifth, not Fourth or Sixth.
[10:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.6-16; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.45, p.51-52, p.60; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #1 p.2, #22 p.32; UPSC CSE 2019 key; First Plan ch.12 (co-operative village management); app notes 3:10 sub 0, 3
[10:0:18] - **Second Plan drafting:** led by **P.C. Mahalanobis** (First Plan: **K.N. Raj**); heavy industry in the public sector; balancing industry and agriculture proved difficult.
[10:0:19] - **Second Plan:** **district and village plans** first prepared in its preparatory exercise.

## SUB 5 | Plans Cut Short, Plan Holiday and the Rolling Plan
[10:5:0] TABLE head: Plan | Cause | Effect
  [10:5:0.0] Third | 1962 and 1965 wars + 1965-66 drought | Plan Holiday (1966-69) declared after the Third Plan
  [10:5:0.1] Fifth | Emergency, new elections, Janata Party elected; Janata government did not want to continue it | Terminated a year early (1978); Rolling Plan (1978-80)
  [10:5:0.2] Eighth | 1990-91 political instability + BoP crisis | Postponed two years; Annual Plans 1990-92
[10:5:1] - **Rolling Plan** = the Janata government's **Sixth Plan (1978-83)**, advocated by Gunnar Myrdal; emphasis on **employment**; ended 1980; Congress launched a new Sixth Plan. Not introduced in any of the Third, Fourth or Fifth Plans.
[10:5:2] - Rolling Plan structure: a plan for **one year**, a plan for **3, 4 or 5 years** renewed every year, and a **perspective plan** for 10, 15 or 20 years.
[10:5:3] - **Two wars in one plan:** the Third (1962 China, 1965 Pakistan).
[10:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.10-17; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.37, p.52; app notes 3:10 sub 2
[10:5:5] - **Janata Sixth Plan (1978-83):** never official; gave new life to **Panchayati Raj** (Asoka Mehta Committee 1977-78).
## SUB 6 | Second Plan Outlay; Eleventh and Twelfth Plan Targets
[10:6:0] - **Second Plan:** planned public outlay **Rs 4,800 crore** (private Rs 3,100 crore); actual **Rs 4,600 crore** (Rs 3,650 crore investment + Rs 950 crore current).
[10:6:1] - **Why pruned:** food and capital shortages, **inflation**, closed-economy assumption, **1957-58 foreign-exchange crisis** (not falling inflation).
[10:6:2] TABLE head: Criticism of the Nehru-Mahalanobis strategy | Detail
  [10:6:2.0] Agriculture | Neglected → food shortages
  [10:6:2.1] Employment | Capital-intensive industry → few jobs
  [10:6:2.2] Prices | High inflation by the late 1950s

  [10:6:4.2] Health | IMR 28; MMR 1 per 1,000 live births; TFR 2.1 | IMR 25

  [10:6:4.4] Outlay | Rs 36,44,718 crore | Rs 76,69,807 crore

[10:6:6] - **Twelfth:** fewer CSS with a **flexi-fund**; social-sector PPPs; plan/non-plan distinction reviewed by the **Rangarajan Committee**; largest allocation to **social services (~34.7%)**.

## SUB 7 | Achievements and Failures of the Plans
[10:7:0] TABLE head: Achievements | Failures
  [10:7:0.0] Steel plants Bhilai, Durgapur, Rourkela; Chittaranjan, Perambur; IITs | Persistent poverty and inequality; Eighth Plan – "the poor became poorer"
  [10:7:0.1] Food self-sufficiency – Green Revolution, FCI (1965), National Seeds Corporation | Job growth lagged (Eighth: 2% vs 2.6%)
  [10:7:0.2] SBI from the Imperial Bank (First Plan period); NABARD (1982) | Regional imbalance both across and within States
  [10:7:0.3] Poverty 48.3% (1977-78) → 37.4% (1983-84) | Eighth Plan public-sector share 34.3% vs 45.2% target
[10:7:1] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.8, p.11, p.18, p.23; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 02 p.5; app notes 3:10 sub 8-9
[10:7:2] - **Each Five Year Plan** reviewed the previous plan and set future goals – 'an assessment of the past and a call for the future'.
[10:7:3] - **Agriculture** (with irrigation) kept a roughly steady share (~20-24%) of plan outlay; energy's share rose, transport's fell.
[10:7:4] - **'Decade of jobless growth':** the **1990s (1991-2000)** – organised employment lagged far behind GDP growth.
[10:7:5] - **Second Plan steel plants:** Bhilai (USSR), **Durgapur (UK)**, Rourkela (W. Germany).

  Which of the following pairs of Five Year Plan and objective is correctly matched?
  Second Plan – Growth with stability and progressive self-reliance | Fifth Plan – Self-reliant and self-generating economy | *Third Plan – Self-reliant and self-generating economy | Fourth Plan – Removal of poverty (Garibi Hatao)

  x: Option B is incorrect: the First Plan put agriculture first, along with food, rehabilitation after Partition, and price stability. Heavy industry was the Second Plan's priority.

=== NOTES 3:11 | Overall Achievements and Failures of Planning in India; End of the Plan Era (2017)
## SUB 0 | Achievements, Failures and Critics of Planning
[11:0:0] TABLE head: Achievements | Failures
  [11:0:0.0] Rise in national income, savings, investment, per-capita income (Plans I-XI averaged ~4.5% growth vs ~1% before Independence) | High rural poverty; rising unemployment – root cause of poverty
  [11:0:0.1] Self-sufficiency in basic, capital and consumer-goods industries | Income inequality not reduced; widened after reforms
  [11:0:0.2] Foodgrain self-sufficiency – Green Revolution (1966-67), FCI (1965) | Land reforms poorly implemented; unequal land ownership persists
  [11:0:0.3] Infrastructure – transport, irrigation, power, telecom | Regional disparities persist (a failure, not an achievement)
  [11:0:0.4] Education, scientific manpower, IT, space; IITs | Neglect of agriculture, lop-sided (capital-intensive) employment strategy, excessive emphasis on PSUs
[11:0:1] # Drawbacks of the planning process
[11:0:2] - Drawbacks named by the books: **implementation failure** (the UN expert team called implementation and enforcement "the principal shortcomings"), a **wrong / absent financial strategy** (Ramesh Singh), **misplaced faith in investment** alone, centralisation, politicisation.
[11:0:3] - APPSC Group 2 Mains 2017 asked for "the chief drawback", and **"All the given answers"** (financial strategy, faith in investment, implementation failure) was keyed. When only one of these is offered, the key is **implementation failure**.
[11:0:4] # Origin and critics
[11:0:5] - The idea of planning came from **Soviet Russia** (USSR five-year plans from 1928).
[11:0:6] TABLE head: Book | Author
  [11:0:6.0] Planning and the Poor (1974) | B.S. Minhas (also asked as "Planning for the Poor")
  [11:0:6.1] India: Planning for Industrialization (1970) | Jagdish Bhagwati and Padma Desai
[11:0:7] - **Padma Desai**: critic of India's planned economy; **first Asian woman** to get a **PhD in Economics from Harvard (1960)**.
[11:0:8] > Distractors for Minhas: Y.K. Alagh, Jagdish Bhagwati, L.G. Patel, D.R. Gadgil, Charan Singh, Rudra Dutt, Manmohan Singh.
[11:0:9] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.5 p.5.36-5.38 (criticism of planning; wrong financial strategy); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 03 p.3-5 (regional disparity, inequality); app notes 3:11 sub 3-4
## SUB 1 | Planning After 1991 and the End of the Plan Era
[11:1:0] - After 1991 planning moved from **"directed" to "indicative"**: the plan shows **priority sectors**; the private sector invests.
[11:1:1] - Plans were kept after 1991 because they give a **long-term perspective** to a market economy; planning is **not a constitutional requirement**.
[11:1:2] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [11:1:2.0] Last plan | Twelfth (2012-17), ended 31 March 2017
  [11:1:2.1] Planning Commission | Scrapping decided August 2014 (Cabinet 13 Aug; PM's Independence Day speech 15 Aug); last Deputy Chairman M.S. Ahluwalia
  [11:1:2.2] Successor | NITI Aayog, 1 January 2015, by Union Cabinet resolution
  [11:1:2.3] NDC (1952) | Inactive; its work passed to the NITI Governing Council; formal abolition pending
[11:1:3] - Abolition ended **discretionary plan grants**; NITI has **no financial powers** – the Governing Council coordinates policy, it does not redistribute funds.
[11:1:4] # Documents that replaced the Five Year Plans
[11:1:5] TABLE head: Document | Period
  [11:1:5.0] 15-year Vision | Up to 2030
  [11:1:5.1] 7-year Strategy | 2017-18 to 2023-24
  [11:1:5.2] Three Year Action Agenda | 2017-18 to 2019-20 (released 1 Aug 2017)
[11:1:6] - Action Agenda on jobs: "unemployment is the lesser of India's problems; the more serious problem is **severe underemployment**" (one job done by two or more workers).
[11:1:7] - **11th Governing Council** (11 June 2026): PM asked States to estimate **district-level GDP**.
[11:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #22-24 p.32-34; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.4-5; NITI Aayog Three Year Action Agenda 2017-18 to 2019-20 (news reports 27 Aug 2017); Wikipedia "Planning Commission (India)"; app notes 3:11 sub 5-7
## SUB 2 | Plan Record – First Plan, Third Plan Failure, Plan Holiday, Fourth Plan
[11:2:0] - **First Plan** launched **1 April 1951**; focus **agriculture and irrigation**.
[11:2:1] - **Third Plan** grew only **2.2%** vs **5.6%** target – **Sino-Indian War (1962)**, **Indo-Pak War (1965)**, **1965-66 droughts**.
[11:2:2] - **Plan Holiday 1966-69** (three Annual Plans) followed the **failure of the Third Plan**.
[11:2:3] - **Fourth Plan (1969-74)**, **Gadgil strategy**: **growth with stability** + progress towards **self-reliance**; targets agriculture **5%** a year, exports **~7%** a year; achieved **3.3%** vs **5.7%** (droughts, 1971 war); **14 banks nationalised (1969)**.
[11:2:4] TABLE head: Formula for central plan assistance to States | Fact
  [11:2:4.0] Gadgil formula | 1969 (Fourth Plan)
  [11:2:4.1] Gadgil-Mukherjee formula | 1991; highest weight to population (1971 Census) – 60%; per capita income 25%; fiscal performance 7.5%; special problems 7.5%
  [11:2:4.2] Special Category States | 90% grant : 10% loan; General Category 30 : 70
[11:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 01 p.6-12; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #22 p.32; rebuilt notes book 3 row 10 (Gadgil-Mukherjee weights); app notes 3:11 sub 0-2

=== NOTES 3:12 | Niti Aayog – Structure, Mandate, Verticals, Differences from the Planning Commission
## SUB 0 | NITI Aayog – Basics, Date and Status
[12:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [12:0:0.0] Full form | National Institution for Transforming India
  [12:0:0.1] Set up | 1 January 2015 (not 2012, 2014 or 2016; not 26 Jan)
  [12:0:0.2] Mode | Union Cabinet resolution – an executive order, not an Act or amendment
  [12:0:0.3] Replaced | Planning Commission (not the Finance, Law or Human Rights Commission)
  [12:0:0.4] Status | Non-constitutional and non-statutory; apex public policy think tank; advisory
  [12:0:0.5] Chairperson | Prime Minister (ex officio) – no full-time Chairman
[12:0:1] - A **think tank, not a fund allocator** – it does **not** make Five Year Plans.
[12:0:2] - "Not a statutory body": **NITI Aayog** – Finance Commission (Art. 280), UPSC and Election Commission are **constitutional**.
[12:0:3] - **Zonal Councils** = **statutory** (States Reorganisation Act, 1956), chaired by the **Union Home Minister**.
[12:0:4] > Statements asked: "set up in 2015 to replace the Planning Commission" ✓; "constitutional body making Five-Year Plans" ✗.

## SUB 3 | Approach, Objectives and Functions
[12:3:0] - Guiding principle: **Cooperative federalism** (not competitive, collateral or compulsive) – also called **"marble-cake" federalism** (shared roles, vs layered "layer-cake").
[12:3:1] - **Bottom-up** approach (vs Planning Commission's **top-down, one-size-fits-all**); bottom-up and top-down are strategies of **information processing**.
[12:3:2] - State rankings (SDG India Index etc.) → **competitive federalism**; competition among States and cities = **competitive sub-federalism**.
[12:3:3] # Objectives in the Cabinet resolution
[12:3:4] - **Shared vision** of national priorities with the States; structured support to States (strong States make a strong nation).
[12:3:5] - **Credible plans at the village level, aggregated progressively at higher levels** of government.
[12:3:6] - **Antyodaya**, inclusive and participatory development; focus on **small enterprises** (not large ones); monitoring and evaluation; knowledge and innovation hub.
[12:3:7] - **Four mandate areas:** knowledge and innovation; NITI for States; driving transformational change; monitoring and evaluation.
[12:3:8] # NOT a function
[12:3:9] - **Allocating central funds to States** / **finalising financial resource allocation** – that was the Planning Commission's role (now Finance Ministry / Finance Commission).
[12:3:10] > Assertion-Reason (APPSC G2 Mains 2025): A (non-constitutional advisory body) and R (village-level plans aggregated upwards) are **both true, but R does not explain A**.
[12:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 03 p.8-10; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #24 p.34 (cooperative federalism + bottom-up); NITI Aayog Cabinet Resolution 1 Jan 2015; app notes 3:12 sub 3

  [12:4:0.1] Atal Innovation Mission | 2016, NITI flagship; AIM 2.0 (2024) Rs 2,750 crore to March 2028; fills ecosystem gaps, scales innovations
  [12:4:0.2] NILERD | Autonomous institute; formerly IAMR

  [12:4:0.4] State Support Mission / SETU | State transformation units – Assam SITA, Maharashtra MITRA; SETU Steering Committee chaired by the CEO
[12:4:1] - NITI also runs the **Aspirational Districts Programme** and the **SDG India Index**.

## SUB 5 | Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog
[12:5:0] TABLE head: Aspect | Planning Commission | NITI Aayog
  [12:5:0.0] Set up | 15 March 1950, Cabinet resolution; first chairman Nehru | 1 January 2015, Cabinet resolution
  [12:5:0.1] Status | Non-constitutional, non-statutory | Same
  [12:5:0.2] Funds | Allocated plan funds and grants to States | No fund-allocation power
  [12:5:0.3] Approach | Top-down, one-size-fits-all | Bottom-up, cooperative federalism
  [12:5:0.4] States' role | NDC and annual plan talks | Every CM on the Governing Council
  [12:5:0.5] Members | Up to 8 full-time; no part-time | Full-time + up to 2 part-time
  [12:5:0.6] Top officials | Deputy Chairman + Member-Secretary | Vice-Chairperson + CEO
[12:5:1] - Constituted in **1950** (not 1947 or 1955); its plans went to the **NDC** for approval.
[12:5:2] - Statement traps: Finance Commission is **constitutional** (Art. 280), not "non-statutory"; Planning Commission was **not statutory**; **RBI nationalised 1 January 1949** (not 26 Jan 1949) – so "none of the above" is correct.

## SUB 6 | Andhra Pradesh and NITI Aayog
[12:6:0] - AP sought NITI's help for its own policy body: **State Institution for Transformation** (2023, State Support Mission).
[12:6:1] - **Swarna Andhra @2047** presented by CM **N. Chandrababu Naidu** at the **11th Governing Council** (11 June 2026).
[12:6:2] - **Visakhapatnam Economic Region** plan made with NITI under the **City and Regional Growth Hubs (G-HUB)** initiative – one of **four** pilot cities; USD **750-800 billion** economy by 2047.
[12:6:3] - **NITI Aayog** built, with the AP government, a **dashboard for real-time monitoring of district progress** (Aspirational Districts).
[12:6:4] ~~ Sources: APPSC EO Grade-III 2023 paper; Praveen CA360 Jun 2026; app notes 3:12 sub 8

  Through what was the Planning Commission set up on 15 March 1950, and who was its first chairman?

=== NOTES 3:14 | Economic Growth vs Economic Development; Measures of Development
## SUB 0 | Growth vs Development – Concepts and the New View
[14:0:0] TABLE head: Basis | Economic growth | Economic development
  [14:0:0.0] Meaning | Rise in real output / income (GDP, GNP, per capita income) | Growth plus better quality of life – health, education, nutrition, less poverty, unemployment, inequality
  [14:0:0.1] Nature | Quantitative; value-neutral (can be negative) | Qualitative + quantitative; normative
  [14:0:0.2] Scope | Narrow | Wider – includes growth
  [14:0:0.3] Relation | Necessary but not sufficient | The end; needs conscious public policy
[14:0:1] - Growth can be measured; development is a **policy intervention endeavour aimed at the economic and social well-being of people** – the definition asked by APPSC is **economic development** (not "sustainable growth").
[14:0:2] - Rise in absolute and per capita real GNP is **not** higher development if **poverty and unemployment increase** (UPSC 2018).
[14:0:3] - **Best / most appropriate measure of growth:** growth of **per capita real income** year to year – not national income at current prices (inflation, population), not GDP/NDP/NNP totals.
[14:0:4] - **Western (modernisation) model** (Rostow): key factor = **economic growth** (industrialisation, GDP).
[14:0:5] - **New view** (1970s): **Dudley Seers**, *The Meaning of Development* (**1969**) – development = falling **poverty, unemployment and inequality**; it does **not** stress the **simple growth rate**. Its key part: **eradication of poverty**.
[14:0:6] - **Trickle-down theory:** benefits of growth **percolate down** to the poor automatically (early Plans).
[14:0:7] - **UNDP HDR 1996:** five bad growths – **jobless, ruthless, voiceless, rootless, futureless**.
[14:0:8] - **Social development** = comprehensive change – economic, political, social and cultural.
[14:0:9] - **Negative economic development** (development going backward) is called **regression**; falling output itself is a **recession** / negative growth.
[14:0:10] - Economic welfare is linked to trickle-down benefits, sustainable development and reduced inequality – **not** to larger imports of consumption goods.
[14:0:11] - Development planning breaks obstacles to raise **income and employment**.
[14:0:12] - A-R asked: "development = improving living standards and welfare" (A) and "per capita income growth is not a sufficient measure" (R) – both true, **R explains A**.
[14:0:13] - **Other models:** **Gandhian** – decentralisation and village industry; **Directive Principles** – adequate livelihood and less inequality, not just higher national income; **capability approach** – broader than GDP.
[14:0:14] - **Indicators of development:** institutional change, inclusive growth, human resource development, rising capital formation and **structural transformation** (shift from agriculture to industry and services; best sign: rising share of **manufactured goods in exports**). A **larger GDP share from the primary sector** is NOT an indicator.
[14:0:15] > Kerala model: high human development at modest per capita income – a State with a lower income rank can do better in human development.
[14:0:16] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.2 p.2.2-2.4 (growth, development, Seers 1969); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.37 (growth = quantitative rise); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #69 p.100; Wikipedia "Economic development" (policy intervention definition); app notes 3:14 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Amartya Sen and Development Economists
[14:1:0] TABLE head: Fact | Detail
  [14:1:0.0] Nobel | 1998, Economic Sciences – welfare economics and social choice; first Indian economics laureate (only Indian-born winner until Abhijit Banerjee, 2019)
  [14:1:0.1] Approach | Capability approach (1980s); poverty as entitlement failure (famines)
  [14:1:0.2] Coined | "Missing women" (1990)
  [14:1:0.3] Books | *Development as Freedom*; *The Argumentative Indian* (essays on Indian history, culture, identity); *Inequality Reexamined*
  [14:1:0.4] Advice for India | Planning should attend to people rather than commodities; priority to primary education and health; people-oriented growth, security for the poorest, safeguards on integration with the world economy
  [14:1:0.5] LSE | Amartya Sen Chair in Inequality Studies set up at the LSE
[14:1:1] - **Mahbub ul Haq** built the human development approach and HDI on Sen's capability ideas.
[14:1:2] - **Bina Agarwal**: **Leontief Prize** (Tufts GDAE) for gender, land rights and environment – shared with Daniel Kahneman; announced 2009, presented **2010** (books say "Leontief Award 2009").
[14:1:3] - **Manmohan Singh**: *India's Export Trends and Prospects for Self-Sustained Growth* (**1964**, his Oxford DPhil thesis).
[14:1:4] TABLE head: Nobel in Economics | Laureates / area
  [14:1:4.0] First, 1969 | Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen (Samuelson 1970)
  [14:1:4.1] 1971 | Simon Kuznets
  [14:1:4.2] 1997 | Merton and Scholes – financial economics (option pricing)
  [14:1:4.3] 1998 | Amartya Sen
[14:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #36 p.53, #67 p.96-97 (Sen, Haq, Bina Agarwal); nobelprize.org (1969, 1997, 1998 prizes); bu.edu/eci Leontief Prize recipients 2010; lse.ac.uk (Amartya Sen Chair); app notes 3:14 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Determinants of Growth – Economic and Non-economic Factors
[14:2:0] TABLE head: Economic factors | Non-economic factors
  [14:2:0.0] Capital formation, savings, investment, natural resources, technical progress, foreign exchange / foreign trade, marketable agricultural surplus | Human resources, social organisation / social behaviour, institutions, political stability, corruption, rule of law
[14:2:1] - **Capital formation** = the factor that **necessarily** brings growth in a country (UPSC 2013); Planning Commission: the most important factor.
[14:2:2] - Capital formation depends on **savings** and effective **financial institutions**; **investment** is its essential factor – both statements true.
[14:2:3] - **Saving is one of the determinants** of growth – not the only or the major one.
[14:2:4] - "Not a major factor of growth": **technocrats and bureaucrats**; "not a non-economic factor": **market surplus in agriculture**.
[14:2:5] - Population and development affect **each other** (both directions true).
[14:2:6] - **Steel plough replacing a wooden one** = **capital-augmenting** technical progress (better tool, UPSC 2015).
[14:2:7] - **Resource curse / paradox of plenty**: resource-rich countries showing less growth, less democracy and less development.
[14:2:8] - Capital formation may fail to raise output when capital is idle or misused, complementary inputs (skills, infrastructure) are missing or demand is weak – **all of these**.
[14:2:9] - Workers moving out of agriculture raise productivity; **social overhead capital** and **human resource development** are part of development.
[14:2:10] - **Harrod-Domar**: saving (investment-income) ratio ÷ capital-output ratio = growth rate of **national income**; higher ICOR = lower growth.
[14:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.50 (capital formation in X); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #68 p.98 (capital-output ratio); pmfias.com PYQ 2015 (steel plough); app notes 3:14 sub 7
## SUB 3 | Theories of Development and Books
[14:3:0] TABLE head: Theory / idea | Economist
  [14:3:0.0] Vicious circle of poverty – "a country is poor because it is poor" | Ragnar Nurkse – *Problems of Capital Formation in Underdeveloped Countries* (1953)
  [14:3:0.1] Balanced growth | Nurkse (with Rosenstein-Rodan)
  [14:3:0.2] Big push – large simultaneous investment in industry | Paul Rosenstein-Rodan (1943)
  [14:3:0.3] Unbalanced growth | A.O. Hirschman – *The Strategy of Economic Development* (1958)
  [14:3:0.4] Critical minimum effort | Harvey Leibenstein
  [14:3:0.5] Unlimited supplies of labour (dual economy) | W. Arthur Lewis (1954)
  [14:3:0.6] Stages of growth | W.W. Rostow
  [14:3:0.7] Cumulative causation | Gunnar Myrdal – *Economic Theory and Underdeveloped Regions* (1957)
  [14:3:0.8] Strategic Factors in Economic Development | Charles P. Kindleberger
  [14:3:0.9] Basic needs / welfare approach | ILO (1976) and Paul Streeten / Pigou
[14:3:1] - **Rostow's stages:** traditional society → pre-conditions → **take-off** → drive to maturity → high mass consumption.
[14:3:2] - **Criticisms of Rostow** – data contradict the take-off thesis, no explanation of growth after take-off, stages hard to test empirically: **all of the above**.
[14:3:3] - ***The Limits to Growth*** (1972, **Donella Meadows** and colleagues, Club of Rome): interactions of **population, resources and pollution** would limit growth (the geometric-ratio idea is Malthus).
[14:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #36 p.53, #67 p.96 (Nurkse); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 (vicious circle argument); app notes 3:14 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Measures of Development – Per Capita Income, PQLI, HDI, GNH
[14:4:0] TABLE head: Measure | Developer / year | Components
  [14:4:0.0] Per capita income | Simon Kuznets, US, 1934 (Nobel 1971) | Income only – oldest; hides distribution
  [14:4:0.1] PQLI | Morris D. Morris, Overseas Development Council, mid-1970s (book 1979) | Literacy, infant mortality, life expectancy at age one; 0-100 – no income
  [14:4:0.2] HDI | UNDP, 1990; Mahbub ul Haq (with Sen, Inge Kaul) | Life expectancy at birth, education, GNI per capita (PPP); 0 to 1
  [14:4:0.3] MPI | OPHI + UNDP, 2010 | Health, education, living standards
  [14:4:0.4] BNI | Economic Survey | Water, sanitation, housing
  [14:4:0.5] GNH | Bhutan, 4th King Jigme Singye Wangchuck, 1970s | Alternative to GDP
  [14:4:0.6] MEW / NEW | Nordhaus-Tobin (1972) / Paul Samuelson | Welfare-adjusted income
[14:4:1] - **Order of introduction:** per capita income → **PQLI** → **HDI** (→ MPI).
[14:4:2] - "Most suitable estimate of physical quality of life": **infant mortality rate and literacy**.
[14:4:3] - Basic indices of quality of life in developing countries: **real income, health and educational attainment** (the HDI trio).
[14:4:4] - First State to publish a Human Development Report: **Madhya Pradesh**.
[14:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.38 (PQLI Morris 1979; HDI team Haq and Kaul); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #52 p.77 (index table), #69 p.100; Ramesh Singh ch.2 p.2.4-2.6 (GNH Bhutan); app notes 3:14 sub 4

=== NOTES 3:15 | Distributive Justice and Inclusive Growth
## SUB 0 | Inclusive Growth in the Five Year Plans – 11th and 12th
[15:0:0] TABLE head: Plan | Period | Theme / objective
  [15:0:0.0] 9th | 1997–2002 | Growth with social justice and equality
  [15:0:0.1] 10th | 2002–07 | Faster growth with development
  [15:0:0.2] 11th | 1 Apr 2007 – 31 Mar 2012 | "Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth" – the approach paper's theme; first Plan to make inclusive growth its core objective
  [15:0:0.3] 12th | 2012–17 | "Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth" – adds the sustainable focus; the last Five Year Plan
[15:0:1] - Questions that say "inclusive growth" alone → **11th Plan**; "sustainable growth" or the three-word theme → **12th Plan**. "Growth with social justice" is the 9th Plan, not the 11th.
[15:0:2] - Short forms used in options all mean the 12th Plan theme: "faster sustainable inclusive growth", "faster, sustainable and more inclusive growth"; a "theme = faster growth + more inclusive growth + sustainable growth" question → **all of these**.
[15:0:3] - **11th Plan inclusive-growth components** (NextGen): **agricultural growth; employment generation and poverty reduction; reduction of regional and other disparities; equitable growth** – plus 27 monitorable national targets (income and poverty, education, health, women and children, infrastructure, environment). **Strengthening the capital market** and "exclusive dependence on urban services" are **not** components.
[15:0:4] - **12th Plan aims:** cut poverty, improve regional equality, better living conditions of SC/ST/OBC/minorities; it **emphasised inclusive growth** (not corporate, competitive or cooperative growth).
[15:0:5] - The basic, constant goal of all Indian Plans: **growth** (with self-reliance, employment, equity) – not curbing private enterprise or communes.
[15:0:6] - **Plan era ended 31 March 2017** (Planning Commission replaced by **NITI Aayog**, 1 Jan 2015); a 2012 question "which Plan are we in?" = **12th Plan** – now there is no Five Year Plan.
[15:0:7] > Repeat angle: 20 PYQs (APPSC, UPSC 2010/2014, NDA 2016, UPPSC, UKPSC, RAS) ask only "which theme belongs to which Plan".
[15:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 02 p.6-8 (11th Plan, 27 targets), 03 p.4 (components); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #22 p.32 (Plan themes); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.37; app notes 3:15 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Inclusive Growth – Meaning, Requirements and Inclusive Governance
[15:1:0] - **Inclusive growth** = **broad-based, shared and pro-poor** growth: growth that advances **equitable opportunities** for all economic participants, with benefits reaching **every section** of society; it raises people's **participation** in the growth process.
[15:1:1] - It looks at both the **pace and the pattern** of growth (who benefits), plus gender and regional balance.
[15:1:2] - **Three pillars** of India's model: **Market Economics, Empowerment, Pragmatism** (APPSC-GS 2025) – not "Antyodaya, Empowerment, Poverty and Unemployment".
[15:1:3] TABLE head: Requirement | Role (Rocket #70)
  [15:1:3.0] Infrastructure development | Expands access and economic opportunities
  [15:1:3.1] Agricultural revival | Benefits the rural population
  [15:1:3.2] Education, vocational training | Improves capabilities – the answer for "underutilised and unskilled manpower"
  [15:1:3.3] Health, social services | Improves human capital
  [15:1:3.4] Employment, credit to farmers | Enables participation and productive activity
  [15:1:3.5] SHGs | Financial / economic participation (bottom-up)
  [15:1:3.6] MSMEs | Employment and entrepreneurship
  [15:1:3.7] Right to Education | Brings disadvantaged children into the mainstream
[15:1:4] - Inclusive growth "would necessitate" infrastructure, agricultural revival and social services → **all of the above**; SHGs, MSMEs and the RTE Act all further it → **1, 2 and 3** (UPSC 2011).
[15:1:5] - Inclusive growth is **NOT** expected to come from a **high national-income growth rate by itself**; it comes from rural development, agriculture and adequate farm credit. Focusing solely on urban areas, raising import tariffs or cutting social spending do not help.
[15:1:6] - Target segments: marginal farmers, landless labourers, SC/ST – **not** semi-urban persons alone (UPPSC 2016).
[15:1:7] - **Inclusive governance** (UPSC 2012): **District Planning Committees** in all districts, **more public-health spending**, **stronger Mid-day Meal** → **2, 3 and 4**; permitting NBFCs to do banking is **not** part of it.
[15:1:8] - **OECD (with the G20):** "Promoting Strong, Sustainable and Inclusive Growth" – the OECD's publication / theme for G20 policy coordination.
[15:1:9] - Instruments in numbers: **DAY-NRLM** 10.05 crore women in **90.09 lakh** SHGs; **MSMEs** 31.1% of GDP, 35.4% of manufacturing output, **48.58%** of exports; **VB-G RAM G** replaced MGNREGA, **100 → 125 days**; **Aspirational Districts** (Jan 2018, 49 KPIs, 5 themes), **Aspirational Blocks** (Jan 2023, 500 blocks).
[15:1:10] - **AP:** Navaratnalu (2019–24: Amma Vodi, YSR Rythu Bharosa) → **Super Six**: **Talliki Vandanam** ₹15,000 per school child; **Annadata Sukhibhava** ₹20,000 per farmer; **Deepam-2** 3 free LPG cylinders; **Stree Shakti** free bus travel for women (15 Aug 2025); AP Rural Inclusive Growth Project (five components).
[15:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.37 (broad-based, shared, pro-poor); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #70 p.101 (requirements; inclusive governance); UPSC CSE 2011/2012 papers; app notes 3:15 sub 0, 5
[15:1:12] - **Inclusive governance** = governance and service delivery with **equal access to government facilities, participation and inclusion**, and public health, **planning and welfare services**.
## SUB 2 | Distributive Justice – Constitution and Socialism
[15:2:0] TABLE head: Article | Provision
  [15:2:0.0] 38 | Social order with social, economic and political justice; 38(2) (44th Amendment, 1978): minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities
  [15:2:0.1] 39(b) | Ownership and control of the material resources of the community distributed to subserve the common good
  [15:2:0.2] 39(c) | Operation of the economic system must not result in concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment
  [15:2:0.3] 31C | 25th Amendment, 1971: protects laws giving effect to 39(b) and 39(c)
[15:2:1] - **Socialism** aims at **distributive justice** – fair distribution of income, wealth and resources; both statements of 39(b) and 39(c) are **present** in the Constitution (DPSP, Part IV).
[15:2:2] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Directive Principles (Art. 38, 39, 31C); app notes 3:15 sub 1
## SUB 3 | Approaches to Poverty and the Bhagwati–Sen Debate
[15:3:0] TABLE head: Approach | Illustration
  [15:3:0.0] Trickle-down | Part of the income of the asset-owning class filters down to the assetless; early Plans' growth-first strategy (criticised: widens inequality)
  [15:3:0.1] Direct attack | 5th Plan "Garibi Hatao"; wage-employment and livelihood missions
  [15:3:0.2] Welfare | Nordic states
  [15:3:0.3] Bottom-up | SHG movement
[15:3:1] - **Bhagwati–Sen debate** – growth first vs social infrastructure first:
[15:3:2] TABLE head:  | Jagdish Bhagwati (with Arvind Panagariya) | Amartya Sen (with Jean Drèze)
  [15:3:2.0] Priority | Economic growth first – rapid market-led growth creates jobs and revenue for welfare | Investment in social infrastructure first – health, education, nutrition
  [15:3:2.1] Book (2013) | *Why Growth Matters* | *An Uncertain Glory*
[15:3:3] - The debate (APPSC G1 2017) is **growth first vs social infrastructure first** – not industry vs agriculture, rural vs urban or private vs public investment.
[15:3:4] - Sen: backward countries should give top priority to **primary education and health** (APPSC-GS 2007).
[15:3:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.2 (trickle-down); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #36; app notes 3:15 sub 2-3
[15:3:6] - *An Uncertain Glory* (2013) was co-written by **Amartya Sen and Jean Drèze**.
## SUB 4 | Measuring Inclusion – WEF Inclusive Development Index and Poverty Data
[15:4:0] - **WEF Inclusive Development Index (IDI)** – pillars: **growth and development; inclusion; intergenerational equity and sustainability**.
[15:4:1] TABLE head: Edition | Top (developing / emerging) | India
  [15:4:1.0] IDI 2017 (16 Jan 2017, Davos) | Lithuania (then Azerbaijan, Hungary) | 60th of 79 developing economies
  [15:4:1.1] IDI 2018 (Jan 2018) | Lithuania | 62nd of 74 emerging economies
[15:4:2] - Inclusion is measured by **HDI**, poverty rates, literacy, access to basic services and gender equality – not by GDP, industrial output or employment alone.
[15:4:3] - **World Bank:** extreme poverty ($3/day) **27.1% (2011-12) → 5.3% (2022-23)**; at $4.20 a day 57.7% → **23.9%**. World Inequality Database: income inequality **rising**.
[15:4:4] ~~ Sources: WEF Inclusive Growth and Development Report 2017 (Deccan Herald, GKToday 16 Jan 2017); WEF IDI 2018; World Bank Poverty & Equity Brief India (2025); app notes 3:15 sub 6

=== NOTES 3:16 | Human Development Index – Components, Methodology, India's Rank and Trend
## SUB 0 | Human Development and the HDR – Origin, UNDP, Concept and Pillars
[16:0:0] - **UNDP** was the first to focus on the **human aspect of development**: first **Human Development Report (HDR), 1990**, which contained the first **HDI**; HDRs released most years since.
[16:0:1] - The HDR **compares countries on educational levels, health status and per capita income** ("Human Development Report" – not a population, education or quality report).
[16:0:2] - **Mahbub ul Haq** introduced the concept and **created the HDI (1990)**; **Amartya Sen** worked with him on the first HDRs (team incl. Inge Kaul, Paul Streeten, Frances Stewart). Sen = **capability approach**; **Martha Nussbaum** extended it with a list of central capabilities.
[16:0:3] - Human development = enlarging people's **choices, freedoms and opportunities**; people, not growth alone, are the criteria; income is a **means**, not the end.
[16:0:4] - **Four pillars of human development:** **Equity, Sustainability, Productivity, Empowerment** (CDS 2020) – not "inclusion" or "gender".
[16:0:5] TABLE head: Approach to human development | Idea
  [16:0:5.0] Income | Higher income = higher human development (oldest)
  [16:0:5.1] Welfare | People as passive beneficiaries of welfare spending
  [16:0:5.2] Minimum / basic needs (ILO) | Health, education, food, water, sanitation, housing – India's Minimum Needs Programme (5th Plan) = investment in human (resources) approach
  [16:0:5.3] Capabilities | Amartya Sen
[16:0:6] - **HDR 2016** ("Human Development for Everyone"): **universalism** is the key to human development.
[16:0:7] - UNDP identifies two categories of poverty: **income poverty** and **human poverty** – both.
[16:0:8] - **Same GNI, different HDI** shows the role of **national policy choices** (Malaysia richer than Chile, but Chile ~7 years more life expectancy and 3 more years of expected schooling).
[16:0:9] TABLE head: Basis | GDP / per capita income | Human development
  [16:0:9.0] Nature | Primarily economic measure | Broader, people-centred
  [16:0:9.1] Dimensions | One-dimensional | Multidimensional
[16:0:10] - **Countries covered:** HDR 2018 update **189**; HDR 2021/22 191; HDR 2023-24 and 2025 **193**.
[16:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 15 p.1-6 (concept, Haq and Sen, four pillars, approaches, policy choices); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #4 p.5, #53 p.79; UNDP HDR 2016 and 2018 Statistical Update (hdr.undp.org); app notes 3:16 sub 0
## SUB 1 | HDI Dimensions, Indicators and Methodology
[16:1:0] TABLE head: Dimension | Indicator | Min | Max
  [16:1:0.0] Long and healthy life | Life expectancy at birth | 20 | 85
  [16:1:0.1] Knowledge | Expected years of schooling | 0 | 18
  [16:1:0.2] Knowledge | Mean years of schooling (adults 25+) | 0 | 15
  [16:1:0.3] Decent standard of living | GNI per capita (PPP $), log | $100 | $75,000
[16:1:1] - HDI = composite of **life expectancy, educational attainment and per capita income**; base = **health, education, standard of living**. Before 2010 the income indicator was per capita **GDP**.
[16:1:2] - **NOT in the HDI:** **ownership of basic assets**, **access to banking**, **employment**, poverty, nutritional status, quality of life, environment, urbanisation, human security, gender, inequality (that is the **IHDI**).
[16:1:3] - Method: dimension index = (actual − min)/(max − min); education index = **arithmetic mean** of its two sub-indices; income uses the **logarithm** (diminishing returns); **HDI = geometric mean** of the three indices (**since 2010**), equal weights.
[16:1:4] - **PPP dollars** allow fair comparison across price levels.
[16:1:5] TABLE head: Category | HDI value
  [16:1:5.0] Very high | 0.800 and above
  [16:1:5.1] High | 0.700–0.799
  [16:1:5.2] Medium | 0.550–0.699
  [16:1:5.3] Low | below 0.550
[16:1:6] - India **0.685** (HDR 2025, for 2023) = **Medium**, just below 0.700.
[16:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 15 p.6-9 (indicators, goalposts, groupings), 16 p.1 (geometric mean since 2010); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #52 p.77; UNDP HDR 2025 Technical notes; app notes 3:16 sub 1-3
## SUB 2 | India's HDI Rank by Edition
[16:2:0] TABLE head: Report (released) | India's rank | HDI value
  [16:2:0.0] HDR 2010 | 119th of 169 | –
  [16:2:0.1] HDR 2011 (Nov 2011) | 134th of 187 (slipped from 119) | 0.547
  [16:2:0.2] HDR 2014 (July 2014) | 135th of 187 | 0.586
  [16:2:0.3] HDR 2015 (Dec 2015) | 130th of 188; lowest among BRICS | 0.609
  [16:2:0.4] HDR 2018 update | 130th of 189 | 0.640
  [16:2:0.5] HDR 2019 (9 Dec 2019, HDI 2018) | 129th of 189 | 0.647
  [16:2:0.6] HDR 2020 (HDI 2019) | 131st of 189 | 0.645
  [16:2:0.7] HDR 2021/22 (Sept 2022, HDI 2021) | 132nd of 191 – slipped from 130 (2020 value) | 0.633
  [16:2:0.8] HDR 2023-24 (Mar 2024, HDI 2022) | 134th of 193 | 0.644
  [16:2:0.9] HDR 2025 (6 May 2025, HDI 2023) | 130th of 193 | 0.685
[16:2:1] - "India's HDI rank in 2019" in exams of 2020 = **129** (HDR released Dec 2019); the HDR 2020 later gave 131 for HDI 2019.
[16:2:2] - HDR 2025 recalculated India's 2022 value as 0.676 (rank 133). Inequality cuts India's HDI by **30.7%**. No newer HDR had been released as of Nov 2026.
[16:2:3] - **HDI trend 1990–2017:** 0.427 → 0.640 (nearly **50%** rise, HDR 2018 update).
[16:2:4] - HDR 2025: Sri Lanka and Maldives above India; Bangladesh tied at 130; India **lowest among the five original BRICS**.
[16:2:5] ~~ Sources: UNDP HDR 2011, 2014, 2015, 2019, 2021/22, 2023-24, 2025 (hdr.undp.org; UNDP India press release 6 May 2025; Business Standard 14 Dec 2015 – 130 of 188); app notes 3:16 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Country Comparisons and HDR Themes
[16:3:0] TABLE head: Report | Top / theme
  [16:3:0.0] HDR 2004 | "Cultural Liberty in Today's Diverse World"
  [16:3:0.1] HDR 2016 | "Human Development for Everyone" – universalism
  [16:3:0.2] HDR 2018 update | Norway 1st
  [16:3:0.3] HDR 2021/22 | "Uncertain Times, Unsettled Lives"; Switzerland 1st; Hong Kong 4th > Australia 5th > Japan 19th > Russia 52nd
  [16:3:0.4] HDR 2023-24 | "Breaking the Gridlock"; Switzerland (0.967)
  [16:3:0.5] HDR 2025 | "A Matter of Choice: People and Possibilities in the Age of AI"; Iceland (0.972) 1st, South Sudan last
[16:3:1] - **HDI 2019 (HDR 2020) ranks:** Brazil 84, China 85, South Africa 114, India 131 → ascending order of rank **Brazil, China, South Africa, India**.
[16:3:2] - India has the **lowest GDP per capita** compared with China, Indonesia and Sri Lanka.
[16:3:3] - Best human development among Asian options (UPSC 2000 table): **South Korea** (life expectancy 71.7, adult literacy 98%).
[16:3:4] ~~ Sources: UNDP HDR 2004, 2018, 2020, 2021/22, 2023-24, 2025 (hdr.undp.org); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.2 p.2.9 (HDR 2004); app notes 3:16 sub 4-5
## SUB 4 | Human Development in Indian States – NHDR and State HDRs
[16:4:0] TABLE head: Report | Year | Fact
  [16:4:0.0] First State HDR | 1995 | Madhya Pradesh; released by Amartya Sen in Delhi; HDI for the State and all districts
  [16:4:0.1] First NHDR | April 2001 | Planning Commission; Kerala top, Punjab 2nd, UP 13th, Bihar 15th (descending: Kerala, Punjab, UP, Bihar)
  [16:4:0.2] Second NHDR (India Human Development Report) | 2011 | Planning Commission / IAMR; Kerala 1st
  [16:4:0.3] First AP HDR | 2007 (released 2008) | CESS, Hyderabad; sponsored by Planning Commission + UNDP
[16:4:1] - The Indian Human Development Report gives, for each sample village, **education, health and infrastructure-and-amenities** indices – **no unemployment index**.
[16:4:2] - **Kerala** consistently tops ("Kerala Model"); Bihar, UP, MP at the bottom (Bihar 0.650 vs India 0.685, 2023).
[16:4:3] - **HDI and SDG ranking** of States are **positively related** because SDG targets rest largely on **education and health** (UPPSC 2019: A and R true, R explains A).
[16:4:4] ~~ Sources: Planning Commission NHDR 2001 (planningcommission.nic.in); UNDP India, MP HDR 1995; app notes 3:16 sub 8
[16:4:5] - UNDP's national HDI for India is **0.685**; the sub-national (Global Data Lab) national average is **0.732**.

=== NOTES 3:17 | Related Undp Indices – Ihdi, Gii, Gdi, Mpi
## SUB 0 | Timeline of the UNDP Indices
[17:0:0] TABLE head: Index | Introduced | Note
  [17:0:0.0] HDI | HDR 1990 | Health, education, income
  [17:0:0.1] GDI (Gender-related Development Index) and GEM (Gender Empowerment Measure) | HDR 1995 | Gender inequalities in HDI achievements / in empowerment
  [17:0:0.2] Capability Poverty Measure (CPM) | HDR 1996 | Lack of three basic capabilities
  [17:0:0.3] Human Poverty Index (HPI) | HDR 1997 | Deprivation; HPI-1 developing, HPI-2 developed countries
  [17:0:0.4] MPI, GII, IHDI | HDR 2010 | MPI replaced HPI; GII replaced GDI/GEM as the gender-inequality measure
  [17:0:0.5] PHDI | HDR 2020 | HDI adjusted for planetary pressures
  [17:0:0.6] Gender Social Norms Index | 5 March 2020 (first) | UNDP; social beliefs blocking gender equality
[17:0:1] - Order: 1995 GDI/GEM → 1996 CPM → 1997 HPI → 2010 MPI/GII/IHDI → 2020 PHDI and GSNI.
[17:0:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.36 (GDI and GEM 1995); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 16 p.4-6; UNDP HDR 1997, 2010 (hdr.undp.org); UNDP GSNI 2020 press release; app notes 3:17 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Human Poverty Index, Capability Poverty Measure and Income vs Human Poverty
[17:1:0] - UNDP's two categories of poverty: **income poverty** and **human poverty** – both.
[17:1:1] - **HPI** measures deprivation in **longevity, knowledge and a decent standard of living** (APPSC-GS 2018 key: it indicates the **standard of living**).
[17:1:2]   - HPI-1 (developing): survival to 40, adult illiteracy, no safe water, underweight children (**social services**).
[17:1:3]   - HPI-2 (developed) adds **income poverty** and **long-term unemployment** (social exclusion) → income, literacy, social-services and employment deprivations are **all** covered (CDS 2013).
[17:1:4] - **CPM (HDR 1996)** indicators: **children under 5 underweight** (child malnutrition), **births unattended** by trained personnel, **female illiteracy** – not male illiteracy, male labour-force participation or drinking water.
[17:1:5] ~~ Sources: UNDP HDR 1996 (CPM) and HDR 1997 / 2009 technical notes (HPI-1, HPI-2) (hdr.undp.org); app notes 3:17 sub 1-2
## SUB 2 | Gender Indices – GDI, GEM and GII
[17:2:0] TABLE head: Index | Dimensions / indicators | Reading
  [17:2:0.0] GDI | Female vs male health (life expectancy), knowledge (schooling), living standard (earned income) | Ratio female HDI / male HDI; 1 = parity, below 1 = women behind; India 0.874 (HDR 2025, Group 5)
  [17:2:0.1] GEM (1995) | Political participation (parliament seats), economic participation (managers, professionals), power over economic resources (earned income) | Empowerment – no health or education indicator
  [17:2:0.2] GII (2010) | Reproductive health (MMR, adolescent birth rate); empowerment (parliament seats, secondary education 25+); labour market (LFPR 15+) | 0 = equality, higher = more inequality
[17:2:1] - **GDI and GEM indicate inequalities in gender** (not income, expenditure or regions).
[17:2:2] - The GDI does **not** cover **gender violence**.
[17:2:3] - **India's GII:** **108th** (HDR 2023-24, for 2022; value 0.437) → **102nd**, 0.403 (HDR 2025, for 2023).
[17:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 16 p.4, p.6-7 (GDI, GII); UNDP HDR 1995 (GEM); UNDP HDR 2023-24 and 2025 tables 4-5 (hdr.undp.org); app notes 3:17 sub 3
## SUB 3 | IHDI, PHDI and Beyond-HDI Statements
[17:3:0] - **IHDI** discounts each HDI dimension for inequality: **no inequality → IHDI = HDI**; otherwise IHDI < HDI. HDI = "potential", IHDI = "actual"; **HDI − IHDI = loss due to inequality** – that loss is **not** part of the HDI itself.
[17:3:1] - **PHDI** (2020) adjusts HDI for **CO2 emissions and material footprint**; it captures **intergenerational** inequality just as the IHDI captures **intragenerational** inequality.
[17:3:2] - **HDR 2021/22**: a **new uncertainty complex** – dangerous planetary change, sweeping societal transformations and **polarisation**.
[17:3:3] - A GDI **below 1** means women's HDI is **lower** than men's (not higher); same GNI with different outcomes shows the role of **policy**, not "growth over development".
[17:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 16 p.2-3 (IHDI); UNDP HDR 2020 (PHDI), HDR 2021/22 overview (uncertainty complex) (hdr.undp.org); app notes 3:16 sub 6
## SUB 4 | MPI – Design and the Global MPI
[17:4:0] - **Global MPI** (2010): **OPHI (Oxford) + UNDP**, presented in HDR 2010; proposed by **Sabina Alkire and Maria Emma Santos**; method **Alkire-Foster**; uses household-survey micro-data; **not** a $1-a-day measure of extreme poverty.
[17:4:1] - **MPI = Headcount ratio (H) × Intensity (A)** – not a sum; MPI-poor = deprived in at least **one-third** of weighted indicators. Most suitable for the **intensity of poverty**.
[17:4:2] TABLE head: Dimension | Global MPI indicators (10) | Weight
  [17:4:2.0] Health | Nutrition, child mortality | 1/6 each
  [17:4:2.1] Education | Years of schooling, school attendance | 1/6 each
  [17:4:2.2] Standard of living | Cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets | 1/18 each
[17:4:3] - **India in the Global MPI** (UNDP-OPHI editions):
[17:4:4] TABLE head: Edition | India
  [17:4:4.0] HDR 2013 | 53.7% multidimensionally poor
  [17:4:4.1] Global MPI 2018 | 271 million out of poverty (2005-06 to 2015-16); Bihar poorest State
  [17:4:4.2] Global MPI 2022 (UNDP + OPHI) | MPI 0.069 (2019-21); headcount 16.4%; about 415 million (books: 414 million) out (2005-06 to 2019-21)
  [17:4:4.3] Global MPI 2023 (released 11 July 2023 by UNDP and OPHI) | Same India data; 415 million out in 15 years
  [17:4:4.4] Global MPI 2024 → 2025 | MPI 0.064 → 0.061
[17:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC Exams 16 p.4-5 (MPI indicators); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Economy #52 p.77; UNDP-OPHI Global MPI 2018, 2022, 2023 reports (hdr.undp.org, ophi.org.uk); app notes 3:17 sub 4, 6
## SUB 5 | National MPI (NITI Aayog), States and Andhra Pradesh
[17:5:0] TABLE head: Feature | National MPI
  [17:5:0.0] By | NITI Aayog (with UNDP, OPHI); baseline Nov 2021; monitored under GIRG
  [17:5:0.1] Method | Alkire-Foster – same as the Global MPI
  [17:5:0.2] Indicators | 12 = 10 global + maternal health + bank account; standard of living has 7 (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account) – years of schooling is an education indicator
[17:5:1] - **Progress Review 2023** (NFHS-4 → NFHS-5): headcount **24.85% → 14.96%**; MPI 0.117 → 0.066; intensity 47% → **44.39%**; about **13.5 crore** out; **rural fell faster** (32.59% → 19.28%) than urban (8.65% → 5.27%).
[17:5:2] - NFHS-5: **J&K 4.80%** and **Himachal 4.93%** both under 6%; UP 22.93%. Lowest MPI: **Kerala 0.002**, Goa 0.003, Tamil Nadu 0.009; highest (2019-21): **Bihar 0.16**, Meghalaya 0.133, Jharkhand 0.131, UP 0.103. **Bihar** had the largest fall in headcount (**51.89% → 33.76%**).
[17:5:3] - NITI Discussion Paper (Jan 2024): 29.17% (2013-14) → 11.28% (2022-23); 24.82 crore out; UP largest fall (5.94 crore).
[17:5:4] - **PM Garib Kalyan Package** (2020) included free foodgrain entitlements (PMGKAY).
[17:5:5] - **Andhra Pradesh:** State MPI report (2018, Planning Dept + OPHI): **41.6% (2005-06) → 21% (2016-17)**; NITI MPI 2023: AP **6.06%** (India 14.96%), MPI **0.053 (2015-16) → 0.025** (2019-21), intensity 41.12%, rural 7.71% / urban 2.20%; AP **9th**; lowest-poverty district **West Godavari 2.42%** (then Guntur 4.36%, Krishna 4.38%, Chittoor 5.66%).
[17:5:6] ~~ Sources: NITI Aayog National MPI Progress Review 2023 and Discussion Paper Jan 2024 (niti.gov.in); OPHI news "Andhra Pradesh releases its first MPI report" (ophi.org.uk); app notes 3:17 sub 5, 7-8
[17:5:7] - World Bank 2022 ($4.20/day) **23.9%** vs NITI MPI 2022-23 **11.28%** – they use **different poverty lines and count poverty differently** (income vs deprivations).

=== NOTES 3:19 | Environmental Degradation As A Development Challenge; Green Accounting and Green Gdp
## SUB 0 | Functions of the Environment, Absorptive and Carrying Capacity
[19:0:0] TABLE head: Function | Meaning
  [19:0:0.0] Supplies resources (first function) | Both renewable (trees, fish – replaced naturally or inexhaustible) and non-renewable (fossil fuels – exhausted with use)
  [19:0:0.1] Assimilates waste | Absorbs and neutralises wastes
  [19:0:0.2] Sustains life | Genetic and biodiversity
  [19:0:0.3] Aesthetic services | Scenery and amenity
[19:0:1] - **Renewable resources** = those that **can be replaced naturally over time or are inexhaustible** – used without the resource becoming depleted.
[19:0:2] - **Absorptive capacity** = ability of the environment to absorb degradation = the **maximum amount of pollutants an ecosystem can process and neutralise without harmful effects**.
[19:0:3] - **Carrying capacity** (NCERT): the environment works without interruption as long as **resource extraction is not above the rate of regeneration** and **wastes are within the assimilating capacity** of the environment.
[19:0:4] - **Crisis**: when **extraction > regeneration** and waste > absorptive capacity, the environment **cannot sustain life** – "we are today at the threshold of environmental crisis".
[19:0:5] - **Recycling** is NOT a function of the environment; "supplies renewable resources only" is wrong.
[19:0:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.52 (functions, renewable resources, absorptive capacity); NCERT Indian Economic Development Class 11 ch.9; app notes 3:19 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Resource Depletion and Causes of Environmental Degradation
[19:1:0] - **Resource depletion** = use faster than regeneration; **overuse of natural resources → resource depletion** (not conservation or sustainability).
[19:1:1] - Best illustration of depletion with long-term impact: **overfishing in a coastal area** harming the whole marine ecosystem and livelihoods. A forest managed **sustainably for timber while keeping biodiversity** is NOT depletion.
[19:1:2] TABLE head: Resource | Cause of depletion
  [19:1:2.0] Groundwater | Deep bore tubewells for irrigation
  [19:1:2.1] Topsoil | Brick production
  [19:1:2.2] Biodiversity habitats | Expansion of agriculture
[19:1:3] - **Causes vs conservation practices:**
[19:1:4] TABLE head: Human-driven causes | NOT causes (conservation)
  [19:1:4.0] Deforestation (primary cause) | Sustainable agriculture
  [19:1:4.1] Chemical-intensive farming | Renewable energy production
  [19:1:4.2] Groundwater over-extraction, dams | Wildlife conservation
  [19:1:4.3] Road and urban expansion, industrial emissions, overfishing | –
[19:1:5] - **Deforestation** is driven by urbanisation, agricultural expansion and timber extraction, and **reduces** biodiversity – "more biodiversity" is false.
[19:1:6] - India's **two threats**: **poverty-induced degradation** + **pollution from affluence** and a rapidly growing industrial sector.
[19:1:7] - Green Revolution: HYV monoculture and chemical fertilisers cut soil fertility; **HYV irrigation needs** depleted the water table. **Urea ≈ 56%** of fertiliser use; low-carbon alternative **green urea** (green hydrogen + captured CO2).
[19:1:8] - India's low EPI score: **urban particulate pollution and coal-based power**.
[19:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.53 (two threats); NCERT Indian Economic Development Class 11 ch.9; app notes 3:19 sub 1-2
## SUB 2 | Green Economy, Green GDP and Green Accounting
[19:2:0] - **Green economy** (UNEP) = **low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive**; reduces environmental risks; focuses on **fostering green industries and creating green jobs**. **Green jobs** preserve or restore environmental quality.
[19:2:1] - **Green GDP** = conventional GDP with the **environmental consequences** of growth factored in = GDP **net of natural-resource depletion and degradation**. The term **Green GNP** emphasises **sustainable development** (not mere growth of GNP or per capita income).
[19:2:2] - **Uttarakhand** = first State to adopt green GDP, as **Gross Environment Product (GEP)**.
[19:2:3] TABLE head: Person / body | Contribution
  [19:2:3.0] Sir Partha Dasgupta | Chaired the Expert Group on Green National Accounts (set up 2011, report 2013)
  [19:2:3.1] Paul Samuelson | NEW (Net Economic Welfare)
  [19:2:3.2] Nordhaus and Tobin | MEW (Measure of Economic Welfare)
  [19:2:3.3] World Bank | Green Index; 2013 cost-of-degradation estimate
  [19:2:3.4] MoSPI | Environment accounts on UN SEEA; EnviStats India (annual)
[19:2:4] - **SEEA** Central Framework adopted by the UN Statistical Commission in **2012**; MoSPI ecosystem accounts since 2018.
[19:2:5] - EnviStats India – six components: conditions and quality; resources and use; **residuals**; **extreme events**; **human settlements and health**; protection and management.
[19:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.38 (green GDP; NEW – Samuelson); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy ch.2 (green GDP, NEW, MEW); PMF Environment 02 (green GDP); MoSPI EnviStats India (mospi.gov.in); app notes 3:19 sub 5-6
## SUB 3 | Environmental Kuznets Curve and the Growth vs Environment Debate
[19:3:0] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [19:3:0.0] X-axis | Per capita income
  [19:3:0.1] Y-axis | Environmental degradation
  [19:3:0.2] Shape | Inverted U – pollution rises at low income, falls after a turning point
  [19:3:0.3] Origin | Simon Kuznets' curve: income vs income inequality; for environment first shown by Grossman and Krueger (1991)
[19:3:1] - **Growth vs environment debate:**
[19:3:2] TABLE head: View | Argument
  [19:3:2.0] Trade-off view | Environmental rules slow growth; "grow first, clean up later"
  [19:3:2.1] Necessity view | Degradation raises health costs and lowers labour efficiency
[19:3:3] - Conventional GDP **ignores depletion** of natural resources, so growth can hide the loss of natural capital.
[19:3:4] ~~ Sources: Grossman and Krueger (1991, NBER); Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy ch.2; app notes 3:19 sub 3-4
## SUB 4 | Cost of Degradation and Land Degradation Data
[19:4:0] - **World Bank (2013)**: India's annual cost of environmental degradation ≈ **5.7% of GDP** (**Rs 3.75 lakh crore**, 2009) – through higher **healthcare spending** and lower **labour productivity**.
[19:4:1] - Global: about one-third of land transformed by humans; **60%+ of rivers** dammed or diverted; about **40%** of land degraded.
[19:4:2] TABLE head: ISRO-SAC Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (2021) | Degraded area
  [19:4:2.0] 2003-05 | 94.53 Mha (28.76%)
  [19:4:2.1] 2011-13 | 96.40 Mha (29.32%)
  [19:4:2.2] 2018-19 | 97.85 Mha (29.77%)
[19:4:3] - Leading process: **water erosion (10.98%)**, then vegetation degradation (8.91%); desertification rose in **28 of 31** States/UTs.
[19:4:4] - **21.76 Mha** restored in 2011-2020; **Telangana first (4.18 Mha)**. Most desertification-vulnerable AP districts: **Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa**.
[19:4:5] ~~ Sources: World Bank, India: Diagnostic Assessment of Select Environmental Challenges (2013); ISRO-SAC Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas of India 2021 (sac.gov.in); app notes 3:19 sub 8
## SUB 5 | Policy Tools – EIA, Green Credit and AP Zoning
[19:5:0] TABLE head: Tool | Year | Provision
  [19:5:0.0] EIA | First used 1978 | River valley projects
  [19:5:0.1] EIA Notification | 1994, revised 2006 | Clearance compulsory for 39 project categories
  [19:5:0.2] Green Credit Rules | 2023 | Under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
[19:5:1] - **AP Common Zoning Regulations 2026** – development-restricted: **forests, hills, water bodies, eco-sensitive areas, CRZ**.
[19:5:2] ~~ Sources: MoEFCC EIA Notification 2006 and Green Credit Rules 2023 (moef.gov.in); app notes 3:19 sub 7
