=== NOTES 3:20 | Sustainable Development – Definition, Brundtland Report, Sdgs and India's Progress
## SUB 0 | Meaning and Goals of Sustainable Development
[20:0:0] - **Definition (Brundtland, 1987):** development that **meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**.
[20:0:1] - It is a case of **inter-generational** sensibility in the use of **natural resources**; present use with **minimum degradation** of natural resources = sustainable development; "**saving energy and other resources for the future without sacrificing people's comfort in the present**"; **balancing the need to use resources and conserve them for the future**.
[20:0:2] - **Main goal:** **balanced growth of environment and economy** – not growth only or protection only. Base of sustainable development = **environmental approach**.
[20:0:3] - It matters for the **well-being of human society** because of the definition itself (A-R: both true, R explains A).
[20:0:4] - Intertwined with **carrying capacity** (UPSC 2010) – Earth's finite capacity.
[20:0:5] - **Three pillars / components:** **economic growth, social inclusion, environmental protection** – not "scientific association", political or military.
[20:0:6] TABLE head: Is an objective | NOT an objective
  [20:0:6.0] Meet present needs while keeping choices for the future | Prioritise individual wealth accumulation
  [20:0:6.1] Balance economy, society and environment | Profit maximisation, growth at any cost
  [20:0:6.2] Intergenerational equity | Unrestricted resource exploitation
[20:0:7] - **Green Agenda** = **concern for environment and for the future generations**.
[20:0:8] - Mid-1980s debate on the **negative aspects of development**: degradation of natural resources, pollution, **displacement and rehabilitation** – not "politics and development".
[20:0:9] - Major challenge to SDG 1 (no poverty): **economic inequality and unequal distribution of resources**.
[20:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.53 (definition); PMF Environment 06 p.6 (Brundtland definition); NCERT Indian Economic Development Class 11 ch.9; app notes 3:20 sub 0, 3
## SUB 1 | Milestones – Club of Rome to Rio+20
[20:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Milestone | Key fact
  [20:1:0.0] 1968 (Apr) | Club of Rome founded, Rome | First advocated resource conservation in a systematic way at the international level (NCERT)
  [20:1:0.1] 1972 | "The Limits to Growth" (Club of Rome) | A book on computer simulation of growth with finite resource supplies
  [20:1:0.2] 1972 | Stockholm – UN Conference on the Human Environment | Created UNEP
  [20:1:0.3] 1980 | World Conservation Strategy (IUCN with UNEP and WWF) | Term "sustainable development" first introduced
  [20:1:0.4] 1983 | WCED set up by UNGA | Chair Gro Harlem Brundtland (Prime Minister of Norway)
  [20:1:0.5] 1987 | "Our Common Future" – Brundtland Report | Defined and popularised sustainable development (first clear modern explanation)
  [20:1:0.6] 1992 | UNCED, Rio (Earth Summit) | Rio Declaration, Agenda 21 (signed 1992, not 1995), UNFCCC, CBD
  [20:1:0.7] 2002 | Johannesburg – World Summit on SD (Rio+10) | Johannesburg Declaration
  [20:1:0.8] 2012 | Rio+20 = UN Conference on Sustainable Development | "The Future We Want"; SDGs born
  [20:1:0.9] 2015 | Agenda 2030, 25 Sep 2015 | 17 SDGs
[20:1:1] - The Brundtland Report is **not** "The Limits to Growth"; the term was defined by the **Brundtland Commission**, not WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF or UNDP.
[20:1:2] - **2017** = UN International Year of **Sustainable Tourism for Development**.
[20:1:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.6-8 (Brundtland, Rio, Rio+20); Rocket Sheets Environment (Agenda 21, Rio+20); NCERT Contemporary India II ch.1 (Club of Rome 1968); IUCN World Conservation Strategy 1980; app notes 3:20 sub 1-2
## SUB 2 | MDGs, Agenda 2030 and the 17 SDGs
[20:2:0] - **MDGs:** **8** goals from the **Millennium Summit, September 2000**, New York; period 2000-2015.
[20:2:1] - **SDGs:** **17** goals, **169** targets, **231** unique indicators; adopted **25 Sep 2015** by the UN; 2016-2030.
[20:2:2] TABLE head: Goal | Theme
  [20:2:2.0] 1 | No poverty
  [20:2:2.1] 2 | Zero hunger
  [20:2:2.2] 4 | Quality education – free and compulsory education, school infrastructure and digital transformation
  [20:2:2.3] 5 | Gender equality
  [20:2:2.4] 6 | Clean water and sanitation – water availability and its sustainable management
  [20:2:2.5] 7 | Affordable and clean energy
  [20:2:2.6] 9 | Industry, innovation and infrastructure
  [20:2:2.7] 10 | Reduced inequalities
  [20:2:2.8] 11 | Sustainable cities and communities
  [20:2:2.9] 13 | Climate action – urgent action to combat climate change
  [20:2:2.10] 14 | Life below water
  [20:2:2.11] 15 | Life on land – terrestrial ecosystems
[20:2:3] - Agenda 2030 emphasises **ending all discrimination and violence against women and girls**; principles: universal, leave no one behind, integrated and indivisible.
[20:2:4] - **UN Secretary-General** presents an **annual SDG Progress Report** (global indicator framework); the **Global Sustainable Development Report** is produced **every four years** for the quadrennial review – not every quarter.
[20:2:5] - **National Indicator Framework** for SDGs is developed by **MoSPI**, not NITI Aayog; **Mission LiFE** (**Lifestyle for Environment**, 2021) aims to change individual demand, industry supply and **government and industrial policy** for sustainable consumption and production; SDG 4 "global citizenship" is education for global citizenship – not flexible citizenship rights.
[20:2:6] - **Roots of Agenda 2030:** the **MDGs** + the **Rio+20** outcome; grounded in the **UDHR**, human rights treaties, the Millennium Declaration and the 2005 World Summit Outcome; informed by the **Declaration on the Right to Development**. **Three** of the 8 MDGs were health goals (4, 5, 6) – merged into **SDG 3**.
[20:2:7] - **India's success is critical** for the global SDGs because India has nearly **one-sixth** of the world population (A-R: R explains A).
[20:2:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.8-9 (MDGs, SDGs); Rocket Sheets Environment (SDG numbers); UN Agenda 2030 (sdgs.un.org) and UN SDG Report / GSDR (un.org); MoSPI National Indicator Framework; PIB Mission LiFE; app notes 3:20 sub 6-7
## SUB 3 | India's SDG Progress – NITI Aayog Index and SDSN Report
[20:3:0] TABLE head: SDG India Index (NITI Aayog) | Fact
  [20:3:0.0] 2018 (1st) | Kerala, HP top; Gujarat a Performer (64)
  [20:3:0.1] 2019-20 | Front Runners incl. Kerala, HP, AP, TN, Telangana; Gujarat 64 – Performer
  [20:3:0.2] 2020-21 | Top five: Kerala 75; HP and TN 74; AP, Goa, Karnataka, Uttarakhand 72 – Gujarat (69) not in top five; AP 1st in SDG 7 (score 100)
  [20:3:0.3] 2023-24 (4th, Jul 2024) | India 71; Kerala and Uttarakhand 79 (top); Bihar 57; AP 74, 9th, still 1st in SDG 7
[20:3:1] - Categories: Achiever 100; **Front Runner 65-99**; Performer 50-64; Aspirant below 50.
[20:3:2] - **NITI Aayog** coordinates SDGs in India; **MoSPI** builds the National Indicator Framework (2026: 277 indicators).
[20:3:3] - India's **first VNR: 2017**, 7 SDGs (1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 14, 17).
[20:3:4] - **SDSN Sustainable Development Report** (lead author Jeffrey Sachs): India **99th of 167** (2025, first time in the top 100) → **94th** (2026); Finland 1st.
[20:3:5] - **Poverty under the MDG reporting** (Tendulkar method, 2011-12): **21.9%** of India's population below the poverty line.
[20:3:6] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.310-311 (Table 11.1, SDG 7 rank 1 in 2020-21 and 2023-24); NITI Aayog SDG India Index 2018, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2023-24 (niti.gov.in); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.36 (VNR); SDSN SDR 2025-26; app notes 3:20 sub 8
## SUB 4 | Andhra Pradesh and the SDGs
[20:4:0] - AP's SDG framework is part of the **Real-time Outcome Monitoring System (ROMS)** of the Planning Department; indicators tracked at State, district and village/ward secretariat level.
[20:4:1] - **NITI Aayog** with the AP government built a **dashboard to monitor district progress in real time**; **APSDPS** runs dashboards for **Swarna Andhra @2047**.
[20:4:2] - **Jan 2017**: Nobel Laureate **Muhammad Yunus** at Andhra University, Visakhapatnam, inaugurated a symposium on **social business for sustainable development**.
[20:4:3] - **Jul 2026**: AP-**UN-Habitat** (HQ **Nairobi**) MoU for a Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs, Amaravati – **SDG 11**.
[20:4:4] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 ch.11 (ROMS); news reports Jan 2017 (Andhra University, Yunus); app notes 3:20 sub 9
## SUB 5 | Related Concepts and Rio Principles
[20:5:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [20:5:0.0] Carrying capacity | Maximum population an environment can support indefinitely without degradation
  [20:5:0.1] Earth Overshoot Day | Date when humanity's yearly demand exceeds what Earth regenerates; Global Footprint Network
  [20:5:0.2] Intergenerational equity | Fairness between present and future generations
[20:5:1] - **Rio 1992 endorsed:** **precautionary principle** (lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone action), **polluter pays**, **CBDR** (developed countries carry more – historical emissions, greater capacity). **Not endorsed:** unrestricted resource exploitation.
[20:5:2] ~~ Sources: Rio Declaration 1992 (un.org); Global Footprint Network; app notes 3:20 sub 4-5

=== NOTES 3:21 | India's Environmental Policy Framework – Nep, Eia, Polluter Pays and Precautionary Principles
## SUB 0 | Environmental Acts and Bodies – Years
[21:0:0] TABLE head: Act / body / plan | Year | Key fact
  [21:0:0.0] Wildlife (Protection) Act | 1972 | Wildlife and habitats; regulates hunting; Schedules of species
  [21:0:0.1] Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act | 1974 | CPCB set up under it (1974, statutory); SPCBs; later given Air Act functions too
  [21:0:0.2] Water Cess Act | 1977 | Cess on water use by industries
  [21:0:0.3] Forest (Conservation) Act | 1980 | Central approval to divert forest land
  [21:0:0.4] Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act | 1981 | Amended 1987 (stricter penalties, noise added)
  [21:0:0.5] Environment (Protection) Act | 1986 | Passed by Parliament in May 1986 (in force 19 Nov 1986); umbrella law; enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy (2-3 Dec 1984, methyl isocyanate, Union Carbide); under Art. 253 to implement the Stockholm Conference, 1972; Sec. 3 powers; EIA, CRZ, ESZ, GEAC all rest on it
  [21:0:0.6] Ganga Action Plan | 1986 | Launched at Varanasi on 14 January 1986 (Central Ganga Authority set up 1985; some books give "first phase 1985") – never 1982
  [21:0:0.7] Coastal Regulation Zone notification | 1991 (revised 2011, 2019) | Under the EP Act; CRZ = land from the High Tide Line up to 500 m landward + the area between LTL and HTL
  [21:0:0.8] Environmental Protection Fund Rules | 2026 | Sec. 16 of the EP Act; pools fines collected under three Acts
[21:0:1] - **Abbreviation:** **EPA** = **Environmental Protection Agency** (the US federal body, 1970); in India "EPA" in notes usually means the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
[21:0:2] - **SPCB compensation powers:** **Sec. 33A Water Act** and **Sec. 31A Air Act** (Supreme Court, Aug 2025).
[21:0:3] > Most repeated angle (8 PYQs): "the Environment (Protection) Act was enacted / passed in **1986**" and "Act passed after Bhopal = EP Act 1986". Traps: 1981 = Air Act, 1972 = Wildlife Act, 1974 = Water Act / CPCB. Incorrect pair (APPSC JL): **Ganga Action Plan 1982** – it is 1986.
[21:0:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Environment p.10 (EP Act: 1986, umbrella, Bhopal, Art. 253, Stockholm), p.11 (CPCB under Water Act 1974), p.3 (GAP first phase 1985); NextGen Environment - APPSC 11 p.11, p.13 and 12 p.2; Shankar Environment 10th ed. part 06 p.1 (GAP launched 14 Jan 1986), part 05 p.1 (CRZ categories); MoEFCC CRZ Notification 1991/2011 (moef.gov.in); app notes 3:21 sub 3
## SUB 1 | Eco-Mark and AP Institutions
[21:1:0] - **Eco-Mark (1991):** Government of India (MoEF) scheme labelling **environment-friendly** consumer products that meet environmental criteria plus **BIS** quality standards; certified by the **BIS** (not CPCB); logo **earthen pot**.
[21:1:1]   - Not about purity, protein content or economic viability – the recurring distractors.
[21:1:2]   - Products: soaps, detergents, paper, plastics, cosmetics, aerosols, food items; **not drugs/antibiotics**.
[21:1:3] - **APPCB:** constituted **24 Jan 1976** under the Water Act; air role from **1981**; gives consents. **White** = practically non-polluting; **Green** = low pollution (Jul 2026).
[21:1:4] - **EPTRI** (Hyderabad): environment training and research.
[21:1:5] > Asked 4 times (UPSC 1998, CDS 2011, UPPCS 2022, IAS 1998): Eco-Mark = **environment friendly**.
[21:1:6] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. part 21 p.11 (26.4 Eco Mark); NextGen Environment - APPSC 12 p.1 (Ecomark issued by BIS); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.55; app notes 3:21 sub 8
## SUB 2 | Environmental Principles
[21:2:0] TABLE head: Principle | Meaning
  [21:2:0.0] Precautionary | Take preventive action even without full scientific certainty of harm; burden of proof on the actor to show the activity is harmless (Rio Principle 15)
  [21:2:0.1] Polluter Pays | Polluter bears the cost of remediation + compensation for the damage
  [21:2:0.2] Public trust | The State holds natural resources in trust for the public
  [21:2:0.3] Absolute liability | Hazardous industries – liable with no exceptions
  [21:2:0.4] Sustainable development | Development that meets present needs without compromising future generations
[21:2:1] - **Environmental sustainability** aims to **conserve natural resources and protect global ecosystems** – not humans, wildlife or animals alone.
[21:2:2] - The NGT must apply sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle in its orders.
[21:2:3] > APPSC 2024-25 (Endowment, others): precautionary = act even when not completely sure of the harm; trap = "only after full scientific proof".
[21:2:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.95 (NGT applies the three principles), PMF Environment 04 p.46 (polluter pays), p.51 (public trust); app notes 3:21 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Landmark Cases and Doctrines
[21:3:0] TABLE head: Case | Year | Doctrine / outcome
  [21:3:0.0] Ratlam Municipality v Vardhichand | 1980 | Municipal duty on public nuisance; health, sanitation
  [21:3:0.1] M.C. Mehta (Oleum gas, Delhi) | 1986 | Absolute liability
  [21:3:0.2] Subhash Kumar v Bihar | 1991 | Pollution-free water and air in Art. 21
  [21:3:0.3] T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad | 1995 (petition; key order Dec 1996) | "Forest" regardless of ownership
  [21:3:0.4] Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum | 1996 | Precautionary + Polluter Pays; tanneries, Palar (TN)
  [21:3:0.5] Bichhri (Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action) | 1996 | Polluter Pays; Rajasthan chemical units
  [21:3:0.6] M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath | 1997 (decided 13 Dec 1996, (1997) 1 SCC 388) | Public trust doctrine – Span Motels on the Beas, Himachal
  [21:3:0.7] Taj Trapezium (M.C. Mehta v UoI) | 1997 (order 30 Dec 1996) | Industries near the Taj to switch to natural gas (CNG) or relocate
[21:3:1] - Vellore = both principles; Bichhri = Polluter Pays only; Kamal Nath = public trust; Oleum gas = absolute liability.
[21:3:2] - Gaurav Bansal v UoI (2015) = disaster-management compensation, not public trust.
[21:3:3] > APPSC FRO screening: public trust upheld in **M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath**.
[21:3:4] ~~ Sources: M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997) 1 SCC 388 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._C._Mehta_v._Kamal_Nath, citing the judgment); PMF Environment 04 p.51 (public trust); app notes 3:21 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Constitutional Provisions
[21:4:0] - **Article 48A** (DPSP) = duty of the **State**; **Article 51A(g)** (FD) = duty of the **citizen** (both added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976).
[21:4:1] - **Article 21** read to include a clean environment (Subhash Kumar, 1991).
[21:4:2] - **Article 253**: Parliament legislates to implement international agreements – basis of the Air Act and EP Act.
[21:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Environment p.10-11; app notes 3:21 sub 2
## SUB 5 | National Environment Policy 2006
[21:5:0] - **Year:** adopted in **2006** (approved 18 May 2006) – India's overarching environment policy.
[21:5:1] - Core idea: **conservation and livelihood security go together**.
[21:5:2] - Objectives: conserve critical resources; **inter-generational equity**; livelihood security for poor tribal communities; **integrate environment into development plans**; efficient resource use.
[21:5:3] - Principles: **precautionary + polluter pays + public trust**.
[21:5:4] - NOT an NEP objective: ending all development in ecologically sensitive areas.
[21:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Environment p.5 (NEP 2006); app notes 3:21 sub 4
## SUB 6 | Environmental Impact Assessment
[21:6:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [21:6:0.0] First used | 1978, river valley projects
  [21:6:0.1] Notifications | 1994 under the EP Act; revised 2006
  [21:6:0.2] Category A | Cleared by MoEFCC
  [21:6:0.3] Category B | Cleared by State SEIAA; B1 full EIA, B2 exempt
  [21:6:0.4] Stages | Screening -> Scoping -> Public consultation -> Appraisal
[21:6:1] - **Draft EIA 2020** controversy: **post-facto clearance**; public notice cut from **30 to 20 days**; wider B2 exemptions.
[21:6:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC 12 p.1 (EIA governed by the EP Act; stages); app notes 3:21 sub 5
## SUB 7 | National Green Tribunal
[21:7:0] - **NGT Act 2010**; in force **18 Oct 2010**; replaced the National Environment Appellate Authority.
[21:7:1] - **Principal Bench: Delhi**; zonal: **Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai**.
[21:7:2] - Civil cases on substantial environmental questions under **7 Acts** in Schedule I.
[21:7:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.95; NextGen Rocket Sheets Environment p.24; app notes 3:21 sub 6
## SUB 8 | NAPCC 2008 and Climate Programmes
[21:8:0] - **NAPCC:** released **30 June 2008** with **eight** national missions: Solar; Enhanced Energy Efficiency; Sustainable Habitat; Water; Himalayan Ecosystem; **Green India**; **Sustainable Agriculture**; Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. Climate change and human health is also listed (2026).
[21:8:1] - **Coastal Security** is NOT a NAPCC mission.
[21:8:2] - **Long-Term Ecological Observatories (LTEO):** announced by India at **COP-21 (Paris, 2015)** – eight observatories for **climate change** studies, under the Climate Change Action Programme.
[21:8:3] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. part 18 p.1 (23.19 LTEO); app notes 3:21 sub 7

=== NOTES 3:22 | National Income Concepts – Gdp, Gnp, Ndp, Nnp, Factor Cost vs Market Price, Gva, Deflator
## SUB 0 | National Income – Meaning, NNP at Factor Cost and Formulas
[22:0:0] # Meaning
[22:0:1] - **National income (NI):** the **money value of all final goods and services** produced by the **normal residents** of a country during a year (UPSC 2013; G2 Prelims 2019) – only **final** goods, so no double counting.
[22:0:2]   - Distractors: "total value of goods and services produced by the nationals" (no "final"), "consumption + investment", "sum of personal incomes".
[22:0:3] - **Income view:** NI = **sum of factor incomes** (wages, rent, interest, profit) earned by normal residents (Police Constable 2019) – not government income, budget or PSU profits.
[22:0:4] - **Source:** generated only from **productive activity** (SSC 2011) – not "any money-making activity".
[22:0:5] - **Flow, not stock:** NI is measured over a period; **national wealth** is a stock at a point of time.
[22:0:6] - **Product = income:** the value of output (national product) is distributed as factor incomes, so national product and national income are **synonymous**; production by labour and capital **automatically generates income** (G1 Prelims 2024 A-R: both true, R explains A).
[22:0:7] # The standard measure
[22:0:8] - **National income = NNP at factor cost** (UPSC 1997, 2001; G2 Mains 2017; SSC 2012) – not GDP/GNP at market prices, not NDP.
[22:0:9] TABLE head: Route | Formula
  [22:0:9.0] From NNP at MP | NI = NNP(MP) − (indirect taxes − subsidies) (Chhattisgarh 2023)
  [22:0:9.1] From GNP at MP | NI = GNP(MP) − depreciation − indirect taxes + subsidies (UPSC 2001)
  [22:0:9.2] From NDP | NI = NDP(FC) + net factor income from abroad (AEE 2012)
  [22:0:9.3] National product at FC | = national product at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies (CDS 2012)
  [22:0:9.4] NNP at FC | = National Income (State PSC) – not "GNP at FC − net indirect taxes"
  [22:0:9.5] Worked example | GDP(MP) 110 + NFIA 10 = GNP 120; − dep 15 = NNP(MP) 105; − NIT 5 = NI 100
[22:0:10] > Most asked angle in this row: "National income = **NNP at factor cost**" (8 PYQs, UPSC/APPSC/SSC). Traps: GNP at MP, NDP at FC, "NNP at basic price".
[22:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.17, p.22-23 (NI = NNP at FC = NNP(MP) − indirect taxes + subsidy; flow not stock); NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.40 (NI = GNP(MP) − depreciation − indirect taxes + subsidies; NI = NNP at FC); Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 03 p.47; app notes 3:22 sub 2
[22:0:12] - **Worked example 2:** GDP(MP) 500, depreciation 50, NFIA −10, NIT 40 → GNP 490; NNP(MP) 440; **NI 400**.
## SUB 1 | Nominal vs Real Income; Measuring Growth
[22:1:0] # Nominal and real
[22:1:1] TABLE head: Basis | Nominal (current prices) | Real (constant prices)
  [22:1:1.0] Prices used | Current-year prices | Prices of a single base year
  [22:1:1.1] Includes price rise | Yes | No – price effect removed
  [22:1:1.2] Use | Size of the economy in rupees | Growth of output
[22:1:2] - **Real GDP** = value of total production at **prices of a single year** = GDP at **constant prices** (SSC 2006; APPSC G2 PYQ; G2 Mains flashcard).
[22:1:3] - **Real national income** = NI at **constant prices** (G2 2011); market value of national output in base-year prices = **GNP at constant prices** (AMVI).
[22:1:4] - **Real NI = nominal NI ÷ price index × 100**: base 1990-91, NI Rs 20,000 crore, index 250 → **Rs 8,000 crore** (G2 Mains 2019).
[22:1:5] - **Prices and money income both doubled** → real income **unchanged** (UPPCS 2004).
[22:1:6] - Per capita income grows **faster at current prices** than at constant prices because the constant-price series allows for the **rise in the price level** (UPSC 2000).
[22:1:7] - **India (UPSC 2015):** GDP at market prices in rupees has **risen steadily**; real GDP growth has **fluctuated** (e.g. contraction in 2020-21) → "Only II".
[22:1:8] - **Base year:** **2022-23** in the new series released **27 Feb 2026** (earlier 2011-12); it uses **double deflation** and Supply-Use Tables. GDP at current prices 2024-25 = **Rs 318.07 lakh crore** (new series).
[22:1:9] - Nominal growth exceeds real growth by roughly the **inflation rate**; 2025-26 estimates (old series): nominal **8.0%**, real **7.4%**.
[22:1:10] # Measuring economic growth
[22:1:11] - **Growth** = rise in **real** output: a growing country has **rising GNP at constant prices** (APRO 2008); GDP growth data is the usual yardstick (Polytechnic Lect. 2020).
[22:1:12] - **Best measure / sign of growth** = a **sustained increase in real per capita income** (per capita product) (UPPCS 2013; RAS 2013).
[22:1:13] - **Not** a growth measure: growth in **financial aid from the World Bank** (Jharkhand 2013); GDP, GNP and per capita GNP are.
[22:1:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.39 (real GVA: base year removes price changes); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.21 (nominal at current, real at constant prices); Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 03 p.46, p.48 (current vs constant prices); MoSPI press release 27 Feb 2026 (new series base 2022-23); app notes 3:22 sub 6, 7, 9
## SUB 2 | Personal, Disposable and Per Capita Income
[22:2:0] TABLE head: Measure | Derivation
  [22:2:0.0] Personal income (PI) | NI − undistributed corporate profits − social security contributions − corporate tax + government and business transfer payments + net interest paid by government
  [22:2:0.1] Personal disposable income (PDI) | PI − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments (fines, fees) (CDS 2019)
  [22:2:0.2] PI − PDI | = direct taxes (AMVI flashcard)
  [22:2:0.3] Per capita income (PCI) | National income ÷ population = NNP ÷ total population (SSC 2012; Endowment) – not GDP ÷ population
  [22:2:0.4] National savings | National disposable income − consumption
[22:2:1] - **PCI = average income** of a country (APPSC G2 PYQ); it shows the **standard of living** (UPPCS 2013) and **regional imbalances** (ACF).
[22:2:2] - **PCI falls while NI rises** when **population grows faster than NI** (G1 2023 A-R: both true, R explains A); PCI rises only when NI grows faster than population.
[22:2:3] - **Statements (Sachivalayam):** PCI is a better welfare measure than GNP ✓; "GNP is always higher than GDP" ✗ (India's NFIA is negative); disposable income is less than personal income ✓ → **I and III**.
[22:2:4] - **Chhattisgarh 2020:** NDP = GDP − depreciation (not +); PCI = NI (NNP) ÷ population (not NDP ÷ population); GDP, not NDP, is used to compare economies → **none true**.
[22:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.1-3 (PI, PDI = PI − personal tax − non-tax payments); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.17-18 (PCI = NI/population, average income); app notes 3:22 sub 6
## SUB 3 | GDP and GNP – Definitions and NFIA
[22:3:0] - **GDP (Gross Domestic Product)** = value of **all final goods and services** produced **within the domestic territory** of a country during a year, whoever produces them (Endowment; Sachivalayam; AEE 2008).
[22:3:1]   - "Goods" alone or without "final" is incomplete; GDP = Q × P.
[22:3:2] - **GNP (Gross National Product)** = value of final goods and services produced by the **normal residents** and their property, **inside or outside** the country, in a year = **Gross National Income** (CDS 2014).
[22:3:3] TABLE head: Basis | GDP | GNP
  [22:3:3.0] Based on | Domestic territory (location) | Normal residents (nationality)
  [22:3:3.1] Indians earning abroad | Excluded | Included
  [22:3:3.2] Link | GDP = GNP − NFIA | GNP = GDP + NFIA
[22:3:4] - **Main difference** GDP vs GNP = **net factor income from abroad** (G2 PYQ) – not transfer payments or depreciation.
[22:3:5] - **NFIA** = factor income **received from** abroad − factor income **paid to** abroad; GNP = GDP + X − M (X = income of nationals abroad, M = income of foreigners at home).
[22:3:6] - **GDP = GNP is possible** when NFIA = 0 (e.g. a closed economy) (SSC 2009).
[22:3:7] - **India:** NFIA usually **negative** → GNP **below** GDP. An Indian resident's income earned in Saudi Arabia counts in India's **GNP only**.
[22:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.18-21 (GNP = GDP + X − M; closed economy GDP = GNP; GDP within geographical boundaries); NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.40 (GDP vs GNP table); app notes 3:22 sub 0, 1
## SUB 4 | Income Determination – Consumption, Saving, Investment, Multiplier
[22:4:0] TABLE head: Concept | Meaning
  [22:4:0.0] Consumption function | C = C̄ + cY – C = total consumption spending, C̄ = autonomous consumption, c = MPC (AP High Court)
  [22:4:0.1] MPC | ΔC/ΔY = slope of the consumption function (Degree Lect. 2017)
  [22:4:0.2] Saving | S = Y − C; MPS = ΔS/ΔY
  [22:4:0.3] MPC and MPS | MPC + MPS = 1 (JL/Polytechnic)
  [22:4:0.4] Autonomous spending | Independent of income
  [22:4:0.5] Induced spending / investment | Varies with the level of national income (G2 Mains 2025)
  [22:4:0.6] Aggregate demand | Total demand for final goods and services
  [22:4:0.7] Inventory | Stock of unsold goods
  [22:4:0.8] Multiplier (k) | k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS – a low MPC gives a low multiplier (Asst. Comm. 2018); MPS 0.25 → k = 4
  [22:4:0.9] Accelerator | Induced investment ÷ change in income (J.M. Clark) – works on the change in income
  [22:4:0.10] Marginal efficiency of investment | Invest while MEI > interest rate: MEI 7% > 6% → profitable
[22:4:1] - **Match (JL):** C = C̄ + cY – consumption function; ΔC/ΔY – MPC; S = Y − C – savings; ΔS/ΔY – MPS → **A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4**.
[22:4:2] - **Mobilisation of domestic savings** depends on past behaviour, the **propensity to save** and **tax policy** (G2 2011).
[22:4:3] - Gross vs net investment: net = gross − depreciation; gross investment that only covers depreciation → net investment **zero**.
[22:4:4] - Realised investment = planned + unplanned (unintended change in inventories); equilibrium where planned saving = planned investment.
[22:4:5] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 04 p.77-79 (consumption function C = C̄ + cY, MPC, autonomous consumption); Ramesh Singh 10th ed. glossary (induced investment); app notes 3:22 sub 11
## SUB 5 | Gross to Net – Depreciation, NDP and NNP
[22:5:0] - **Depreciation** (consumption of fixed capital) = loss in value of **machinery** and other fixed capital through wear and tear (SSC CGL 2016) – deducted because output that only replaces worn-out capital is **not new output**.
[22:5:1] TABLE head: Aggregate | Formula
  [22:5:1.0] NNP | GNP − depreciation (SSC 2011, 2015)
  [22:5:1.1] GNP − NNP | = depreciation (G2 Gazetted 2006)
  [22:5:1.2] NNP at MP | GNP at MP − depreciation (RAS 2021)
  [22:5:1.3] NDP | GDP − depreciation (not plus)
  [22:5:1.4] NNP | = GDP + NFIA − depreciation (both forms correct – Uttarakhand 2021)
  [22:5:1.5] GNP | NNP + depreciation
[22:5:2] - **Incorrect combination (NDA 2015):** "NDP(FC) = GDP(MP) − depreciation" – moving to factor cost also needs removing net indirect taxes.
[22:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.21-22 (NNP = GNP − depreciation; why depreciation is deducted); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.5 (consumption of fixed capital); NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.40 (NNP = GNP − depreciation, GNP(MP) − depreciation = NNP(MP)); app notes 3:22 sub 2
## SUB 6 | PPP and India's World Rank
[22:6:0] - **PPP** exchange rates compare the **prices of the same basket** of goods and services in different countries (UPSC 2019 statement I ✓) – estimated under the **International Comparison Program (ICP)** of the UNSD; **World Bank** = global implementing agency; **NSO** = India's nodal agency.
[22:6:1] - India's PPP GDP is much larger than its market-rate GDP because **prices are lower in India**.
[22:6:2] TABLE head: Measure | India's rank
  [22:6:2.0] PPP GDP (World Bank ICP 2021; IMF 2017) | 3rd, after China and the USA – not 6th (UPSC 2019 statement II ✗)
  [22:6:2.1] Nominal GDP, 2025 | 4th (overtook Japan)
  [22:6:2.2] Nominal GDP, IMF WEO April 2026 | 6th (USD 4.15 trillion, behind Japan and the UK – weaker rupee and new base year)
[22:6:3] - **Older facts:** **Japan** was the third largest economy (PPP) when UPPCS 2007 asked; highest per capita income in **World Development Report 2000** = **Luxembourg** (USD 44,640); 2024 highest per capita GNI (PPP) = **Singapore**.
[22:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 15 p.11 (PPP rates vs market exchange rates); Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 03 p.45 (PPP); World Bank ICP 2021 results (icp.worldbank.org); IMF WEO April 2026 (reported by Indian Express, 21 Apr 2026); app notes 3:22 sub 9
## SUB 7 | Factor Cost vs Market Price – Indirect Taxes and Subsidies
[22:7:0] - **MP = FC + indirect taxes − subsidies**; **FC = MP − indirect taxes + subsidies** → **GDP at FC = GDP at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies** (G2 Mains flashcard).
[22:7:1] - **GDP at MP vs GDP at FC** differ by **indirect taxes and subsidies** (net indirect taxes) – **not direct taxes**, not depreciation (G2 PYQ; WBPSC 2020: "indirect taxes").
[22:7:2] - **Subsidy** = a **payment by the government to producers (the business sector)** that lowers the market price below cost (G2 2003; JL 2004) – not government purchase of goods and services (that is government expenditure).
[22:7:3] - Subsidies are **added** when going from MP to FC.
[22:7:4] TABLE head: Tax type | Meaning | Examples
  [22:7:4.0] Production taxes | Levied irrespective of output | Land revenue, stamp duty, property tax
  [22:7:4.1] Product taxes | Per unit of product | Excise, GST
[22:7:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.21 (GDP(FC) = GDP(MP) − indirect taxes + subsidies); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.9 ("Subsidy is a payment that a government makes to a producer"); Ramesh Singh 10th ed. part 03 p.47-48 (factor cost, production vs product taxes); app notes 3:22 sub 3
## SUB 8 | Transfer Payments – Inclusions and Exclusions
[22:8:0] - **Transfer payments** = one-way payments with **no productive service in return** – **old age pensions**, unemployment allowance, scholarships, prizes (G2 2008) – **not included** in national income (AEE/AMVI; G2 Mains 2019).
[22:8:1]   - They are **added** when moving from NI to personal income.
[22:8:2] TABLE head: Included in NI | Excluded
  [22:8:2.0] Wages, rent, interest, profits, dividends | Transfer payments – pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowance
  [22:8:2.1] Value added at each stage | Intermediate goods (double counting)
  [22:8:2.2] Commission on resale (a productive service) | Second-hand sales; interest on public debt (a transfer)
[22:8:3] - **A-R (G2 PYQ):** "transfer earnings" are not included in NI because they are **not payments for factor services** → both true, R explains A (the question uses "transfer earnings" for transfer payments; in micro theory transfer earnings = the minimum payment to keep a factor in its present use).
[22:8:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.1 (transfer payments: pensions, scholarships, prizes); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.43 (transfer payments); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.25 (transfer earnings); app notes 3:22 sub 5
## SUB 9 | GVA and State Domestic Product
[22:9:0] - **GVA** = value added by producers and sectors – a **production-side** measure; **GDP = GVA at basic prices + taxes on products − subsidies on products**.
[22:9:1] TABLE head: Step | Result
  [22:9:1.0] GVA at factor cost + net production taxes | GVA at basic prices
  [22:9:1.1] GVA at basic prices + net product taxes | GVA at market prices = GDP
[22:9:2] - **GVA vs NVA:** GVA **includes** depreciation; **GVA − consumption of fixed capital = net value added**; at State level **GSDP − depreciation = NSDP** (G2 2011).
[22:9:3] - **GVA at basic prices** = headline sectoral measure since the 2011-12 series and still in the 2022-23 series; real GVA uses a base year to remove price changes.
[22:9:4] - **Q1 2026-27 (Sep 2026):** real GDP Rs 81.36 lakh crore vs real GVA Rs 73.82 lakh crore – the gap = **net product taxes**.
[22:9:5] - **State Domestic Product** = aggregate value of all goods and services produced **within the State's boundaries, counted without duplication**, during a year (AEE/AMVI – AP Socio-Economic Survey wording).
[22:9:6] - **Sectors for GSDP (old series):** **9 broad sectors** (G2 Mains 2017); **17 sectors and sub-sectors** in all (G2 2011).
[22:9:7] - **AP per capita income** is computed on **NSDP**: **Rs 2,68,653** vs India **Rs 2,00,162** (2024-25 FAE).
[22:9:8] - **Goa** = highest per capita income among States; **Maharashtra** = largest GSDP (Tamil Nadu 2nd, 2024-25).
[22:9:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.38-39 (GVA production-side; real/nominal GVA); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.5 (gross and net value added); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.18-32 (SDP definition, per capita NSDP); app notes 3:22 sub 3, 4, 10
## SUB 10 | GDP Deflator and GNP Deflator
[22:10:0] - **GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100** = ratio of GDP at **current prices to constant prices** (G2 Mains 2025) – not real ÷ nominal.
[22:10:1] - **GNP deflator** = nominal GNP ÷ real GNP, as a percentage (G2 PYQ).
[22:10:2] - **Most comprehensive measure of inflation:** covers **all goods and services in GDP**; WPI, CPI use fixed baskets.
[22:10:3] - A rising deflator → higher prices → **purchasing power of money falls**.
[22:10:4] - **Double deflation** (2022-23 series): output and input prices deflated separately for manufacturing and agriculture.
[22:10:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh 10th ed. ch.7 (GDP deflator, index p.13 of part 03); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.5-8 (inflation measures); app notes 3:22 sub 8

  ₹105 | ₹120 | ₹90 | *₹100
  x: NFIA +10 gives GNP 120; minus depreciation 15 gives NNP 105; minus NIT 5 gives NI 100.

  Which item is deducted from NNP at market prices to obtain national income?
  Depreciation | Net factor income from abroad | *Net indirect taxes | Transfer payments
  x: National income is NNP at factor cost = NNP at market prices minus (indirect taxes minus subsidies).
[g38ce9072e0a5] sub0

1. National income is NNP at factor cost.
2. National income is equal to NDP at factor cost plus NFIA.
3. National income is GDP at market prices.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  1 only | *1 and 2 only | 2 and 3 only | 1, 2 and 3
  x: National income = NNP at factor cost = NDP at factor cost + NFIA; GDP at market prices is a different, wider aggregate.
[n75bc786385a] sub0
  Which of the following combinations represents the components of national income at factor cost?
  Indirect taxes, subsidies, depreciation and exports | Consumption, investment, government expenditure and imports | *Wages, rent, interest and profits earned by the country's normal residents | Only wages and salaries earned within domestic territory
  x: National income is the sum of wages, rent, interest and profits earned by factors belonging to the country, including the adjustment for NFIA.
[n71f5df02633] sub0
  What kind of concept is national wealth, measured at a point of time?
  *stock | nominal | real | flow
  x: National wealth is a stock measured at a point of time; national income is a flow measured over a period.
[nb19198aed10] sub0
  A country has GDP at market prices of ₹500 crore, depreciation of ₹50 crore, NFIA of –₹10 crore and net indirect taxes of ₹40 crore. What is its national income?
  *₹400 crore | ₹410 crore | ₹440 crore | ₹490 crore
  x: GNPMP = 500 – 10 = ₹490 crore; NNPMP = 490 – 50 = ₹440 crore; NNPFC = 440 – 40 = ₹400 crore. NNP at factor cost is national income.
[nce2ac7a2e5f] sub1
  A country's nominal GDP rises from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,200 crore, while its price index rises from 100 to 120. What happens to its real GDP?
  It rises by 20 per cent | It falls by 20 per cent | *It remains unchanged | It rises by 40 per cent
  x: The increase in nominal GDP is exactly matched by the increase in the price index from 100 to 120, so output measured at constant prices remains unchanged.

=== NOTES 3:23 | Methods of Measuring National Income – Product, Income and Expenditure Methods; Difficulties
## SUB 0 | The Three Methods – Names and Non-methods
[23:0:0] TABLE head: Method | Also called | What is summed
  [23:0:0.0] Product / production | Output method, value added method, net product method, inventory method | Value added by every producing unit (output − intermediate consumption) = total final product
  [23:0:0.1] Income | Factor income / factor payment / distributed share method | Compensation of employees + rent + interest + profit + mixed income
  [23:0:0.2] Expenditure | Consumption-and-investment method, final expenditure method, outlay method | C + I + G + (X − M) – spending on final goods and services
[23:0:1] - **Only three methods:** product, income, expenditure (NextGen: "National income is calculated by three methods").
[23:0:2] - **NOT methods (frequent distractors):** **Export-Import method** (AEE 2012; Deputy Jailors 2012), **Savings approach** (SSC 2013), **Diminishing cost method** (State PSC), **Gross Value method** (Civil Asst Surgeon), **Cost and Accounting method** (G2 2025); balance of trade, net exports, foreign reserves are not methods either.
[23:0:3] - **"Net product method"** = the product method (G1 2007).
[23:0:4] - **"Final product method":** standard texts (NCERT/NIOS, NextGen) place it under the **product method** – value of final goods produced (the other variant being value added); one APPSC flashcard key gave "expenditure method".
[23:0:5] - All three give the **same total** (product = income = expenditure).
[23:0:6] > Most asked angle: "Which is NOT a method?" – 5 PYQs. Answer = the odd one (export-import, savings, diminishing cost, gross value).
[23:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.3-7 (three methods; product method = total final product); OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.65-71 (product/value added, expenditure, income methods); NIOS Economics 318 L25 (final product and value added variants of product method); app notes 3:23 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Income Method – Factor Incomes, Inclusions and Exclusions
[23:1:0] - **National income = income of factors of production** (Sachivalayam Cat-II) – rent + wages + interest + profit; not government income, PSU profits as such, or a State budget.
[23:1:1] - **Factor income** = income accruing to a factor of production in return for services rendered to the production unit (Degree Lecturers 2023).
[23:1:2] - Economic Survey formula: **GDP = compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital + (taxes on production − subsidies on production) + gross operating surplus**.
[23:1:3] - **Transfer income** = income **not produced by any production process** – received without any service in return (SSC 2012); pensions, scholarships, gifts, old-age allowances.
[23:1:4] TABLE head: Item | In NI? | Reason
  [23:1:4.0] Rent, wages, interest on productive loans, dividends, undistributed profits, mixed income | Yes | Factor incomes
  [23:1:4.1] Profits of public enterprises | Yes | Factor income (profit) of the State's enterprises
  [23:1:4.2] Imputed rent of owner-occupied houses; income from agriculture; self-consumed farm output | Yes | Production / imputed service
  [23:1:4.3] Change in inventories (production − sales) | Yes | Part of output
  [23:1:4.4] Pension, scholarships, gifts | No | Transfer payments (SSC 2011)
  [23:1:4.5] Tax revenue | No | Transfer to government, not a factor income (G1 2023)
  [23:1:4.6] Interest on public debt | No | Treated as a transfer
  [23:1:4.7] Housewife's services | No | Not marketed (HWO 2017)
  [23:1:4.8] Second-hand sales | No | Only the dealer's / broker's commission counts
  [23:1:4.9] Shares and bonds | No | Financial transaction – no new production
  [23:1:4.10] Transfer earnings | No | Not payments for current factor services
[23:1:5] > Imputed rent and PSU profits = IN; tax revenue, pension, interest on public debt, housewives' work = OUT.
[23:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.5-6 (income method: rent + wages + interest + profit; Economic Survey formula); NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.40; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.71; app notes 3:23 sub 0, 3
## SUB 2 | Expenditure Method – C + I + G + (X − M) and Capital
[23:2:0] - **GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)** – consumption + investment + government purchases + **net exports** (G2 Mains 2019; Town Planning 2012 open economy: **Y = C + I + G + (X − M)**; "C + I + G + X" omits imports).
[23:2:1] TABLE head: Component | Fact
  [23:2:1.0] Private consumption (C) | Largest – about 59% of GDP; 11th Plan (2007-12) average about 59% (APPSC flashcard); keeps India less exposed to global swings
  [23:2:1.1] Government spending (G) | Second largest
  [23:2:1.2] Business investment (I) | Most volatile component
  [23:2:1.3] Net exports (X − M) | Effect of foreign trade
[23:2:2] - **Q1 2026-27**: GFCF **34.3% of GDP** (from 31.4%); real GFCF grew **11.9%**; private consumption grew **7.1%** (Sep 2026).
[23:2:3] TABLE head: Fixed capital | Working capital
  [23:2:3.0] Lasts many production cycles – farmer's plough, computer, machines, buildings | Used up in one cycle – yarn used by the weaver, petrol, raw materials
[23:2:4] - **IAS Prelims 2024** pairs: plough–working ✗, computer–fixed ✓, yarn–fixed ✗, petrol–working ✓ → **only two** correct.
[23:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.6-7 (C + I + G + (X−M); consumer spending about 59%, investment most volatile); OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.70-71 (GDP = C + I + G + X − M); NCERT Class XI Indian Economic Development (fixed vs working capital); MoSPI Q1 2026-27 GDP release; app notes 3:23 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Product (Value Added) Method and Double Counting
[23:3:0] - **Value added = value of output − intermediate consumption**; summing value added at every stage = value of the final product.
[23:3:1] - **Double counting:** adding sales at every stage (cotton farmer → weaver → tailor) counts the cotton again and again. Remedy: count **only final goods** or the **value added** at each stage; **intermediate goods are excluded**. Both routes give the same total.
[23:3:2] - **Gross value added − depreciation = net value added**.
[23:3:3] - **Sum of net value added at factor cost** of all sectors within the domestic territory = **Net Domestic Product at factor cost (domestic income)**; + NFIA = NNP at FC = national income.
[23:3:4] - **Change in inventories = production − sales**; treated as investment.
[23:3:5] - **Double deflation** (2022-23 series): **real GVA = real output − real intermediate consumption**, output and inputs deflated separately.
[23:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.4-5 (value added = production − intermediate goods; GVA − depreciation = NVA); OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.69 (value added, GVA/NVA, inventories); NIOS Economics 318 L25 (sum of NVA at FC = NDP at FC); app notes 3:23 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Methods by Sector in India; State Income
[23:4:0] - India uses a **combination of the production and income methods** (NextGen).
[23:4:1] TABLE head: Method | Sectors
  [23:4:1.0] Production (value added) | Agriculture and allied, mining, manufacturing
  [23:4:1.1] Income | Services – trade, transport, banking, real estate, public administration
  [23:4:1.2] Expenditure (commodity flow) | In part for construction; PFCE data as a cross-check
[23:4:2] - **2026**: new 2022-23 series integrates **Supply and Use Tables** (cuts the gap between production- and expenditure-side GDP) and uses **double deflation + volume extrapolation**.
[23:4:3] TABLE head: State income term | Meaning
  [23:4:3.0] Income originating | Value of goods and services produced within the State's boundaries (= GSDP) (G2 2011)
  [23:4:3.1] Income accruing | Adds income of the State's residents earned outside the State (G2 2011)
  [23:4:3.2] GSDP (market prices) | GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies
  [23:4:3.3] NSDP | GSDP − depreciation; AP per capita income is based on NSDP
  [23:4:3.4] Production taxes / subsidies | Stamp duties, property taxes / apprentice and interest subsidies
[23:4:4] - **DES, AP** compiles AP's GSDP (NSO compiles national accounts); States use the **production (income-originating) approach**.
[23:4:5] - AP GSDP in **9 sectors**: agriculture-forestry-fishing; mining; manufacturing; electricity-gas-water; construction; trade-hotels; transport-storage-communication; finance-real estate; community and social services (no separate tourism sector).
[23:4:6] - APSES 2024-25 figures at **2011-12** prices; manufacturing GVA was allocated to States by **ASI shares** (now GST data too); **May 2026**: MoSPI uniform guideline for **GSVA on base 2022-23**.
[23:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.7 (combination of production and income methods); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 ch.2; MoSPI GSVA guideline May 2026; app notes 3:23 sub 2, 7
## SUB 5 | Circular Flow, Output = Income and Equilibrium
[23:5:0] TABLE head: Flow | Direction
  [23:5:0.0] Real flow – factor services | Households → firms
  [23:5:0.1] Real flow – goods and services | Firms → households
  [23:5:0.2] Money flow – factor payments | Firms → households
  [23:5:0.3] Money flow – consumption spending | Households → firms
[23:5:1] # Leakages and injections
[23:5:2] TABLE head: Leakages | Injections
  [23:5:2.0] Saving (S) | Investment (I)
  [23:5:2.1] Taxes (T) | Government spending (G)
  [23:5:2.2] Imports (M) | Exports (X)
[23:5:3] - **Two-sector equilibrium: planned Savings = planned Investment (S = I)** (G2 2008) – the same as aggregate income = aggregate expenditure (Y = C + I).
[23:5:4] - **Open economy: S + T + M = I + G + X** (leakages = injections).
[23:5:5] - **Output = income:** production pays out factor incomes, so national product = national income; **J.R. Hicks** (*The Social Framework*): "**Net Social Product and Social Income are one and the same thing**" (G1 PYQ).
[23:5:6] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 03 p.65 (circular flow); NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics ch.4 (S = I equilibrium); J.R. Hicks, The Social Framework (1942); app notes 3:23 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Definitions of National Income by Economists
[23:6:0] TABLE head: Economist | Core of the definition
  [23:6:0.0] Alfred Marshall | "National dividend" – net aggregate of commodities and services produced annually by labour and capital acting on natural resources (net of depreciation, plus income from abroad)
  [23:6:0.1] A.C. Pigou | Part of community income, incl. income from abroad, measurable in money – suits developed countries
  [23:6:0.2] Irving Fisher | Consumption-based – services received by ultimate consumers
  [23:6:0.3] Simon Kuznets | Net output flowing to ultimate consumers or into net additions to capital stock
[23:6:1] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:23 sub 4 (standard textbook definitions, e.g. M.L. Jhingan, Macroeconomic Theory)
## SUB 7 | Difficulties in Measuring National Income in India
[23:7:0] TABLE head: Difficulty | Example
  [23:7:0.0] Non-monetised economy | Subsistence output, farm produce kept for home use
  [23:7:0.1] Large informal sector | Unorganised units without proper accounts
  [23:7:0.2] No occupational specialisation | One person both farmer and weaver
  [23:7:0.3] Black money / parallel economy | Unrecorded income
  [23:7:0.4] Valuation problems; data gaps | Depreciation, inventories; missing records
  [23:7:0.5] Double counting risk | Intermediate goods counted again
[23:7:1] - **IMF review (Dec 2025)**: persistent **gaps between production- and expenditure-side GDP** show only **partial capture of informal activity**; the new series uses **Supply and Use Tables** to reduce the discrepancy.
[23:7:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.7; IMF Article IV India (Dec 2025); app notes 3:23 sub 6

## SUB 1 | Who Compiles National Income – CSO to NSO (MoSPI)
[24:1:0] - National income was computed by the **Central Statistical Organisation (CSO)** – the key in every older PYQ; not the NSSO (surveys), ISI, NCAER, Indian Standards Institution, RBI, Finance Ministry or Planning Commission.
[24:1:1] - **2019**: CSO + NSSO merged into the **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under **MoSPI**, headed by the **Chief Statistician of India** (also Secretary, MoSPI) – NSO now releases GDP, GNI, NNI and per capita income (UP RO/ARO 2023).
[24:1:2] - **CSO** grew out of the Central Statistical Unit (1949) and was set up on **2 May 1951**; National Accounts Division = GDP, consumption, capital formation; **Economic Statistics Division (ESD) compiled the IIP**; Industrial Statistics Wing, Kolkata conducts the **ASI**.
[24:1:3] - **P.C. Mahalanobis** = **architect of independent India's statistical system** – first Statistical Adviser to the Cabinet (Jan 1949), founder of the **ISI (1931)** and the **NSS (1950)**; P.V. Sukhatme built agricultural statistics.
[24:1:4] TABLE head: Body | Role
  [24:1:4.0] NSC (2006) | Part-time Chairperson + 4 part-time members; CEO of NITI Aayog ex officio
  [24:1:4.1] ISI | Autonomous, ISI Act 1959
  [24:1:4.2] State DES | State Domestic Product
  [24:1:4.3] NSO | Follows IMF SDDS; nodal agency for the ICP; not monetary policy
[24:1:5] - **Economic Census:** the **6th Economic Census** fieldwork ran **January 2013 – April 2014** (MoSPI).
[24:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.8 (CSO + NSSO merged into NSO, Chief Statistician of India); NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.17-18 (NSO estimates national income); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.33 (Mahalanobis – architect of the statistical system; Sukhatme; ISI); MoSPI 6th Economic Census highlights; app notes 3:24 sub 1
[24:1:7] - **NSO role:** umbrella body for national accounts, IIP, CPI and the NSO surveys (PLFS, ASUSE, HCES).
## SUB 2 | Base Year – Meaning and Revisions
[24:2:0] - **Base year** = year whose prices value real GDP (constant prices); index base = 100; revised every 5-10 years.
[24:2:1] - Sequence: **1948-49, 1960-61, 1970-71, 1980-81, 1993-94, 1999-2000, 2004-05, 2011-12, 2022-23** – nine base years; **2009-10 was never a base year**.
[24:2:2] TABLE head: Series | When released | Base it replaced
  [24:2:2.0] 1993-94 | Feb 1999 (UPSC 2000) | 1980-81
  [24:2:2.1] 1999-2000 | 2006 | 1993-94 (still "present" base at UPPCS 2009)
  [24:2:2.2] 2004-05 | Jan 2010 | 1999-2000
  [24:2:2.3] 2011-12 | Jan 2015 | 2004-05 (APPSC 2012-2023 and UPPCS 2015-16 asked this 5 times)
  [24:2:2.4] 2022-23 | 27 Feb 2026 (current) | 2011-12
[24:2:3] - **2015 change = both base year and method** (RAS 2013 re-exam): GDP at factor cost dropped; headline = **GVA at basic prices**; GDP at market prices; **MCA-21** corporate database partly replaced ASI.
[24:2:4] - **AP GSDP base**: 1999-2000 at the 2008 exam; AP still reports at **2011-12** (APSES 2024-25), moving to 2022-23.
[24:2:5] - Other new bases (Feb 2026): IIP **2022-23**; CPI **2024** (from calendar 2012); first new CPI print **2.75%** (Jan 2026).
[24:2:6] - **Real income** = current income × 100 / price index; e.g. Rs 30,000 crore × 100 / 150 = **Rs 20,000 crore**.
[24:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.39 (base year removes price changes); MoSPI press releases Jan 2015 and 27 Feb 2026 (new series); RAS 2013 explanation (base year and method changed); app notes 3:24 sub 3, 4
## SUB 3 | 2011-12 and 2022-23 Series – Changes and Data Debates
[24:3:0] - **2011-12 series criticism:** manufacturing growth not matching physical indicators; private corporate sector overestimated via MCA-21. **Arvind Subramanian** (former CEA, 2019): select indicators and GDP growth **"flipped" post-2011**; 2011-17 growth about **4.5%**, not ~7%.
[24:3:1] - **2022-23 series** (NSO, 27 Feb 2026): follows **UN SNA 2025**; 2022-23 chosen as a "normal" year (not 2017-18 GST, 2019-21 COVID, 2021-22 base effects).
[24:3:2] - Changes: **double deflation**; **Supply and Use Tables**; GST, e-Vahan, PFMS data; PFCE benchmarked on **HCES 2022-23**; four institutional sectors – government, public corporations, private corporations, households (**not exports**).
[24:3:3] TABLE head: Item | Revision
  [24:3:3.0] 2023-24 growth | 9.2% → 7.2%
  [24:3:3.1] 2024-25 growth | 6.5% → 7.1%
  [24:3:3.2] Size | GDP cut 3-4%; 2022-23 nominal Rs 269 → Rs 261 lakh crore
[24:3:4] ~~ Sources: Arvind Subramanian, "India's GDP Mis-estimation", CID Harvard Working Paper 354 (June 2019); MoSPI press release 27 Feb 2026; app notes 3:24 sub 4, 5

## SUB 7 | Savings and Capital Formation
[24:7:0] - **MoSPI/NSO** estimates saving and capital formation by institutional sector; **K.N. Raj Committee (1981)** on saving and capital formation estimates.
[24:7:1] - **Household sector = largest contributor** to gross domestic savings (WBCS 2017); descending order: **household > private corporate > public corporations/enterprises > government** (UP Lower Sub. 1998).
[24:7:2] - Gross domestic saving rate: about **18%** of GDP in the early 1980s (G1 1983-84); 2001-10 peak in **2007-08** (about 37% of GDP, UPPCS 2009).
[24:7:3] - Household saving **18.6% → 18.1%** of GDP (2022-23 → 2023-24, NAS 2025); private corporate investment **11.2%** of GDP (FY24).
[24:7:4] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 (gross domestic savings by sector); RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy (GDS rate series); NAS 2025; app notes 3:24 sub 8
## SUB 8 | AP – GSDP by DES

=== NOTES 3:25 | Trends in India's National Income, Per Capita Income and Sectoral Shares; Inter-state Gsdp Comparison
## SUB 0 | Growth Record – Real GDP Growth Year by Year
[25:0:0] # The long run
[25:0:1] - **First Plan (1951-56):** achieved growth **3.6%** against a 2.1% target – the figure APPSC 2019 keys as "GDP growth 1950-51" (strictly it is the First Plan average, not a single-year rate).
[25:0:2] - **1950-80:** about **3.5%** a year (NextGen: 3.52%) = **"Hindu rate of growth"**; 1980s: **5.13%** a year.
[25:0:3] - Trend is **not a steady rise**: contractions in **1979-80** (drought + oil shock) and **2020-21** (COVID-19), then a **sharp rebound in 2021-22**.
[25:0:4] - **Since 1991:** the economy grew **"almost 12 times"** – the APPSC key (2018, 2020); in US $ terms it is about **10 times** ($270 bn in 1991 → $2.7-2.9 trillion by 2019-20).
[25:0:5] - **IAS 2010:** GDP did **not** rise four-fold in 2000-10 (about three-fold at current prices); the **public sector's share of GDP declined** after liberalisation.
[25:0:6] # Year-by-year figures asked
[25:0:7] TABLE head: Year | Figure asked | Answer
  [25:0:7.0] 2010-11 | GNP growth (APPSC 2012) | About 8.3-8.4% (CSO 2011-12 estimates) → "None of the above" to 9.3 / 9.6 / 7.5; 9.3% came only in the Jan 2013 revision of GDP
  [25:0:7.1] 2012-13 | Budget 2012-13 assumption | 7.6% (± 0.25)
  [25:0:7.2] 2014-15 | Real GDP growth | 7.3% – first estimate on the new 2011-12 base (May 2015)
  [25:0:7.3] 2016-17 | Nominal GDP growth, Provisional Estimates (31 May 2017) | 11.0% (₹151.84 lakh crore); real growth 7.1% (the distractor)
  [25:0:7.4] 2014-15 to 2017-18 | Average real growth | 7-7.9% (about 7.4, 8.0, 8.2, 7.0)
  [25:0:7.5] 2022-23 | Real GDP growth | 7.2% (older series)
  [25:0:7.6] 2023-24 | Real GDP growth | First printed 8.2% (May 2024); later 9.2% (old series), 7.2% (new series)
  [25:0:7.7] 2024-25 | Real GDP growth | 7.1% (new series; old 6.5%)
  [25:0:7.8] 2025-26 | Real GDP growth | FAE 7.4% → SAE 7.6% (Feb 2026) → Provisional Estimates (5 Jun 2026) 7.7%; agriculture 3.1% (4.6% the year before)
  [25:0:7.9] Q1 2026-27 | Quarterly estimate | Real GDP 7.8% (RBI projected 7.0%); real GVA 8.2%; nominal GDP 10.3%
[25:0:8] > Number questions: answer the **first official estimate current at the exam date**; real vs nominal is the usual trap (2016-17: 7.1 real, 11.0 nominal).

[25:2:1] - **Two biggest economies:** **USA and China**; China = **2nd since 2010** (2020 too). In **2005 Japan was 2nd** (US $4.9 trillion vs China $2.3 trillion).

## SUB 3 | Inter-state Comparison – GSDP, Per Capita Income and Growth
[25:3:0] - **Largest GSDP:** **Maharashtra** (13.3% of national GDP in 2023-24, down from 14.5% in 1990-91); **Tamil Nadu 2nd**, then Karnataka and Gujarat; Karnataka grew fastest of the big four since 2021-22 (about 65%).
[25:3:1] - **Highest per capita income (per capita NSDP):** **Goa** (₹3.58 lakh, 2023-24; Sikkim 2nd, Delhi 3rd); **Bihar lowest**.
[25:3:2] - **Among big States, dated:** **Punjab** led till about 2004-05; **Maharashtra** led Gujarat, Punjab and West Bengal in the 2004-05 series used in 2012; EAC-PM now shows Gujarat ahead.
[25:3:3] - **Highest GSDP growth 2010-11** among Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu: **Bihar** (about 14.8%).
[25:3:4] - **Bihar:** a backward State; it has internal regional disparities, but those do not explain its backwardness (A-R: both true, R not the explanation).

## SUB 4 | Sectoral Shares and Structural Shift
[25:4:0] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [25:4:0.0] Largest contributor at Independence | Agriculture (56.5% of national income in 1950-51)
  [25:4:0.1] Industry share, 1950-51 | About 13%
  [25:4:0.2] Agriculture share | 29% (1990s) → 17.9% (2014) → about 17% (2017-18)
  [25:4:0.3] Services share | 48.5% in 2000-01 → over 50% now
  [25:4:0.4] Order now | Services > Industry > Agriculture
  [25:4:0.5] Services' share of GVA growth | About 69% (2011-12 to 2015-16); 72.5% (2017-18)
[25:4:1] - **"Industry poised to take over as the major contributor to GDP"** (AEE 2008) = **Services**.
[25:4:2] - Agriculture's share fell much faster than its **share of workforce** (72% in 1951, still the largest employer).
[25:4:3] # Institutional sectors

  [25:4:4.0] Household (largely unorganised) | 45.5% (2011-12); 44.8% (2014-15)
  [25:4:4.1] Private corporate | 33.9%, then 35.9% (2014-15)
[25:4:5] - Largest institutional sector = **household**; private sector far exceeds the public sector.

## SUB 5 | Per Capita Income – Meaning, Level and Slow Growth
[25:5:0] - **PCI = National income ÷ Population** (NextGen).
[25:5:1] - At **current prices** PCI rises faster than at **constant prices** (constant prices remove inflation).
[25:5:2] - **Per capita NNI 2025-26** (FAE, Jan 2026, current prices): **₹2,47,487**, up ₹16,025; the 2026 new series **lowered** nominal GDP and PCI.
[25:5:3] - **2016-17:** per capita NNI ₹1,03,219 (+9.7%); **2017-18:** PCI at current prices up about **8.6%** (CSO provisional).
[25:5:4] - **2006-07 (UPSC 2008):** per capita GDP at current prices about **₹37,000**; wheat about **75 mt**; rice about **93 mt** (not 180) → A and C.
[25:5:5] - **Reasons for slow growth of real PCI (UPPCS 2001):** rapid **population growth**, **high price rise**, **slow growth of agriculture and industry**, and (before 1991) **scarcity of foreign exchange**; low farm productivity and a large unorganised sector – a **rising services share is not a cause**.
[25:5:6] - **Size 2025-26:** about **₹345 lakh crore ≈ US $3.9 trillion** (new series); earlier estimate ₹357 lakh crore.
[25:5:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 11 p.17 (PCI = NI ÷ population); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.8; MoSPI PE 31 May 2017 (PCI ₹1,03,219, via Tribune); app notes 3:25 sub 3
## SUB 6 | Growth Concepts – Hindu Rate, Miracle Economies, Middle-income Trap
[25:6:0] - **Hindu rate of growth:** about **3.5%** a year in **1950-80**; term coined by **Raj Krishna**.
[25:6:1] - **Miracle economies:** GDP growth of **7%** for a **decade or more** (NextGen) – not 8, 8.5 or 7.5%.
[25:6:2] - **Middle-income trap:** countries that rose from low to middle income but stagnated there; causes = **poor infrastructure, weak institutions, unfavourable growth conditions** – **climate change is not** one of the listed causes.
[25:6:3] - **GDP does not measure income distribution**; dollar rankings move with exchange rates and base revisions.
[25:6:4] - **World Bank income groups:** low, lower-middle, upper-middle, high; WDR 1994 low income = per capita GNP **US $725 or less**.
[25:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.33 (miracle economies 7%); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.11; NextGen Rocket Sheets Economy p.98 (Hindu rate – Raj Krishna); app notes 3:25 sub 0
## SUB 7 | Latest Macro Snapshot – Economic Survey 2025-26 and Stability (as of 2026)
[25:7:0] - **Economic Survey 2025-26** (tabled **29 Jan 2026**; CEA **V. Anantha Nageswaran**): FY27 growth **6.8-7.2%**; potential growth raised to **7%**; FY27 = **"year of adjustment"**.
[25:7:1] - **Growth drivers:** private consumption (**PFCE**), public **capex** (**3.1% of GDP** in FY26), services, monsoon and rabi prospects.
[25:7:2] TABLE head: Indicator | Latest value
  [25:7:2.0] Retail inflation | 1.7% (Apr-Dec 2025, decade low)
  [25:7:2.1] Union fiscal deficit | 4.8% (FY25), 4.4% (FY26), 4.3% (FY27 BE)
  [25:7:2.2] Debt-GDP | 55.6% (FY27); target 50 ± 1% by 2030-31
  [25:7:2.3] CAD | 0.6% of GDP (2024-25); 0.8% in H1 FY26
  [25:7:2.4] Bank GNPA | 2.2%, multi-decade low
[25:7:3] - RBI cut **repo by 100 basis points** (Feb-June 2025).
[25:7:4] - **S&P (Aug 2025):** **BBB- → BBB**, first major upgrade in nearly two decades.
[25:7:5] - **New GDP series (2026):** **reduced nominal GDP and PCI**, raised FY26 growth to **7.6%**.
[25:7:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:25 sub 5, 6 (Economic Survey 2025-26 and macro figures as carried in the app notes)

=== NOTES 3:26 | Demography of India – Census 2011 Findings, Population Growth, Density, Sex Ratio, Literacy
## SUB 0 | Sex Ratio – National Trend, Child Sex Ratio and Causes
[26:0:0] # Definition and Census 2011 figures
[26:0:1] - **Sex ratio:** number of **females per 1,000 males**; "male : female" questions write it as **1000 : 943**.
[26:0:2] - **Census 2011:** final **943** (provisional **940**) – rural **949**, urban **929**; 2001: **933** (1000 : 933).
[26:0:3] - **Child sex ratio (0-6):** 2011 final **919** (provisional **914**); 2001: 927.
[26:0:4] > 940 vs 943 and 914 vs 919 are the provisional vs final traps: a "provisional figures" stem wants 940 / 914; when only 940 is offered, key 940.
[26:0:5] # Trend 1901-2011
[26:0:6] TABLE head: Census | Sex ratio | Change
  [26:0:6.0] 1901 | 972 | –
  [26:0:6.1] 1941 | 945 | −5
  [26:0:6.2] 1951 | 946 | +1
  [26:0:6.3] 1961 → 1971 | 941 → 930 | −11 (sharpest decline)
  [26:0:6.4] 1981 | 934 | +4
  [26:0:6.5] 1991 | 927 (all-time low) | −7
  [26:0:6.6] 2001 | 933 | +6
  [26:0:6.7] 2011 | 943 | +10
[26:0:7] - Long run **declining with ups and downs** (rises in 1951, 1981, 2001, 2011) – keys call the trend **"fluctuating"**; the 1991 figure itself was a fall (934 → 927).
[26:0:8] - **Child sex ratio** has **fallen continuously** since 1961: **976 (1961), 964 (1971), 962 (1981), 945 (1991), 927 (2001), 919 (2011)**.
[26:0:9] # Causes of the low sex ratio
[26:0:10] - **Female foeticide / sex-determination tests** (the fear for the world sex ratio), **high maternal mortality**, **neglect and higher death rate of girl children**, and the natural **excess of male births** (about 105 boys per 100 girls) – all four are counted.
[26:0:11] - **More boys than girls are born** each year in India (so "more female children are born" is false); boys have the higher biological (neonatal) death risk.
[26:0:12] - **NFHS-5 (2019-21):** overall sex ratio **1,020** (NFHS-4: 991) – first time more women than men; **sex ratio at birth 929** (up from 919).
[26:0:13] # International
[26:0:14] - 2011 decreasing order: **Bangladesh > Pakistan > India > China**; most favourable among Sweden, Switzerland, Netherlands, Finland: **Finland**.
[26:0:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.31 (972 → 927 → 940); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 15 p.17 (child sex ratio 914, 927 in 2001); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Geography p.66 (943, child 919); NCERT Indian Society (OnlyIAS) 03 p.66-67 (Table 9.3, NFHS-5 1,020); app notes 3:26 sub 2-3
## SUB 1 | Sex Ratio – States, UTs, Religions and Cities
[26:1:0] # States (Census 2011)
[26:1:1] TABLE head: Item | Answer
  [26:1:1.0] Highest State | Kerala 1,084 (1,058 in 2001) – the only State above 1,000
  [26:1:1.1] Next after Kerala | Tamil Nadu 996, Andhra Pradesh (undivided) 993, Chhattisgarh 991, Manipur 992, Meghalaya 989
  [26:1:1.2] Lowest State | Haryana 879 (861 in 2001) – lowest in 2001 and 2011, though rich by per capita income
  [26:1:1.3] Next lowest | J&K 889, Sikkim 890, Punjab 895 (2001: Sikkim 875, Punjab 876)
  [26:1:1.4] UP | 912 (898 in 2001)
  [26:1:1.5] Above national 943 | Jharkhand 948-949; Gujarat 919, Maharashtra 929, MP 931 are below
  [26:1:1.6] Provisional descending | Kerala, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh
[26:1:2] - **2001 among States asked:** lowest **Gujarat (920)** vs TN 987, Chhattisgarh 989, Manipur 978; highest **Chhattisgarh (989)** vs AP 978, HP 968, Jharkhand 941; lowest **Haryana (861)** vs Punjab 876, J&K 892, Sikkim 875, UP 898.
[26:1:3] - **1991-2001:** biggest rise **Arunachal Pradesh (859 → 893)**; rose in **Uttarakhand (936 → 962)**; fell in Delhi (827 → 821), Haryana (865 → 861), Punjab (882 → 876); **biggest fall Daman and Diu (969 → 710)**.
[26:1:4] - Persons aged **7+** (2011 P): males outnumber females in **Bihar, Maharashtra, UP and West Bengal** (all four).
[26:1:5] # Union Territories
[26:1:6] - **Lowest:** **Daman and Diu 618** (2001: 710) – lowest of all States/UTs; then Dadra and Nagar Haveli 774, Chandigarh 818.
[26:1:7] - **Females outnumber males:** **Puducherry 1,037** (1,038 P) – the UT answer to "region with more women than men".
[26:1:8] # Child sex ratio (0-6), 2011
[26:1:9] - **Lowest: Haryana 834** (830 P) – lowest in **both rural and urban** areas; most boys per 100 girls: **Haryana (120)**; fewest: **Arunachal Pradesh (102)**, which has the highest child sex ratio (972).
[26:1:10] - 2011 provisional: **Mizoram 971 > Meghalaya 970 > Punjab 846 > Haryana 830**; among Chhattisgarh, UP, Punjab, Haryana the highest is **Chhattisgarh** (964 P, 969 final).
[26:1:11] # Religion and cities
[26:1:12] - Religious sex ratio (2011, descending): **Christian 1,023 > Buddhist 965 > Jain 954 > Muslim 951**; lowest: **Sikh (903)** (religion data released 25 Aug 2015).
[26:1:13] - Metros: **Chennai** highest (957 in 2001; 985 in 2011 P) – above Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai.
[26:1:14] - Cities: northern cities have an **unbalanced sex ratio**; eastern cities are **scattered**, western cities **concentrated**; western cities have a **lower share of rural immigrants**.
[26:1:15] ~~ Sources: Wikipedia "List of states and union territories of India by sex ratio" (Census 2001/2011 columns, fetched in this job); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Geography p.67 (Kerala highest, Haryana lowest, Arunachal highest child sex ratio); app notes 3:26 sub 3

## SUB 3 | Literacy
[26:3:0] # Definition and national figures
[26:3:1] - **Literate (Census):** a person aged **7 years or above** who can **read and write with understanding** in any language.
[26:3:2] - **2011 provisional:** **74.04%** (male **82.14%**, female **65.46%**); **final 72.98% (73.0%)** – male 80.9%, female **64.6%**; national gender gap **16 points**.
[26:3:3] - **2001:** 64.84% final (65.38% P); **female 53.67% final (54.16% P)**. **1951:** 18.33% (male 27.2%, female 8.9%).
[26:3:4] # States and UTs
[26:3:5] TABLE head: Item | Answer
  [26:3:5.0] Highest State | Kerala (93.9% P; 94.0% final; 90.9% in 2001)
  [26:3:5.1] Second | Mizoram (91.3%) – also 2nd in urbanisation (52.1%, after Goa); 2nd in male literacy too
  [26:3:5.2] Descending | Kerala > Mizoram > Goa > Maharashtra (2001 and 2011)
  [26:3:5.3] Descending (2011 P) | Tripura 87.75 > Himachal 83.78 > Sikkim 82.20 > Nagaland 80.11
  [26:3:5.4] Lowest | Bihar (63.82% P; 61.8% final)
  [26:3:5.5] Lowest four, ascending (P) | Bihar < Arunachal < Rajasthan < Jharkhand
  [26:3:5.6] Maximum rise 2001-11 (among Bihar, Gujarat, Rajasthan, UP) | Bihar (47.0 → 61.8)
  [26:3:5.7] Highest UT | Lakshadweep (91.8%) – also highest UT female literacy
  [26:3:5.8] Highest rural (among Maharashtra, Manipur, Goa, Gujarat) | Goa; overall highest rural – Kerala

## SUB 4 | Population Growth – Phases, Decadal Record and the Great Divide
[26:4:0] # Phases
[26:4:1] TABLE head: Phase | Feature
  [26:4:1.0] 1901-21 | Stagnant (stationary); population fell in 1911-21
  [26:4:1.1] 1921 | "Year of the Great Divide" / "Demographic Divide"
  [26:4:1.2] 1921-51 | Steady growth
  [26:4:1.3] 1951-81 | Rapid growth / population explosion (1961-71 the peak decade)
  [26:4:1.4] 1981-2011 | High but declining growth
[26:4:2] - **1921:** the **only Census with negative decadal growth (−0.31%)**; growth accelerated after it. **1951 is NOT the demographic divide** – but India's growth **since 1951 has been phenomenal** (36.1 crore → 102.9 crore by 2001).
[26:4:3] # Decadal record
[26:4:4] TABLE head: Decade | Decadal growth | Annual exponential
  [26:4:4.0] 1951-61 | 21.64% | 1.96%
  [26:4:4.1] 1961-71 | 24.80% (highest) | 2.20%
  [26:4:4.2] 1971-81 | 24.66% | 2.22% (highest)
  [26:4:4.3] 1981-91 | 23.87% | 2.16%
  [26:4:4.4] 1991-2001 | 21.54% | 1.97%
  [26:4:4.5] 2001-11 | 17.64% P / 17.7% final – lowest since 1921; sharpest fall since Independence | 1.64%
[26:4:5] - **2001-11:** population rose by **18.1 crore** (181 million); India = **17.5%** of the world (not 18.5%) – "**one in six persons**" is Indian; with its high growth India was expected to overtake China (it did in 2023, UNFPA).
[26:4:6] - **Urbanisation:** largest decadal urban growth **1971-81 (46.1%)**; UP's urban population also grew fastest in **1971-81 (60.9%)**.
[26:4:7] - **UPPCS 2006:** "40% below the poverty line" was false (official estimate about 26-27%).
[26:4:8] - World population by religion (descending): **Christians > Muslims > Hindus > Buddhists**.
[26:4:9] - **Replacement level:** TFR **2.1**. **UNFPA SWOP 2025:** India **1,463.9 million**.
[26:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.23-24, 30 (great divide 1921, phases, 1911-21 fall); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 15 p.10, 12 (decadal table, 17.64%, 1.97/1.64%); NCERT Indian Society (OnlyIAS) 03 p.60 (Table 9.1); PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.51-53; app notes 3:26 sub 1
[26:4:11] - **World (2008):** about **60-61%** of the world's population lives in **Asia**.
[26:4:12] - **Census 2001:** the literacy **gender gap narrowed** (24.8 points in 1991 → 21.6); the **35 million-plus cities** held about **38%** of the urban population.
## SUB 5 | Census – History, Organisation and India at a Glance 2011
[26:5:0] - **Census:** official enumeration of population, every **10 years**; **first attempted 1872** (non-synchronous, operations 1867-72; often loosely "1871-72"); **first complete / synchronous 1881**, regular since.
[26:5:1] - **Census Organisation:** under the **Ministry of Home Affairs** – **Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India**, on a permanent footing since **1961**; Census Act 1948.
[26:5:2] - **Census 2011:** **15th** national Census (7th after Independence); motto **"Our Census, Our Future"**; first with a **"No religion"** category.
[26:5:3] # India at a glance (2011)
[26:5:4] TABLE head: Indicator | Figure
  [26:5:4.0] Population | 121.09 crore (121.02 crore P) – "121 crores"; 2001: 102.87 crore; 1991: 84.6 crore
  [26:5:4.1] Decadal growth | 17.7%
  [26:5:4.2] Density | 382
  [26:5:4.3] Sex ratio / child sex ratio | 943 / 919 (P 940 / 914)
  [26:5:4.4] Literacy | 72.98% (P 74.04%)
  [26:5:4.5] Rural : urban | 68.84 : 31.16 (P; final 68.9 : 31.1); 2001 rural 72.2%
  [26:5:4.6] SC / ST | 16.6% / 8.6%
[26:5:5] - **India's share of world population:** about **17.5%** (2.4% of the world's land); older papers round it to **16-17%**.
[26:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.55, 60 (1872, 1881, every tenth year); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.23 (RGCC, 15th Census, motto); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC 15 p.10, 19-21 (totals, 72.19 → 68.84% rural); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Geography p.66; app notes 3:26 sub 0, 2
[26:5:7] - **Child (0-6) share of rural population, 2011:** lowest **Kerala (about 10.4%)**; Punjab 11.2, Haryana 13.2, J&K 17.5.
