=== NOTES 3:27 | Demographic Transition Theory and India's Position; Demographic Dividend and Its Window
## SUB 0 | Vital Rates – India, States and the World
[27:0:0] # India – headline figures
[27:0:1] TABLE head: Indicator | Figure
  [27:0:1.0] IMR 1951 → 2010 → 2014 | 146 → 47 → 39 per 1,000 live births
  [27:0:1.1] IMR 2020 (National Health Profile 2021, SRS) | 28
  [27:0:1.2] IMR / U5MR (SRS 2024) | 24 (25 in 2023) / 28
  [27:0:1.3] CBR / CDR (SRS 2024) | 18.3 / 6.4 per 1,000 (CDR 7.6 in 2005 – "below 9")
  [27:0:1.4] MMR (2023) | 80.5 per 1,00,000 live births (130 in 2014-16)
  [27:0:1.5] Life expectancy at Independence | about 32 years
  [27:0:1.6] Life expectancy (SRS 2016-20) | 70.0 years; highest NCT Delhi 75.8, lowest Chhattisgarh 65.1
  [27:0:1.7] Elderly 60+ (SRS 2024) | 9.7% (Kerala highest 15%)
[27:0:2] # States (SRS 2024 unless stated)
[27:0:3] TABLE head: Indicator | Highest | Lowest
  [27:0:3.0] CBR | Bihar 26.8 | Goa 10.7
  [27:0:3.1] CDR | Chhattisgarh 8.4 | Delhi 4.5 (not Kerala)
  [27:0:3.2] IMR | Chhattisgarh 36 | Manipur 2
[27:0:4] - **Kerala** has the lowest IMR among Kerala, Karnataka, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh; lowest **urban IMR** too (SRS 2023: Kerala 5, Maharashtra 10, Tamil Nadu 11, Gujarat 15).
[27:0:5] - **2011:** IMR below the all-India average among the options – **Tamil Nadu** (UP, Rajasthan, MP above).
[27:0:6] - **Census 2001:** lowest child mortality **Kerala (16)**; Goa 36, Maharashtra 49, TN 53. Highest child mortality (UNICEF, then): **Odisha**.
[27:0:7] - **CDR 2015:** lowest among Maharashtra, West Bengal, Gujarat, Karnataka – **Maharashtra (5.8)**.
[27:0:8] # World
[27:0:9] - Highest life expectancy: **Japan** (about 85 years) – ahead of Canada, Germany, Norway, Switzerland, Denmark, USA.
[27:0:10] - Highest birth rate in South Asia (options): **Afghanistan**; highest MMR among Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Nepal: **Nepal**.
[27:0:11] - Female labour force participation: India **36.7% (2005-06) → about 26% (2018)**; highest economically active women (1996, options USA/China/Russia/S. Korea): **China**.
[27:0:12] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:27 sub 3 (SRS 2024 table, SRS 2023 urban IMR, CDR 2015, 1947 life expectancy); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.31 (1951 vital data); PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.60-61 (IMR definition, SRS life expectancy); PYQ explanations (SRS / UNFPA SWOP 2025 figures)
## SUB 1 | Vital Rates – Definitions and Key Terms
[27:1:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning / base
  [27:1:0.0] Fertility | Ability of women to give live birth (actual reproductive performance)
  [27:1:0.1] CBR / CDR | Births / deaths per 1,000 mid-year population
  [27:1:0.2] IMR | Deaths of infants before age 1 per 1,000 live births
  [27:1:0.3] Neonatal mortality | Death within the first four weeks (28 days) of life
  [27:1:0.4] MMR (maternal mortality ratio) | Maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births
  [27:1:0.5] TFR | Average number of live births a woman would have over her reproductive span at current age-specific fertility rates
  [27:1:0.6] Replacement-level TFR | 2.1 children per woman (zero growth in the long run)
  [27:1:0.7] Growth rate (natural increase) | Birth rate − death rate in a given period (CBR 30 − CDR 10 = 20 per 1,000 = 2.0%)
  [27:1:0.8] Dependency ratio | (0-14 + 65+) ÷ (15-64)
  [27:1:0.9] Youth (National Youth Policy 2014) | 15-29 years (approved 9 Jan 2014, replaced NYP 2003)
[27:1:1] - Population change = **births, deaths, emigration and immigration** – all four.
[27:1:2] - **Zero population growth:** births (+ immigrants) = deaths (+ emigrants), so the population does not change.
[27:1:3] - Birth-rate data arranged **year by year** = **chronological** classification.
[27:1:4] - **SRS TFR:** 2016 – **2.3** (rural 2.5, urban 1.8); 2018 – 2.2; **NFHS-4 (2015-16) 2.2**; **NFHS-5 (2019-21) 2.0**; NFHS-5 highest Bihar 3.0; AP 1.7.
[27:1:5] - SRS 2024: TFR below replacement for the **fifth year running**.
[27:1:6] > IMR is per 1,000 live births; MMR per 1,00,000 – the classic base trap.
[27:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.60-62 (IMR, U5MR, definitions); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.23-24; Wikipedia "Zero population growth" (births plus in-migrants = deaths plus out-migrants, seen in web search); app notes 3:27 sub 2 and 4
## SUB 2 | Demographic Transition and Population Theories
[27:2:0] # The model
[27:2:1] TABLE head: Stage | Birth rate | Death rate | Result
  [27:2:1.0] I | High | High | Slow growth (pre-industrial)
  [27:2:1.1] II | High (rises or stays high) | Falling | Population explosion
  [27:2:1.2] III | Falling significantly | Low | Growth slows
  [27:2:1.3] IV | Low | Low | Stable or slow growth
[27:2:2] - Order with development: **high birth & high death → high birth & low death → low birth & low death** (UPSC 2012: 2, 3, 1).
[27:2:3] - Third stage = **significant fall in the birth rate** (death rate never becomes zero).
[27:2:4] - Theory: early form **Warren Thompson (1929)**; formal theory **Frank Notestein** (1940s-50s).
[27:2:5] - **India:** late Stage 3, moving into Stage 4; Stage-4 States (2011, low fertility): **Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh**.
[27:2:6] - **Urbanisation reduced both birth and death rates** (education, work, medical care).
[27:2:7] - Low birth rates / ageing / declining population in news: **Italy, Japan, South Korea** (not Nigeria, South Africa).
[27:2:8] # Population theories
[27:2:9] TABLE head: Theory | Propounder
  [27:2:9.0] Principle of Population (1798): population grows geometrically, food arithmetically; positive and preventive checks | T.R. Malthus – a theory of population
  [27:2:9.1] Optimum population | Edwin Cannan
  [27:2:9.2] The Population Bomb (1968) | Paul Ehrlich
[27:2:10] - Population growth: **larger working population is not an adverse effect**; smaller holdings, unemployment and less food per head are.
[27:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.23 (Thompson 1929, Notestein); PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.35-36 (stages, UPSC 2012); NextGen Society Group 2 Prelims 02 p.16 (effects of population growth); app notes 3:27 sub 0-1
## SUB 3 | Demographic Dividend and Its Window
[27:3:0] - **Demographic dividend / bonus / window:** growth potential from a rising share of the **working-age (15-64)** population – all three names are used (APPSC G2 2019: "All of these").
[27:3:1] - India is called a dividend country because of its **high population aged 15-64** (UPSC 2011); the "demographic bonus" around 2016 = **surge in the productive age group**.
[27:3:2] - Working age about **62.9%** (PMF: over 62% aged 15-59; 54% below 25).
[27:3:3] - **Census 2011 age shares:** aged 20+ **59.29%**; under 14 about **29% (28.67%)**; 65+ about **5% (4.8%)** – the "5-6%" option.
[27:3:4] - **Window:** **2005-06 to 2055-56** (NITI Aayog: until 2055); peak around **2041**, when 20-59 is about **59%** (Economic Survey 2018-19).
[27:3:5] - 0-19 share **41% (2011) → 25% (2041)**; 60+ **8.6% → 16% (2041)** and **20.5% (2051)**.
[27:3:6] - To obtain full benefits: **promote skill development** (UPSC 2013); without health, education, skills and jobs it becomes a **"demographic nightmare"**.
[27:3:7] - Broad-based age pyramid (underdeveloped country): **many young people and few old people**.
[27:3:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.43-44 (definition, until 2055, Economic Survey 2018-19, nightmare); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.49 (skill development); NextGen Society Group 2 Prelims 02 p.14-15 (2041 peak, shares); app notes 3:27 sub 5
## SUB 4 | Dependency Ratio and Harnessing the Dividend
[27:4:0] - **Dependent population** in the pyramid: **0-14** (and 65+); working age 15-64.
[27:4:1] - India's dependency ratio is falling because the **15-59 (working-age) share is relatively high**, itself due to the **fall in fertility**: **79% (1975) → 58% (2008) → about 48% (2021)**.
[27:4:2] - **Old-age dependency ratio (2011): 14.2%** (60+ ÷ 15-59; 10.9% in 1961).
[27:4:3] - Lower dependency ratio → **potential demographic dividend**.
[27:4:4] - **Female LFPR (PLFS):** 23.3% (2017-18) → **41.7% (2023-24)**; cutting it would weaken the dividend.
[27:4:5] - RBI typology: **ageing – Kerala, Tamil Nadu**; wide window – Bihar, UP; narrowing – Telangana, Uttarakhand; Kerala 60+ **22.8% by 2036**.
[27:4:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:27 sub 6-8; PMF Human & Economic Geography 01 p.43 (working age); PYQ explanation UPPCS 2016 (old-age dependency 14.2, MoSPI)
## SUB 5 | Fertility Determinants, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh
[27:5:0] - Birth rate falls with **female education and later marriage**, **child survival**, **urbanisation** and **contraception**; **urbanisation lowers the birth rate and high literacy goes with a low birth rate** (UPPCS 2021: both).
[27:5:1] - **Kerala's** lowest population growth: heavy **investment in promoting literacy**, especially female literacy (94% in 2011).
[27:5:2] - **Couple Protection Rate (CPR):** share of eligible couples protected by an approved contraceptive method; a rising CPR cuts the birth rate only when the protected couples are **young** (older couples have finished child-bearing).
[27:5:3] - More boys than girls are born (about **105 : 100**).
[27:5:4] - **Andhra Pradesh:** Stage 4; decadal growth peak **21.13% (1981-91) → 9.21% (2001-11)**; median age **32.5** (India 28); by 2036 under-14 share **25% → 15%**, 60+ **10% → 19%**; NFHS-5 TFR **1.7**.
[27:5:5] - AP: Gram Sabhas (May 2026) for feedback on incentives to reverse falling fertility.
[27:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.57 (CPR one-liner); app notes 3:27 sub 8; PYQ explanations IAS 1993 / 1999

=== NOTES 3:30 | Poverty Estimation Committees – Alagh, Lakdawala, Tendulkar, Rangarajan; Niti Aayog Mpi
## SUB 0 | Poverty Committees – Chronology, Chairmen and Firsts
[30:0:0] TABLE head: Committee / study | Set up – report | Chair | Known for
  [30:0:0.0] Planning Commission Working Group | 1962 | – | First official line: ₹20 rural / ₹25 urban per capita per month (1960-61 prices)
  [30:0:0.1] Dandekar and Rath – "Poverty in India" | 1971 | V.M. Dandekar, N. Rath | First systematic assessment of poverty; first to use calories: line = spending adequate for 2,250 kcal/day in both rural and urban areas (1960-61 NSS data)
  [30:0:0.2] Alagh Task Force | Formed 1977 – report 1979 | Y.K. Alagh | Line based exclusively on nutritional requirements: 2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban
  [30:0:0.3] Lakdawala Expert Group | Set up 1989 – report 1993 | D.T. Lakdawala | Poverty estimation methodology; State-specific poverty lines
  [30:0:0.4] Tendulkar Expert Group | Set up Dec 2005 – report Dec 2009 | Prof. Suresh D. Tendulkar | "Fresh look" at poverty lines; revised methodology
  [30:0:0.5] Rangarajan Expert Group | Set up May-June 2012 – report June 2014 | Dr C. Rangarajan | Members Mahendra Dev, K. Sundaram, Mahesh Vyas, K.L. Datta; last Planning Commission group on poverty
  [30:0:0.6] NITI Aayog Task Force on Elimination of Poverty | 2015 | Arvind Panagariya | –
[30:0:1] - **Chronological order:** Dandekar-Rath (1971) → Alagh (1979) → Lakdawala (1989/1993) → Tendulkar (2005/2009) → Rangarajan (2012/2014).
[30:0:2] - **Not poverty-line committees:** Vijay Kelkar (tax / fiscal), S.P. Gupta (employment), Raj Krishna ("Hindu rate of growth"), Amartya Sen (no committee); **Rangarajan also chaired the 12th Finance Commission** – the setting in which other PYQs use his name.
[30:0:3] - Both the **Lakdawala and Tendulkar** groups were poverty-estimation committees; a question asking "which one" usually wants the latest offered (Tendulkar).
[30:0:4] > Most asked angle (APPSC 2011-2025, UPPSC, RAS, JPSC): who chaired which group and when; "first" = Dandekar-Rath; "nutrition only" = Alagh; "2005 fresh look" = Tendulkar; "new committee to identify the poor (2012)" = Rangarajan.
[30:0:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.5-7; Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.4, p.51, p.74; Planning Commission Press Note on Poverty Estimates 2011-12 (22 July 2013, niti.gov.in) para 2-3; governancenow.com (24 May 2012, Rangarajan panel members); app notes 3:30 sub 1-2
## SUB 1 | Calorie Norms and the Method of Each Committee
[30:1:0] TABLE head: Committee | Method / basis
  [30:1:0.0] Dandekar-Rath | 2,250 kcal per day, same for rural and urban
  [30:1:0.1] Alagh | Poverty line = per capita consumption expenditure meeting 2,400 kcal (rural) and 2,100 kcal (urban) – purely nutritional
  [30:1:0.2] Lakdawala | Kept the calorie anchor (₹49.09 rural / ₹56.64 urban per month at 1973-74 prices); State-specific lines; update by CPI-AL (rural) and CPI-IW (urban); stopped scaling to National Accounts
  [30:1:0.3] Tendulkar | Moved away from the calorie anchor; basket covers spending on food, education, health, electricity, clothing and footwear; MRP data; one urban poverty line basket (25.7% urban HCR) used for both rural and urban
  [30:1:0.4] Rangarajan | Separate food and non-food baskets; 2,155 kcal rural / 2,090 kcal urban plus protein and fat norms; MMRP data
[30:1:1] - **Why State poverty lines differ:** **price levels vary from State to State** (inter-state price differentials), not poverty rates, GSDP or PDS quality.
[30:1:2] - "Planning Commission poverty line": **2,400 kcal rural, 2,100 kcal urban** – the rural figure is the higher one.
[30:1:3] - The basis of urban poverty estimation (Lakdawala) = **CPI-IW**; rural = **CPI-AL**.
[30:1:4] > UPSC 2019 (State lines differ because of prices) and the calorie pair 2,400/2,100 are the repeats; "single urban basket" belongs to Tendulkar, not Rangarajan.
[30:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.5-7, p.9; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 05 p.9; Planning Commission Press Note 2011-12 (July 2013) para 7; app notes 3:30 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Tendulkar and Rangarajan Estimates – Lines and Ratios
[30:2:0] TABLE head: Estimate | Rural | Urban | Total
  [30:2:0.0] Tendulkar 1993-94 | 50.1% | 31.8% | 45.3%
  [30:2:0.1] Tendulkar 2004-05 (report Dec 2009) | 41.8% | 25.7% | 37.2%
  [30:2:0.2] Lakdawala 2004-05 (URP, old official) | 28.3% | 25.7% | 27.5%
  [30:2:0.3] Tendulkar 2009-10 (released 19-20 Mar 2012) | 33.8% | 20.9% | 29.8%
  [30:2:0.4] Tendulkar 2011-12 (released 22 July 2013) | 25.7% | 13.7% | 21.9%
  [30:2:0.5] Rangarajan 2011-12 (report 2014) | – | – | 29.5%
  [30:2:0.6] Poverty line | Rural (per capita per month) | Urban | Per day
  [30:2:0.7] Tendulkar 2009-10 (all-India) | ₹672.8 (Andhra Pradesh's own rural line: ₹693.8) | ₹859.6 | about ₹22 / ₹29
  [30:2:0.8] Tendulkar 2011-12 | ₹816 | ₹1,000 | about ₹27 rural / ₹33 urban
  [30:2:0.9] Rangarajan 2011-12 | ₹972 | ₹1,407 | ₹32 rural / ₹47 urban

[30:2:2] - The popular "**₹26 rural / ₹32 urban per day**" was the Planning Commission's 2011 figure (2009-10 Tendulkar lines updated to 2011 prices); exam keys attach it to the Tendulkar line. **₹32 per day is Rangarajan rural but "Tendulkar urban".**
[30:2:3] - The **27.5%** of 2004-05 = Planning Commission, **Uniform Recall Period** (Lakdawala method).
[30:2:4] > Numbers are asked from every exam family: 37.2% (2004-05), 41.8% rural, 29.8% (2009-10), 21.9% (2011-12), 27 crore poor, ₹672.8 rural line 2009-10, Rangarajan ₹32/₹47.
[30:2:5] ~~ Sources: Planning Commission Press Note on Poverty Estimates 2011-12 (22 July 2013, niti.gov.in) para 3, 7-9 and Table 2; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.6; governancenow.com (PTI 20 Mar 2012, 2009-10 lines); deccanchronicle.com (7 July 2014, Rangarajan report); RBI Handbook of Statistics Table 11 (rbi.org.in); app notes 3:30 sub 5-6
## SUB 3 | Recall Periods, NSS Data and Price Indices
[30:3:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [30:3:0.0] URP (Uniform Reference/Recall Period) | 30-day recall for all items; used up to 1993-94
  [30:3:0.1] MRP (Mixed Reference Period) | 365-day recall for five low-frequency items (clothing, footwear, durables, education, institutional medical care), 30 days for the rest; basis of Tendulkar
  [30:3:0.2] MMRP (Modified MRP) | 7-day recall for some food items; first used 2009-10; used by Rangarajan
  [30:3:0.3] CPI-AL / CPI-IW | Update rural / urban lines (Lakdawala)
[30:3:1] - URP and MRP measure the **incidence of poverty** (not exports, urbanisation or demonetisation).
[30:3:2] - The **61st NSS round (2004-05)** gave **both URP and MRP** distributions.
[30:3:3] - Poverty is estimated from NSS **household consumer expenditure** surveys (MPCE), normally every five years; now **HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24**.
[30:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.10; Planning Commission Press Note 2011-12 (July 2013) para 6; app notes 3:30 sub 4
## SUB 4 | BPL Identification Committees
[30:4:0] TABLE head: Person / body | Purpose
  [30:4:0.0] N.C. Saxena (Ministry of Rural Development, report Aug 2009) | Method for the rural BPL Census – automatic exclusion / inclusion, ranking the rest on a 10-point scale
  [30:4:0.1] S.R. Hashim (Planning Commission expert group) | Identification of urban BPL families
  [30:4:0.2] Abhijit Sen (MoRD, 2012) | Use of SECC indicators to choose beneficiaries of rural programmes
[30:4:1] - **Automatic exclusion (Saxena):** income-tax payers, owners of motor vehicles / mechanised farm equipment, salaried above ₹10,000 a month, large landowners.
[30:4:2] - **Automatic inclusion:** **PVTGs**, Maha Dalit groups, single-woman-headed and disabled-breadwinner households, destitute, homeless, bonded labourers.
[30:4:3] - Saxena = rural BPL; **Hashim = urban BPL**; Tendulkar / Lakdawala / Rangarajan = poverty estimation.
[30:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.7, p.9; app notes 3:30 sub 7
## SUB 5 | NITI Aayog National Multidimensional Poverty Index
[30:5:0] - **Body:** **NITI Aayog**, with technical inputs from **OPHI and UNDP**; **Alkire-Foster** method.
[30:5:1] - **3 equally weighted dimensions** – health, education, standard of living; **12 indicators** (Global MPI 10) – the two added are **maternal health and bank account**.
[30:5:2] - Standard-of-living indicators: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account (years of schooling is an **education** indicator).
[30:5:3] - Data: NFHS-4 (2015-16), NFHS-5 (2019-21).
[30:5:4] - **Discussion paper (Jan 2024):** headcount **29.17% (2013-14) → 11.28% (2022-23)**; **24.82 crore** people exited in 9 years. Earlier: 55.3% (2005-06) → 14.96% (2019-21).
[30:5:5] - **AP:** MPI 0.053 → 0.025; headcount 6.06% (2019-21), 9th.
[30:5:6] > New PYQ angle (AP High Court 2026): the 2022-23 MPI headcount, 11.28%.
[30:5:7] ~~ Sources: Economic Survey 2025-26 Highlights part 2 p.14; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.2-4; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.13; app notes 3:30 sub 8
## SUB 6 | Early Estimates and Poverty-Line Debates
[30:6:0] - **Dadabhai Naoroji** ("Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"): subsistence line **₹16-35 per capita per year** at 1867-68 prices – the earliest estimate.
[30:6:1] - **National Planning Committee (1938):** ₹15-20 per month; **Bombay Plan (1944):** ₹75 per year.
[30:6:2] - The Planning Commission estimated poverty from NSS data **since the Sixth Plan**; the Ministry of Rural Development runs the **BPL Census**.
[30:6:3] - **Debate:** a higher line raises fiscal cost, a lower one excludes the needy; Tendulkar line called "too low" → Rangarajan group (2012).
[30:6:4] - **A-R (UPPSC 1997):** there is no clear picture of the extent of poverty (estimates differ by method) **and** poverty-eradication strategy has shifted – both true, but R does not explain A.
[30:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.4-5; Planning Commission Press Note 2011-12 para 3; app notes 3:30 sub 0, 9

  x: The Tendulkar methodology used one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas. It moved away from an exclusive calorie anchor, included private health and education expenditure, and used MRP in place of URP.

[31:0:4] - **Concentration:** more than half of India's poor live in **Bihar, UP, MP and Odisha** (World Bank); the high-poverty belt is Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, MP, Odisha, UP (with Rajasthan) – **Andhra Pradesh and Kerala are not in it**.

[31:0:8] - 2011-12 to 2022-23: rural **Odisha 47.8% → 8.6%**; urban **Bihar 50.8% → 9.1%** (convergence – high-poverty States fell fastest).
[31:0:9] > Highest / lowest State is asked in almost every year (APPSC 2012-2020, UPPSC 2004-2014, MPPSC). Answer from the data of the exam's time: Punjab (1999-2000), J&K (2004-05), Kerala / HP / Goa (2009-10 onward); today Goa.

## SUB 1 | All-India Poverty Trends and Global Goals
[31:1:0] TABLE head: Year (Tendulkar) | All-India | Rural | Urban
  [31:1:0.0] 1993-94 | 45.3% | 50.1% | 31.8%
  [31:1:0.1] 2004-05 | 37.2% | 41.8% | 25.7%
  [31:1:0.2] 2009-10 | 29.8% | 33.8% | 20.9%
  [31:1:0.3] 2011-12 | 21.9% (MRP) | 25.7% | 13.7%
  [31:1:0.4] 2022-23 / 2023-24 (updated line, Economic Survey 2025-26) | 4.7% / 2.3% | – | –
[31:1:1] - Decline accelerated: 0.74 points a year (1993-94 to 2004-05) → **2.18 points a year (2004-05 to 2011-12)**.
[31:1:2] - **After the 1991 New Economic Policy:** the official quinquennial estimates show **both rural and urban poverty declining** (all-India 36.0% in 1993-94 → 26.1% in 1999-2000, Lakdawala); thin-round data showed a short rise in rural poverty in 1991-92.
[31:1:3] - **MDG:** India used the Tendulkar 2011-12 figure **21.9%** in its MDG report; target – halve poverty from 47.8% (1990) to **23.9% by 2015**; India **met the poverty-halving target (Goal 1)** but missed hunger, maternal health and sanitation.
[31:1:4] - **2011 to 2015:** more than **90 million** lifted out of poverty (World Bank).
[31:1:5] - **SDG 1:** **end poverty in all its forms everywhere by 2030** (no numerical ratio).
[31:1:6] - World Bank $3-a-day extreme poverty: 27.1% (2011-12) → **5.3% (2022-23)**; MPI 55.3% (2005-06) → 14.96% (2019-21) → 11.28% (2022-23).
[31:1:7] ~~ Sources: Planning Commission Press Note 2011-12 (July 2013) para 8-10; RBI Handbook Table 11; Economic Survey 2025-26 Highlights part 2 p.14 and Summary part 2 p.40; app notes 3:31 sub 0

  [31:2:0.1] SERP – Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty | People-sensitive support structure: social mobilisation of the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods | 2000

  [31:2:0.5] APMSS – Andhra Pradesh Mahila Sadhikara Samstha | Integrated body for poverty alleviation and empowerment of poor households in both rural and urban areas | –

## SUB 3 | Poverty in Andhra Pradesh
[31:3:0] TABLE head: Measure | AP | India
  [31:3:0.0] Tendulkar 2011-12 total | 9.20% | 21.92%
  [31:3:0.1] Tendulkar 2011-12 rural / urban | 10.96% / 5.81% | 25.70% / 13.70%
  [31:3:0.2] MPI headcount 2019-21 | 6.06% (rural 7.71, urban 2.20) | 14.96%
  [31:3:0.3] MPI value | 0.025 (0.053 in 2015-16) | –
[31:3:1] - **AP trend (Tendulkar):** 44.6% (1993-94) → **29.9% (2004-05)** → **21.1% (2009-10)** → **9.20% (2011-12)** – a fall of **8.8 points** from 2004-05 to 2009-10.
[31:3:2] - **Old official (URP) estimate for 2004-05 (Eleventh Plan):** AP **15.8%** (figure used in the APPSC Group-II 2011 key).
[31:3:3] - **2011-12:** both rural and urban poverty in AP were **below the all-India level**; AP's work participation is **higher** than India's.
[31:3:4] - AP multidimensional poverty: 41.6% (2005-06) → about 21%.
[31:3:5] - **Districts (old 13, MPI):** least poor **West Godavari 2.42%**, YSR Kadapa, Guntur, Krishna; poorest **Kurnool 12.84%**, Vizianagaram 8.66%, Visakhapatnam, Anantapur.
[31:3:6] - Poorer regions: **Rayalaseema** (rain-fed) and **North Coastal Andhra** (tribal ITDA tracts); least poor: **delta districts** (irrigation, productivity).
[31:3:7] ~~ Sources: Planning Commission Press Note 2011-12 (July 2013) Table 2; RBI Handbook Table 11; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.13, p.290; app notes 3:31 sub 4-5
## SUB 4 | Social Groups, Causes and Latest Developments
[31:4:0] - Highest poverty: **Scheduled Tribes** (about 43-45% in 2011-12), then SCs (29%); rural agricultural labour and urban casual labour households about 34%.
[31:4:1] - No formal education: **35.1%** poor vs 14.9% with post-secondary education.
[31:4:2] TABLE head: Cause of regional difference | Effect
  [31:4:2.0] Agricultural productivity and irrigation | Delta gains; rain-fed Rayalaseema lags
  [31:4:2.1] Infrastructure and investment | Investment only in select locales
  [31:4:2.2] Human capital | Low education → higher poverty
  [31:4:2.3] Social transfers | PMGKAY, MGNREGA, PMAY-G cut poverty
[31:4:3] - **Graduation approach (2025-26):** Bihar's **Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana**; Kerala's poverty-eradication model (Kerala moving to extreme-poverty-free status); Centre's **Samaveshi Aajeevika Yojana** under DAY-NRLM.
[31:4:4] - **VB-G RAM G Act, 2025** (passed 18 Dec 2025): rural job guarantee **125 days**.
[31:4:5] - Social protection coverage **22% (2016) → 64.3% (2025)**.
[31:4:6] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 05 p.10; Economic Survey 2025-26 Summary part 2 p.40; app notes 3:31 sub 2, 3, 7

=== NOTES 3:32 | Inequality - Lorenz Curve, Gini Coefficient, Kuznets Hypothesis; Income vs Wealth Inequality in India
## SUB 0 | Economists and Books on Wealth, Poverty and Inequality
[32:0:0] TABLE head: Work / idea | Author
  [32:0:0.0] The Wealth of Nations (1776); "science of wealth" definition; "father of (modern) economics" | Adam Smith
  [32:0:0.1] Theory of surplus value (Das Kapital) | Karl Marx
  [32:0:0.2] Principles of Political Economy and Taxation; rent, comparative advantage | David Ricardo
  [32:0:0.3] General Theory (1936) | J.M. Keynes
  [32:0:0.4] Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (drain of wealth) | Dadabhai Naoroji
  [32:0:0.5] The Economic History of India | R.C. Dutt
  [32:0:0.6] Arthashastra | Kautilya
  [32:0:0.7] Inequality Reexamined | Amartya Sen
  [32:0:0.8] The Price of Inequality (2012) | Joseph Stiglitz
  [32:0:0.9] Capital in the Twenty-First Century; The Economics of Inequality | Thomas Piketty
  [32:0:0.10] Inequality: What Can Be Done? | Anthony Atkinson
  [32:0:0.11] World Inequality Report | World Inequality Lab (Paris School of Economics)
  [32:0:0.12] Inequality reports at Davos | Oxfam International
  [32:0:0.13] Global Wealth Report / Databook | Credit Suisse (now UBS)
[32:0:1] - Strong advocates of the **market economy**: **Adam Smith, Hayek, Friedman** (Keynes favoured intervention; Marx a critic; Galbraith criticised unregulated markets).
[32:0:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.53, p.96-97; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 17 p.4; app notes 3:32 sub 6
## SUB 1 | Lorenz Curve and Gini Coefficient
[32:1:0] TABLE head: Person | Measure | Year
  [32:1:0.0] Max O. Lorenz (American) | Lorenz curve – graphical distribution of income / wealth | 1905 ("Methods of measuring the concentration of wealth")
  [32:1:0.1] Corrado Gini (Italian statistician) | Gini coefficient ("Variability and Mutability") | 1912
  [32:1:0.2] Simon Kuznets | Kuznets curve (inverted U) | 1955
[32:1:1] - **Lorenz curve:** X-axis = cumulative % of population (poorest first); Y-axis = cumulative % of income; **45° line = perfect equality**; the farther the curve bows away, the **greater the inequality**. It is a graph, not a number – it **measures inequality of income / distribution of income**.
[32:1:2] - **Gini coefficient:** **derived from the Lorenz curve** = area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line ÷ whole area under the equality line; measures **income inequality**.
[32:1:3] - Range **0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all income)**; Gini index = coefficient × 100 (0.40 → 40); **higher Gini = more inequality** (so "higher Gini, lower inequality" is wrong).
[32:1:4] - **Relative poverty** within India is measured with the **Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient**; absolute poverty with the **poverty line**.
[32:1:5] - India: consumption Gini (World Bank, Spring 2025) **28.8 (2011-12) → 25.5 (2022-23)**; income Gini (World Inequality Database) 52 (2004) → 62 (2023).
[32:1:6] TABLE head: Curve | Shows
  [32:1:6.0] Lorenz | Distribution of income (inequality)
  [32:1:6.1] Phillips | Inflation vs unemployment
  [32:1:6.2] Laffer | Tax rate vs tax revenue
  [32:1:6.3] Marshall (demand curve) | Price vs quantity demanded
  [32:1:6.4] Kuznets | Inequality vs per capita income
[32:1:7] > Most repeated in this row (UPSC CDS 2019, UPPSC 2018, CGPSC 2018, JPSC 2023, SSC 2005, APPSC): what the Lorenz curve / Gini measures, its year, and the statements on Gini.
[32:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.23-24 (gives Lorenz 1906 – the paper is 1905); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 16 p.9 (relative poverty); NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 18 p.9 and 19 p.8; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenz_curve (Lorenz 1905, Publications of the American Statistical Association 9(70)); Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.96-97; app notes 3:32 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Measuring Inequality in India – Consumption, Income and Wealth
[32:2:0] - **NSSO/NSO indicator of household economic inequality = consumption** (**MPCE**, monthly per capita consumption expenditure) – not income, wealth or social status; poverty too is measured from household consumption expenditure.
[32:2:1] TABLE head: Inequality | Data source | Finding
  [32:2:1.0] Consumption | NSS/HCES (MoSPI), every five years | Looks lower; may understate top-end incomes
  [32:2:1.1] Income | No official survey: PLFS wages, tax data, WID | Top 10% median about 13 times bottom 10% (2023-24)
  [32:2:1.2] Wealth | AIDIS (All India Debt and Investment Survey) | Top 10% hold about 77%
[32:2:2] - **Oxfam, "An economy for the 99%" (Davos, Jan 2017):** India's **richest 1% hold 58%** of total wealth; 57 billionaires = wealth of the bottom 70%; the top 10% share (about 77-80%) is the figure asked.
[32:2:3] - **McKinsey Global Institute, "Poorer than their parents?" (2016):** **65-70% of households** in 25 advanced economies had flat or falling real incomes, 2005-2014.
[32:2:4] - **Sen's poverty index** combines the headcount ratio, the income-gap ratio and the **Gini coefficient of income among the poor** – i.e. it brings in **income inequality**.
[32:2:5] - **Inequality** (of income and assets) is the underlying cause of poverty within a society.
[32:2:6] TABLE head: Survey | Rural MPCE | Urban MPCE | Gap
  [32:2:6.0] NSS 2011-12 | ₹1,430 | ₹2,630 | about 84%
  [32:2:6.1] HCES 2022-23 | ₹3,773 | ₹6,459 | about 71%
  [32:2:6.2] HCES 2023-24 | ₹4,122 | ₹6,996 | about 70%
[32:2:7] - Inter-State: **Bihar** lowest per capita NSDP, **Goa** highest (2023-24). AP's district MPI gap (West Godavari 2.42% to Kurnool 12.84%) measures **intra-State** inequality; **Rayalaseema and North Coastal** lag.
[32:2:8] ~~ Sources: Planning Commission Press Note 2011-12 (July 2013) para 6 (MPCE); Oxfam 2017 and McKinsey 2016 figures – general knowledge, not checked (sources could not be opened); app notes 3:32 sub 3-4
## SUB 3 | Measures to Reduce Inequality
[32:3:0] TABLE head: Direct (redistribute assets) | Indirect (fiscal)
  [32:3:0.0] Ceiling on land holdings, land reforms, tenancy laws | Estate duty, wealth tax, capital gains tax, progressive income tax
[32:3:1] - **K.N. Raj Committee (1972)** on taxation of agricultural wealth and income recommended an **Agricultural Holdings Tax**.
[32:3:2] - **Wealth tax** abolished from **1 April 2016**; **estate duty** abolished **1985**.
[32:3:3] - **Art. 38(2)**: minimise inequalities in income; **Art. 39(c)**: prevent concentration of wealth.
[32:3:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 3:32 sub 5; K.N. Raj Committee – general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 4 | Kuznets Curve and Environmental Kuznets Curve
[32:4:0] TABLE head: Curve | Plots | Shape
  [32:4:0.0] Kuznets hypothesis (Simon Kuznets, 1955) | Inequality vs per capita income: rises in early growth, then falls | Inverted U
  [32:4:0.1] Environmental Kuznets Curve | Environmental degradation vs per capita income: rises then falls after a threshold income | Inverted U
[32:4:1] - The curve that explains the relationship between **economic growth and environmental degradation** = **(Environmental) Kuznets curve** – not Lorenz, Phillips or Laffer.
[32:4:2] - EKC message: "the solution to pollution is **economic growth**".
[32:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.39; NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 19 p.8; app notes 3:32 sub 2

=== NOTES 3:35 | Labour Force Participation, Female Lfpr, Informality and the Quality of Employment
## SUB 0 | Informal Sector and Quality of Employment
[35:0:0] TABLE head: Concept | Meaning
  [35:0:0.0] Formal / organised sector | Public sector + private establishments with 10 or more hired workers; social security, higher wages
  [35:0:0.1] Informal / unorganised sector (enterprise) | Unincorporated private enterprises of individuals / households with fewer than 10 workers
  [35:0:0.2] Informal employment (worker) | Workers without social security, paid leave or dismissal notice – in any sector
[35:0:1] - **Unemployment and underemployment are concentrated in the unorganised sector**; it runs on **cash (currency transactions)** – the "informal, cash-intensive parts of the economy".
[35:0:2] - **NCEUS** (National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector), set up **2004**, chaired by **Arjun Sengupta**.
[35:0:3] - Nearly **82%** of the workforce is in the informal sector and nearly **90%** is informally employed (India Employment Report 2024); 2011-12: only about **6%** in the formal sector (NCERT).
[35:0:4] - **AP:** informal share **62.3% rural, 45.6% urban**; overall about **55%**.
[35:0:5] - **Casual workers (UPSC 2021):** EPF coverage is **not** for all casual workers (depends on establishment size and wage ceiling); they are entitled to regular working hours and overtime (minimum wage rules); the Government may by notification require an establishment to **pay wages only by cheque or into the bank account** (Payment of Wages Amendment 2017) → **2 and 3 only**.
[35:0:6] - **India's wage policy** (minimum wages, DA) is linked to the **cost of living**.
[35:0:7] > APPSC Group-II 2017: NCEUS = Arjun Sengupta; WBCS: unemployment concentrated in the unorganised sector.
[35:0:8] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 05 p.3; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.21 p.83 (cash-intensive informal economy); vajiramandravi.com and testbook.com (UPSC 2021 casual-workers question); app notes 3:35 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Jobless Growth and Employment Elasticity
[35:1:0] - **Jobless growth:** a widening gap between GDP growth and employment growth – more goods and services produced without proportionate jobs; NCERT dates the "disheartening development" to the **late 1990s**; employment growth was near zero again in **2004-05 to 2009-10** (the decade **2001-2010** in the AEE 2016 key).
[35:1:1] - Term coined by **Nick Perna** (early 1990s), not Arthur Lewis.
[35:1:2] - **Main reason after 1991:** reforms were **mainly confined to the formal sector** while most jobs are informal; growth led by **capital-intensive** IT and finance, not **labour-intensive manufacturing** ("**missing middle**").
[35:1:3] - **Post-1991 (UPSC 2020):** rural **non-farm** growth rose and **rural employment growth fell**; productivity rose in rural and urban areas; the rural share of the workforce fell → **III and IV only**.
[35:1:4] - **Employment elasticity** = % change in employment ÷ % change in output; **low** = output grows with little rise in jobs.
[35:1:5] TABLE head: Sector (1999-2000 to 2009-10) | Employment elasticity
  [35:1:5.0] Construction | 1.13
  [35:1:5.1] Finance and real estate | 0.66
  [35:1:5.2] Manufacturing | 0.09
  [35:1:5.3] Agriculture (mixed farming) | 0.04 – very low
[35:1:6] - About **12 million** enter the job market every year; direct factory employment fell 61% → 47% (2011-2023) as **contract workers rose to 42%** (13 Mar 2026).
[35:1:7] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 05 p.1; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 03 p.49; 12th Five Year Plan ch.22 (elasticities, as quoted in the PYQ explanation); app notes 3:35 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Status and Sector of Employment
[35:2:0] TABLE head: India Employment Report 2024 (ILO + IHD), 2022 | Share
  [35:2:0.0] Self-employment | 55.8%
  [35:2:0.1] Casual | 22.7%
  [35:2:0.2] Regular wage / salaried | 21.5%
[35:2:1] - IER 2024 is released by the **ILO and the Institute for Human Development**, not NITI Aayog.
[35:2:2] - Q2 FY26 (Economic Survey 2025-26): self-employment 55.8%; casual labour 18.9%; regular salaried **49.8% of urban jobs**; **56.2 crore** employed (15+); agriculture **42.4%** of the workforce.
[35:2:3] - **Gen Z (22 Jul 2026):** only **14.2%** have a formal contract; **20.1%** have any social security.
[35:2:4] TABLE head: Item | Share
  [35:2:4.0] Agriculture's share of workforce | 72% (1951) → 64.75% (1993-94) → 42.4% (Q2 FY26)
  [35:2:4.1] Rural employment in agriculture, 2025-26 | 57% (self-employment 62.8%)
  [35:2:4.2] Rural households engaged in agriculture (NSSO 70th round, 2013, released 2014) | 57.8%
  [35:2:4.3] AP labour force in agriculture (APPSC Group-II Mains 2019 key) | 55%
[35:2:5] - Efficiency of workers depends on age and the **level of wages**.
[35:2:6] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 04 p.85-86; app notes 3:35 sub 3-4
## SUB 3 | Female Labour Force Participation
[35:3:0] TABLE head: PLFS round | Female LFPR (15+, usual status)
  [35:3:0.0] 2017-18 | 23.3%
  [35:3:0.1] 2020-21 | 32.5%
  [35:3:0.2] 2022-23 | 37.0%
  [35:3:0.3] 2023-24 | 41.7%
  [35:3:0.4] 2025 | about 40% (rural 45.9%, urban 27.7%)
[35:3:1] - **Earlier decline:** female LFPR fell sharply from 2004-05 to 2017-18; the usual explanation – **rising family income (income effect) and more girls in education** (A and R both true, R explains A in UPPSC 2019; some keys say R does not fully explain A).
[35:3:2] - **Economic Survey 2017-18:** most women's indicators improved, but **female labour force participation and the fertility rate declined**.
[35:3:3] - **Rural women = 80%** of the rise in female workers (2017-18 to 2023-24) – subsistence farming, unpaid family work; the **rural-urban gap is widening** (24 Aug 2026).
[35:3:4] - **U-shaped hypothesis:** female LFPR falls with early income growth and rises later with education and service jobs.
[35:3:5] - **Feminisation of agriculture:** basic reason = **rural-to-urban migration of men**.
[35:3:6] - **Barriers:** social norms, unpaid care work, unsafe transport (not the expansion of service jobs).
[35:3:7] - PLFS 2025: LFPR about **59%**, WPR about **57%**, UR about **3%**.
[35:3:8] - **AP (PLFS 2023-24):** female LFPR all ages **35.8%** (India **31.7%**), 15+ **44.8%** (India 41.7%); overall LFPR 47.5% (rural 50.1, urban 41.3).
[35:3:9] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.287-288; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 04 p.84; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.20 p.61-62; app notes 3:35 sub 5, 8
## SUB 4 | Quarterly Employment Survey and Organised-Sector Jobs
[35:4:0] - **QES** by the **Labour Bureau**: establishments with **10+ workers** in **9 sectors** – manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, accommodation and restaurants, IT/BPO, education, health, financial services (not agriculture).
[35:4:1] - **Manufacturing** is the largest QES employer (38.5%, Jan-Mar 2022), then **education** (21.7%).
[35:4:2] - **28th QES (2015, eight sectors):** only **1.35 lakh** jobs added; **IT/BPO led with about 76,000**, then textiles including apparel (72,000) and metals (37,000). Textiles led only the Oct-Dec 2015 quarter.
[35:4:3] - **Organised-sector employment growth declined between 1994 and 2007** (Economic Survey 2009-10); reforms reduced formal-sector employment (NCERT).
[35:4:4] ~~ Sources: millenniumpost.in ("2015 job growth falls to 7-year low: Labour survey", Apr 2016); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. ch.20 p.61; OnlyIAS NCERT Economy 05 p.3; app notes 3:35 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Gig Economy, Labour Codes and e-Shram
[35:5:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [35:5:0.0] Gig economy | Engagement of independent contractors / freelancers instead of permanent workers
  [35:5:0.1] NITI Aayog "India's Booming Gig and Platform Economy" (June 2022) | 77 lakh gig workers (2020-21)
  [35:5:0.2] Projection | 2.35 crore by 2029-30 (about 6.7% of workforce)
  [35:5:0.3] Code on Social Security, 2020 | Defines gig and platform workers; aggregators pay 1-2% of annual turnover to a fund
  [35:5:0.4] Online Labour Index (Oxford Internet Institute) | India is the largest supplier of online freelance labour, mainly software and tech work
[35:5:1] - FY25: gig workforce grew 55% to about **120 lakh**; **PLFS does not yet capture gig workers** separately; most are outside e-Shram.
[35:5:2] - **4 Labour Codes** consolidate **29 central labour laws**, in force from **21 Nov 2025**: Code on Wages 2019, Code on Social Security 2020, Industrial Relations Code 2020, OSH and Working Conditions Code 2020.
[35:5:3] - **e-Shram** portal (**26 Aug 2021**): national database of **unorganised workers**; each gets a **12-digit Universal Account Number**; about **31.89 crore** registrations (Aug 2026).
[35:5:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.72; app notes 3:35 sub 6-7

=== NOTES 3:36 | Employment Generation Schemes - Mgnrega, Pmegp, Ddu-gky, Pm-svanidhi, Atmanirbhar Packages
## SUB 0 | Wage and Self-employment Programmes – Lineage and Chronology
[36:0:0] TABLE head: Wage employment | Self-employment
  [36:0:0.0] RMP (1960), CSRE (1971), FFW (1977), NREP (1980), RLEGP (1983) | IRDP (1978 pilot / 2 Oct 1980), TRYSEM (15 Aug 1979), DWCRA (1982)
  [36:0:0.1] JRY (1989), EAS (1993), JGSY (1999), SGRY (2001), NFFWP (2004) | PMRY (1993), REGP (1995), SGSY (1 Apr 1999), NRLM (2011)
  [36:0:0.2] NREGA / MGNREGS (2006) → VB-G RAM G (1 July 2026) | PMEGP (2008, PMRY + REGP); urban: SJSRY (1997)
[36:0:1] # Launch Years
[36:0:2] TABLE head: Programme | Year | Exam fact
  [36:0:2.0] Rural Manpower Programme | 1960-61 | Earliest rural wage-employment programme
  [36:0:2.1] Crash Scheme for Rural Employment (CSRE) | April 1971 (3 years) | First of the listed wage programmes – before Food for Work
  [36:0:2.2] Food for Work | April 1977 | Janata government
  [36:0:2.3] TRYSEM | 15 Aug 1979 | Training rural youth for self-employment
  [36:0:2.4] IRDP | 1978-79 pilot; nationwide 2 Oct 1980 | Self-employment for rural BPL households
  [36:0:2.5] NREP | Oct 1980 | FFW restructured
  [36:0:2.6] RLEGP | 1983 | Rural landless; NREP + RLEGP → JRY
  [36:0:2.7] DWCRA | 1982 | Women; sub-scheme of IRDP
  [36:0:2.8] JRY | April 1989 | NREP + RLEGP merged
  [36:0:2.9] PMRY | 1993 | Educated unemployed youth; started in the reform period (after 1991)
  [36:0:2.10] EAS | 2 Oct 1993 | Backward blocks
  [36:0:2.11] REGP | 1995 | KVIC; later part of PMEGP
  [36:0:2.12] JGSY | 1 April 1999 | JRY restructured as Jawahar Gram Samriddhi Yojana; rural infrastructure
  [36:0:2.13] SGSY | 1 April 1999 | Single self-employment programme
  [36:0:2.14] PMGY / VAMBAY | 2000-01 / 2001 | After PMRY and REGP
  [36:0:2.15] SGRY | 25 Sept 2001 | JGSY + EAS fully merged
  [36:0:2.16] NFFWP | 14 Nov 2004 | 150 most backward districts
  [36:0:2.17] NREGA | 2005 Act / 2 Feb 2006 launch | NFFWP + SGRY subsumed
  [36:0:2.18] PMJDY | 2014 | –
[36:0:3] - **Order:** TRYSEM 1979 → RLEGP 1983 → JRY 1989 → EAS 1993; IRDP 1980 → DWCRA 1982 → JRY 1989 → EAS 1993 → SGRY 2001 → NREGA 2006; PMRY 1993 → REGP 1995 → PMGY 2000 → VAMBAY 2001; IRDP → SGSY 1999 → NRLM 2011 → DDU-GKY 2014.
[36:0:4] - **1970s motto:** rural development programmes of the 1970s aimed at **creating wage employment and income-generating assets for the rural poor**.
[36:0:5] - **JRY objectives:** employment for the rural unemployed and underemployed **and** strengthening the rural economic and social structure ("all of the above").
[36:0:6] - **JGSY** was implemented **entirely at the level of the Village Panchayat** (Gram Panchayat).
[36:0:7] - **SGRY** (2001) fully absorbed **JGSY and EAS** – not Samagra Awaas Yojana or SGSY.
[36:0:8] - **SGSY (April 1999)** merged **IRDP, TRYSEM, DWCRA, SITRA, GKY and the Million Wells Scheme (MWS)**; it organised the assisted poor into **Self Help Groups** to lift them above the poverty line; restructured as **NRLM (Aajeevika), 2011**.
[36:0:9] - **PMRY** = **self-employment, not wage employment**; implemented through **District Industries Centres (DICs)** with bank loans.
[36:0:10] - **SJSRY (1 Dec 1997)** = urban **employment-generating** scheme; subsumed **NRY, UBSP and PMIUPEP**; it did **not** include PMRY.
[36:0:11] - Not employment-related: **RMSA** (March 2009, secondary education); MGNREGA, NRLM and **STEP** (training for women) are.
[36:0:12] > APPSC asks "not a wage programme" (PMRY), "JRY restructured in 1999" (JGSY), PMRY agency (DIC), chronology codes (UPPSC 2024, BPSC 2015) and SGRY mergers (APPSC 2003).
[36:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.25 (FFW 1977, TRYSEM 15 Aug 1979, DWCRA 1982); Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.4 (FFW 1977-78, IRDP 2 Oct 1980), p.51 (JRY = NREP + RLEGP); Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. p.182 (IRDP 1978, JRY 1989, SGSY 1999, SGRY 2001, NREGP 2006); pubadmin.institute "Evolution of employment schemes" (RMP 1960-61, CSRE 1971-72, NREP, RLEGP, JRY, EAS, JGSY, SGRY, NFFWP dates); app notes 3:36 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Food for Work and NFFWP
[36:1:0] - **Food for Work Programme:** launched **April 1977** by the **Janata government** to use surplus foodgrain stocks; wages paid in **food grains** (in part or full, the rest in cash); renamed **NREP in October 1980**.
[36:1:1] - **First wage programme among exam options:** the **Crash (printed "Cash") Scheme for Rural Employment, 1971** – earlier than Food for Work (1977), NREP (1980) and JRY (1989).
[36:1:2] - **National Food for Work Programme (NFFWP):** **14 November 2004**, by the UPA government, in the **150 most backward districts**, during the **Tenth Plan (2002-07)**; an interim step before NREGA.
[36:1:3] - **NFFWP + SGRY** were subsumed into NREGA in its districts from **2006**.
[36:1:4] - The Planning Commission was **not** a constitutional body (it was set up by a cabinet resolution).
[36:1:5] > APPSC 2004: 150 districts; Group-II 2017: 1977; CDS 2008: FFW in the Tenth Plan.
[36:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.25; Rocket Sheets Indian Economy p.4; pubadmin.institute "Evolution of employment schemes"; app notes 3:36 sub 1
## SUB 2 | MGNREGA 2005 – Enactment, Phases and Name
[36:2:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [36:2:0.0] Idea | First proposed in 1991 by P.V. Narasimha Rao; promised in the UPA's National Common Minimum Programme (2004) – 100 days of work a year
  [36:2:0.1] Passed | Parliament 23 Aug 2005
  [36:2:0.2] Assent | 5 Sept 2005 (Act No. 42 of 2005)
  [36:2:0.3] Notified / enacted | 7 Sept 2005
  [36:2:0.4] Launch | 2 Feb 2006 in 200 backward districts
  [36:2:0.5] Phase 2 | 130 more districts in 2007-08
  [36:2:0.6] Whole country | 1 April 2008 (all 625 districts)
  [36:2:0.7] Renaming | "Mahatma Gandhi" added 2 Oct 2009 (MGNREGA)
  [36:2:0.8] Repealed | Replaced by the VB-G RAM G Act from 1 July 2026
[36:2:1] - **Enacted 2005, scheme launched 2006**: "MGNREGA launched" = **2006**; "Act enacted / passed" = **2005**.
[36:2:2] - The 100-day programme for rural folk = **REGA / NREGA**, not DRDA, SGSY or IAY.
[36:2:3] - **Largest rural employment programme** in India; landmark of the **Manmohan Singh** government with **RTI 2005** and **NFSA 2013** (NEP 2020 is not).
[36:2:4] > 7 Sept 2005 is the date asked as "enacted"; 7 Nov 2005 is a distractor. 625 = 2008 coverage, not the 2006 launch.
[36:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.57; NREGA 2005 Act text (prsindia.org PDF, "5th September, 2005"); MoRD NREGA Operational Guidelines 2008 ("notified on September 7, 2005", via web search); app notes 3:36 sub 2
## SUB 3 | MGNREGA – Entitlement, Eligibility and Objectives
[36:3:0] - **Objective:** "**enhancing livelihood security** in rural areas by providing **at least 100 days of guaranteed wage employment in a financial year** to every **household** whose **adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work**".
[36:3:1] - **Unit = household**, not each adult: "100 days to every adult" is wrong; **150 days** is wrong for the normal guarantee.
[36:3:2] - **Eligible:** adult members of **any rural household** – not only SC/ST, BPL or backward communities.
[36:3:3] - **Unskilled** manual work only – "100 days of **skilled** labour" is not an objective.
[36:3:4] - Other aims: **durable assets** (roads, canals, ponds, wells), rural income, **women's empowerment**, inclusive growth.
[36:3:5] - Work within **5 km**; minimum wages; **legal entitlement** (statutory right, **not a Fundamental Right**); anchored in **Article 41** (DPSP).
[36:3:6] - The Act covers **all rural areas of the country** in notified phases – **not "only selected States"**.
[36:3:7] - **Drought-hit areas:** an extra **50 days** – **150 days** in a year in areas declared drought-affected (as in Feb 2019).
[36:3:8] - **Features of MGNREGS:** guaranteed wage employment, **rights-based**, rural wage employment; **nutritious food is not** a feature.
[36:3:9] - **SDG link:** NITI Aayog's **SDG India Index 2023-24** tracks MGNREGA under **SDG 1 (No Poverty)** – 99.7% of those who demanded work were offered it; Goal 1 score **72**.
[36:3:10] - **World Development Report 2014** (World Bank): "**stellar example of rural development**"; safety net in agrarian distress and **COVID-19**.
[36:3:11] > UPSC 2011 (any household), APPSC Group-II 2017 (household, 100 days), CDS 2020 (skilled labour is not an objective), APPSC Group-I 2023 (nutritious food is not a feature).
[36:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.57; NREGA 2005 Act text (prsindia.org PDF); drishtiias.com SDG India Index 2023-24 (via web search); app notes 3:36 sub 2-3
[36:3:13] - **Olga Tellis (1985)** linked livelihood with **Article 21**; MGNREGA gives the right to work statutory force.
[36:3:14] - **Nodal ministry:** MGNREGA (and VB-G RAM G) = **Ministry of Rural Development**.
[36:3:15] - **Women priority:** at least **one-third** of those given work must be women (Schedule II), not one-half.
## SUB 4 | MGNREGA – Funds, Works, Monitoring and Social Audit
[36:4:0] - **Women:** at least **one-third** of beneficiaries (Schedule II) – not one-half; actual share **about 56% of person-days (2016-17)**.
[36:4:1] - **Work within 15 days** of application, else **unemployment allowance** (**1/4 of wage for the first 30 days, 1/2 thereafter**); wages within **15 days** of work; unemployment allowance is a **transfer payment**.
[36:4:2] - **Funds:** Centre and State money is pooled in the **State Employment Guarantee Fund** (Section 21); the material component and the **14th Finance Commission** grants go directly to **Gram Panchayat** accounts.
[36:4:3] - **Agriculture and allied works:** about **two-thirds (≈68%)** of expenditure in **2016-17**, up from ≈48% in 2013-14.
[36:4:4] - **Permissible works:** water conservation, **percolation tanks**, **fish ponds**, **compost pits**, **cattle sheds**, land development, rural connectivity – all four in the APPSC 2017 question are permissible.
[36:4:5] - **Convergence:** MGNREGS is the textbook example – 90/95 person-days for **PMAY-G** houses, works with agriculture, horticulture and watershed schemes.
[36:4:6] - **Social audit:** **Section 17** – the **Gram Sabha** conducts regular social audits; **NREGA was the first Act** to make social audit a means of continuous public vigilance; a village social auditor must **not be a political person**.
[36:4:7] - **Monitoring:** **GeoMGNREGA** geo-tags assets on ISRO's **Bhuvan mobile platform**; **NREGASoft** MIS; in AP fund flow was tracked on **RAGA soft** (TCS).
[36:4:8] - **Newsletter** of MoRD for MGNREGA in the APPSC key: **Saaransh** (key not verified).
[36:4:9] - **CAPART** and **NIRDPR (Hyderabad)**: autonomous bodies under the Ministry of Rural Development.
[36:4:10] > 15 days twice: allowance if no work within 15 days of application; wages within 15 days of work.
[36:4:11] ~~ Sources: NREGA 2005 Act text (prsindia.org PDF: s.17, s.21, Schedule II one-third women, fifteen days); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 01 p.57; indianemployees.com and Hindustan Times (April 2017) on 68% agri spend (via web search); app notes 3:36 sub 4
[36:4:12] - **Wage payment:** by **DBT** into Aadhaar-linked bank / post-office accounts.
## SUB 5 | VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 – Replacing MGNREGA
[36:5:0] - **Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025**: passed in **December 2025** (18 Dec); in force from **1 July 2026**; nodal **Ministry of Rural Development**.
[36:5:1] TABLE head: Aspect | MGNREGA 2005 | VB-G RAM G 2025
  [36:5:1.0] Guarantee | 100 days/household | 125 days/household, operated over 305 days
  [36:5:1.1] Seasonal pause | None | States may pause up to 60 days (sowing / harvest)

## SUB 0 | IRDP and the Direct-Attack Programmes (1977-1999)
[37:0:0] # Programme → full form, year, aim
[37:0:1] TABLE head: Programme | Full form / aim | Start
  [37:0:1.0] Food for Work (FFW) | Foodgrains as wages for rural works; renamed / restructured as NREP in 1980; revived as NFFWP (14 Nov 2004), merged into NREGA | 1977-78
  [37:0:1.1] IRDP | Integrated Rural Development Programme: subsidy + bank credit (income-generating assets) so that poor rural families come above the poverty line; self-employment; individual family approach | Started in a small way 1978-79 (experimental); all blocks 2 Oct 1980 (6th Plan, 1980-85)
  [37:0:1.2] TRYSEM | Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment; supporting arm of IRDP; a rural development programme | 15 Aug 1979
  [37:0:1.3] NREP | National Rural Employment Programme; wage employment; successor of FFW | Oct 1980 (6th Plan)
  [37:0:1.4] RLEGP | Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme | 1983 (6th Plan)
  [37:0:1.5] DWCRA | Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas; sub-scheme of IRDP for women's groups; "thrift and credit society" in the group; income activities, not natural-resource SHGs | 1982-83 (50 districts)
  [37:0:1.6] JRY | Jawahar Rozgar Yojana = merger of NREP + RLEGP; labour-oriented additional (wage) employment | April 1989 (7th Plan) – not April 1995
  [37:0:1.7] SITRA | Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans – sub-scheme of IRDP | 1992
  [37:0:1.8] Ganga Kalyan Yojana | Bore-well / tube-well irrigation for small and marginal farmers | 1997
  [37:0:1.9] PMRY / REGP | Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (self-employment) / Rural Employment Generation Programme | 1993 / 1995
[37:0:2] - **IRDP main aim:** assistance to **poor rural families to come above the poverty line** on a lasting basis (assets + credit); the **Seventh Plan** strategy = **total household approach**.
[37:0:3] - **IRDP, TRYSEM and NREP** = all for eradication of rural poverty; **NREP and RLEGP** both in the **6th Plan**; IRDP is the programme of the **Sixth Plan** (1980).
[37:0:4] - **"Direct attack on poverty"** = IRDP, NREP, RLEGP, JRY (target-group approach); **Family Planning** is a population measure, NOT direct attack.
[37:0:5] - **Odd-one-out (not anti-poverty):** **MRTP** (1969 Act on monopolies), **NSSF** (2011, ₹1,000 crore social-security fund for unorganised workers), **CRY** (an NGO); MGNREGA, NRLM, SJSRY, TRYSEM, JRY, IRDP are anti-poverty.
[37:0:6] - **Five categories of poverty-alleviation programmes:** self-employment, wage employment, food security, social security, urban poverty alleviation.
[37:0:7] - **Assertion-reason (Sachivalayam):** change in beneficiaries' socio-economic status is due to PAPs (A) and income/employment were created (R) – both true; official key: R not the correct explanation.
[37:0:8] TABLE head: Chronology | Order
  [37:0:8.0] IRDP, RLEGP, PMRY, REGP | IRDP (1978-80) → RLEGP (1983) → PMRY (1993) → REGP (1995)
  [37:0:8.1] IRDP, NREP, DWCRA, JRY | IRDP → NREP (1980) → DWCRA (1982-83) → JRY (1989)
  [37:0:8.2] Long chain | IRDP (1980) → SGSY (1999) → NRLM (2011) → DAY-NRLM (2016)
[37:0:9] > Year angle: "IRDP started" = **1978-79** when 1978-79 is offered; **1980** (nationwide, 2 Oct) when only single years are offered. Avoid "IRDP pilot 1976".

## SUB 2 | Restructuring Chain – SGSY to DAY-NRLM
[37:2:0] TABLE head: Old | New | Year
  [37:2:0.0] IRDP + TRYSEM + DWCRA + SITRA + GKY + Million Wells Scheme (6) | SGSY (Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana) – replaced IRDP | 1 April 1999
  [37:2:0.1] SGSY | NRLM "Aajeevika" | Restructured 2010; launched June 2011; fully replaced SGSY 1 April 2013
  [37:2:0.2] NRLM | DAY-NRLM (Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – NRLM) | 29 March 2016
  [37:2:0.3] SJSRY (1997) | NULM → DAY-NULM | 2013
  [37:2:0.4] PMRY | PMEGP | 2008
[37:2:1] - **SGSY = restructured IRDP and TRYSEM** (with four allied schemes); **group financing** – organising the rural poor into **SHGs**; emphasis on skills of the self-employed; bring assisted BPL families above the poverty line.
[37:2:2] - **IRDP = individual family approach → SGSY = SHG/group approach.**
[37:2:3] - **JRY is not part of SGSY.** SGSY → NRLM = rural chain; SJSRY → NULM = urban chain.
[37:2:4] - "Aajeevika" was NRLM's brand name; there is no "Deendayal Aajeevika Yojana".
[37:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 04 p.25 (TRYSEM merged with SGSY 1 April 1999); app notes 3:37 sub 3
## SUB 3 | DAY-NRLM – Design, Panchasutra and Scale
[37:3:0] - **Ministry of Rural Development**; Centrally Sponsored; funding (Aug 2026): general **60:40**; NE incl. Sikkim **90:10**; UTs **100%**.
[37:3:1] - **Aim:** mobilise rural poor households (one woman per household) into **Self Help Groups and their federations**; the **institutions of the poor** plan and implement interventions for economic development and social justice.
[37:3:2] - **Primary unit** of community institutional design = **Self Help Group**; tiers: **SHG → Village Organisation → Cluster-Level Federation**.
[37:3:3] - **Borrowers:** **women SHGs** (not individual farmers, SMEs or cooperatives); SHG of **10-20 members**; poor identified by **Participatory Identification of Poor (PIP)**, vetted by the **Gram Sabha**; up to **30%** members may be slightly above the poverty line.
[37:3:4] - **Panchasutra (5 conditions):** regular meetings, regular savings, regular internal lending, timely repayment, up-to-date books → SHGs practising it for **3-6 months** get the **Revolving Fund**.
[37:3:5] - **Interest subvention (May 2013):** women SHGs get loans up to **₹3 lakh at 7%**.
[37:3:6] - **Capitalisation support:** ₹5,919.71 crore to SHG women till Nov 2018 (APPSC Panchayat Secretary key; figure not traced in an official release).
[37:3:7] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [37:3:7.0] Coverage (3 Feb 2026) | ~10 crore households; 91 lakh SHGs; 5.35 lakh VOs; 33,558 CLFs
  [37:3:7.1] Lakhpati Didi (2023) | ₹1 lakh+ a year; 2 crore crossed (Feb 2026); target 6 crore by March 2029 (Aug 2026)
  [37:3:7.2] SVEP (2016) | Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme: non-farm enterprises; 4.32 lakh; women ≥60% (Jul 2026)
  [37:3:7.3] Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana | Sub-component of DAY-NRLM for women farmers (not part of NSAP)
[37:3:8] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.276-278 (FNHW and non-farm livelihoods under NRLM); app notes 3:37 sub 4; general knowledge, not checked (Panchasutra, ₹3 lakh at 7%)
## SUB 4 | SHG Concept and SHG-Bank Linkage
[37:4:0] TABLE head: Person / body | Contribution
  [37:4:0.0] Muhammad Yunus, Grameen Bank (1976) | Idea of SHGs / group lending as a tool for poverty alleviation; collateral-free loans to poor women
  [37:4:0.1] MYRADA | Pioneered bank linkage, mid-1980s (not the national programme)
  [37:4:0.2] NABARD | SHG-Bank Linkage pilot 1992 (about 500 SHGs, 1992-93); world's largest microfinance programme; refinances banks, trains and promotes SHGs
[37:4:1] - **SHG:** 10-20 members; **microfinance + thrift** for poor women; **loan decisions taken by the members** themselves; **all members are jointly responsible** for a member's loan.
[37:4:2] - SHG programme first started by **NABARD, not SBI**; **RRBs and scheduled commercial banks** finance SHGs; RBI = regulator.
[37:4:3] - **Savings-linked SHGs (NABARD):** ~**85-87 lakh** (2016-18) → **143.3 lakh** (31 March 2025).
[37:4:4] > Year trap: SHG-BLP = **1992** – not 1990, 1995 or 1999.
[37:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.38 (Grameen Bank, Muhammad Yunus); Sa-Dhan Bharat Microfinance Report 2025 ch.5 Table 5.1 (sa-dhan.net); app notes 3:37 sub 6

## SUB 6 | SHG Movement in Andhra Pradesh – SERP, Stree Nidhi, Unnathi
[37:6:0] TABLE head: Programme | Year | Note
  [37:6:0.0] DWCRA in AP | 1982-83 | With UNICEF; rural BPL women's self-employment
  [37:6:0.1] SAPAP | 1995 | UNDP; Mahabubnagar, Kurnool, Anantapur
  [37:6:0.2] Janmabhoomi | 1997 | AP rural development programme
  [37:6:0.3] SERP | 2000 | Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty; also called Velugu
  [37:6:0.4] Velugu | 2000 | World Bank District Poverty Initiatives Project; federated SHGs into VOs, Mandal Samakhyas
  [37:6:0.5] IKP | 2004-05 | Velugu + DWCRA merged; by SERP
  [37:6:0.6] Pavala Vaddi | 2004 | Interest subsidy for SHGs
[37:6:1] - **Unnathi (PoP):** SERP programme to bring the **poorest of the poor** (SC/ST sub-plan funds) out of poverty; implemented by **Velugu (SERP)**.
[37:6:2] - **SARAS** (Sales of Articles of Rural Artisans Society) – listed among SERP's NRLM non-farm initiatives.
[37:6:3] - **Stree Nidhi** (Credit Cooperative Federation, 2011): livelihood loans to SHG women, rural and urban, through VOs/MS; loan credited **within 48 hours**; about half its credit earmarked for the **poorest of the poor** (APPSC key 50%); loans up to ₹1 lakh at 11%.
[37:6:4] - **Abhaya Hastham** (Velugu Pension and Insurance): for **all women enrolled in SHGs**; member contributes **₹365 a year** (₹1 a day), Government matches.
[37:6:5] - **Pasupu Kumkuma** (2019): one-time assistance to **SHG members**. **Vaddi Leni Runalu**: interest-free loans rewarding prompt repayment.
[37:6:6] - **SERP study of SC SHG CBOs:** about **40-60% of SHGs defunct** (APPSC key).
[37:6:7] - **SHG-Bank Linkage:** AP **1st**, 36% national share, **99.66% recovery**; ~₹32,190 crore rural disbursement (2024-25).
[37:6:8] - AP's SERP/Velugu = template for NRLM; rural = SERP, urban = MEPMA. Challenges: uneven quality, weak market links, debt stress, political interference.
[37:6:9] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.275-278 (SERP, SHG-BLP 36%/99.66%, Unnathi, SARAS, Streenidhi); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 - APPSC 02 p.38 (DWCRA in AP); Stree Nidhi 48-hour credit (web search: Hans India, Stree Nidhi presentation); app notes 3:37 sub 7

=== NOTES 3:38 | Social Security and Dbt – Pm-jdy, Jam Trinity, Aadhaar-enabled Transfers, Pension Schemes
## SUB 0 | Insurance Schemes – PMSBY, PMJJBY, AABY, RSBY and Others
[38:0:0] # PMJJBY vs PMSBY (Jan Suraksha schemes, 9 May 2015, DFS)
[38:0:1] TABLE head: Feature | PMJJBY | PMSBY
  [38:0:1.0] Type | Life – one-year renewable term insurance (death from any cause); NOT health insurance | Accidental death and disability (personal accident cover)
  [38:0:1.1] Age | 18-50 (cover continues to 55) | 18-70 (not 18-50)
  [38:0:1.2] Premium | ₹330 → ₹436/yr (1 June 2022) | ₹12/yr (flat per member) → ₹20/yr from 1 June 2022
  [38:0:1.3] Cover | ₹2 lakh | ₹2 lakh death/total disability; ₹1 lakh partial
  [38:0:1.4] Enrolments | 27.33 crore | 57.92 crore
[38:0:2] - **Jan Suraksha schemes** = **PMSBY, PMJJBY** (+ APY); Sovereign Gold Bond and Kisan Vikas Patra are savings instruments, not Jan Suraksha.
[38:0:3] - PMSBY has **no suicide cover**; 34.18 crore enrolled by Apr 2023.
[38:0:4] # Other social insurance
[38:0:5] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [38:0:5.0] Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana | Launched 2 Oct 2007; LIC; life and disability cover for rural landless households below the poverty line (head or one earning member)
  [38:0:5.1] RSBY | Health insurance for unorganised-sector (BPL) workers; launched by the Ministry of Labour (not Health); enrolment from 1 Apr 2008; now in Ayushman Bharat – PMJAY
  [38:0:5.2] Rajiv Gandhi Shilpi Swasthya Bima Yojana | Health insurance for handicraft artisans – Ministry of Textiles
  [38:0:5.3] Weavers' Health Insurance Scheme (2005-06) | Family of four (self, spouse, two children); at least 50% income from handloom; men and women; no age cap (so "covers up to 60 years" is NOT a criterion); life cover: Mahatma Gandhi Bunkar Bima Yojana
  [38:0:5.4] Krishi Shramik Samajik Suraksha Yojana (1 July 2001) | Pension + insurance for agricultural workers
  [38:0:5.5] Ashraya Bima Yojana (2001) | Social security to workers who lose their jobs; up to 30% of salary for a year
[38:0:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 18 p.5-6 (PMSBY, PMJJBY, APY); PMSBY Rules (sbi.bank.in, "Premium: Rs.12/- per annum per member"); app notes 3:38 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Pension Schemes – APY, NPS, PM-SYM, PM-KMY, PMVVY
[38:1:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Target / entry age | Contribution | Benefit
  [38:1:0.0] Atal Pension Yojana (9 May 2015) | Unorganised workers 18-40 (citizens with a savings bank / post-office account); not taxpayers (from Oct 2022) | Age-linked; Govt co-contribution 50% or ₹1,000/yr for 5 yrs (joined before 31 Dec 2015) – NOT 100% | Guaranteed (defined-benefit) ₹1,000-5,000/month at 60; same pension to spouse for life; any member of a family may join
  [38:1:0.1] PM-SYM (2019) | Unorganised workers 18-40 (not 21-40), income ≤ ₹15,000/month; not in NPS/ESIC/EPFO | Voluntary, age-specific contribution ₹55-200; Centre matches | ₹3,000/month at 60; family pension (50%) to spouse only
  [38:1:0.2] PM Kisan Maan-dhan (12 Sep 2019, Ranchi) | Small and marginal farmers 18-40 | ₹55-200/month; Centre matches | ₹3,000/month at 60
  [38:1:0.3] NPS | Citizens (resident/NRI) and OCI 18-70; minors via NPS Vatsalya; compulsory for Central Govt civilian employees joining on/after 1 Jan 2004 (not Armed Forces); State Govt employees from the date of each State's notification | Voluntary, defined contribution, market-linked | Corpus + annuity
  [38:1:0.4] PM Vaya Vandana Yojana (LIC, 2017) | Senior citizens 60+ | Lump-sum purchase | Assured pension for 10 years – social security in old age, protects the elderly against a future fall in interest rates
  [38:1:0.5] Unified Pension Scheme (2025) | Central Govt employees under NPS | Govt-backed | 50% of average basic pay of last 12 months for 25 years' service

[38:1:2] - NPS: an account **cannot be opened or operated for a third person**.

## SUB 2 | DBT, PAHAL and Ujjwala
[38:2:0] - **DBT** piloted **1 Jan 2013** (7 schemes, 20 districts); scaled up in 2015 with JAM; FY 2024-25: **₹6.9 lakh crore, 327 schemes**; the **DBT Mission** sits in the **Cabinet Secretariat**.
[38:2:1] - **State DBT nodal officer / coordinator:** a **Principal Secretary (Planning/IT/Finance)** or equivalent officer.
[38:2:2] - **MGNREGS:** largest number of DBT transactions in 2018-19 (about 43 crore by Feb 2019); **PAHAL** = largest cash-transfer scheme by beneficiaries.
[38:2:3] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [38:2:3.0] PAHAL (Pratyaksha Hastaantarit Laabh) | DBT of LPG subsidy into the consumer's bank account; 54 districts 15 Nov 2014, national 1 Jan 2015; first JAM application; Guinness record (2015): world's largest cash-transfer programme; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
  [38:2:3.1] PM Ujjwala Yojana | Free LPG connection to women of BPL households – clean cooking fuel to safeguard the health of women and children; 1 May 2016, Ballia (UP); "Swachh Indhan Behtar Jeevan"; ₹8,000 crore for 3 years; 5 crore connections; support ₹1,600 per connection (not ₹2,800); target later raised to 8 crore
[38:2:4] - Schemes vs inequality: PMJDY, MGNREGA, Stand-Up India reduce inequality; **UDAN** (regional air connectivity) does not.
[38:2:5] ~~ Sources: Business Standard/IANS 10 May 2019 (top DBT schemes, MGNREGA 43.24 crore transactions; web search); app notes 3:38 sub 2
## SUB 3 | PM Jan Dhan Yojana, JAM and Aadhaar
[38:3:0] - **PMJDY:** launched **28 Aug 2014**; **Department of Financial Services**; financial inclusion; **zero-balance** account, **RuPay** card; **Guinness World Record** – most bank accounts opened in one week (18 million, 23-29 Aug 2014).
[38:3:1] TABLE head: Feature | Old | Now
  [38:3:1.0] RuPay accident cover | ₹1 lakh | ₹2 lakh
  [38:3:1.1] Overdraft | ₹5,000 | ₹10,000
  [38:3:1.2] Focus (after 14 Aug 2018) | Every household | Every unbanked adult
[38:3:2] - **Phase II (2015-18):** overdraft; Credit Guarantee Fund; unorganised-sector pensions (**Swavalamban**). Accounts (19 Aug 2026): **59.09 crore**; women 32.92 crore; rural 45.95 crore.
[38:3:3] TABLE head: JAM component | Role
  [38:3:3.0] Jan Dhan | Bank account – destination of funds
  [38:3:3.1] Aadhaar | Biometric identity – verifies beneficiary
  [38:3:3.2] Mobile | Communication channel

[38:3:5] TABLE head: India Stack layer | Enabler
  [38:3:5.0] Presence-less | Aadhaar authentication
  [38:3:5.1] Paperless | e-KYC, e-Sign, DigiLocker
  [38:3:5.2] Cashless | UPI, AePS
  [38:3:5.3] Consent | DEPA; Account Aggregator – consent-based data sharing (not ATM cash)
[38:3:6] - **APBS** = DBT routing to Aadhaar-seeded accounts; **AePS** = cash withdrawal at micro-ATMs.
[38:3:7] - **Jeevan Pramaan** (2014): pensioners create a **digital life certificate** (Aadhaar biometrics) for the Pension Disbursing Agency.
[38:3:8] - **Aadhaar Act, 2016, Sec 7:** Aadhaar may be required for subsidies from the Consolidated Fund of India.
[38:3:9] TABLE head: Case | Year | Bench | Ruling
  [38:3:9.0] K.S. Puttaswamy I | 2017 | 9 judges | Privacy a fundamental right under Art. 21
  [38:3:9.1] K.S. Puttaswamy II | 2018 | 5 judges, 4:1 | Sec 7 upheld; Sec 57 (private use) struck down

## SUB 4 | NSAP and Social Security Concepts
[38:4:0] - **NSAP:** from **15 Aug 1995**; **Ministry of Rural Development**; Core of the Core CSS; fulfils **Article 41**; BPL households; chief aim = **old-age pension to the very poor**.
[38:4:1] TABLE head: Component | Who | Benefit
  [38:4:1.0] IGNOAPS | 60-79 / 80+ | ₹200 / ₹500 a month
  [38:4:1.1] IGNWPS | BPL widows | Monthly pension
  [38:4:1.2] IGNDPS | BPL, 18-79, 80%+ disability | ₹300 a month
  [38:4:1.3] NFBS | Family losing breadwinner | Lump sum
  [38:4:1.4] Annapurna | Needy elderly not on IGNOAPS | 10 kg free foodgrains/month
[38:4:2] - **NOT in NSAP / not social security:** **Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana** (DAY-NRLM), **Skill Development Programme**, **SJSRY** (employment generation).
[38:4:3] - ~3.09 crore beneficiaries (FY 2025-26); May 2026: old-age pension lost nearly **half its real value** to inflation.
[38:4:4] - **Universal Basic Income** = an unconditional **minimum income support by the Government to every citizen** (Economic Survey 2016-17).
[38:4:5] - **ILO** = the UN body for social security; about **80% of the world's population** lacked adequate **social security** (ILO).
[38:4:6] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 06 p.87 (UBI); app notes 3:38 sub 6; general knowledge, not checked (ILO 80%)

## SUB 6 | AP Social Security – NTR Bharosa, Chandranna Bima
[38:6:0] - **NTR Bharosa (2014):** a **livelihood pension scheme for the old and disabled** (secure and dignified life for the poor); ₹1,000 a month, **₹1,500 for persons with 80%+ disability** (2014-19).
[38:6:1] - **YSR Pension Kanuka** (2019): doorstep delivery through Village/Ward Secretariat staff.
[38:6:2] - **NTR Bharosa Pension** again (June 2024): old age, widows etc. **₹4,000**; disabled **₹6,000**; fully disabled **₹15,000**; chronic diseases ₹10,000 (from 1 July 2024); first distribution **65.31 lakh** beneficiaries, 28 categories.
